title: Ring announces its first smart lock, solving a major pain point for smart home users
snippet: Today, Amazon’s Ring subsidiary is announcing its first ever smart lock. It solves a key problem that looms over many smart lock owners: dead batteries. Ring has a clever solution to negate that problem, and it’ll be available in Q1 2027. Additionally, the company is announcing a few new security cameras with improved low-light performance. more…
fullText:
Today, Amazon’s Ring subsidiary is announcing its first ever smart lock. It solves a key problem that looms over many smart lock owners: dead batteries. Ring has a clever solution to negate that problem, and it’ll be available in Q1 2027. Additionally, the company is announcing a few new security cameras with improved low-light performance.

Ring Smart Lock

The idea of a smart lock is far from new, but Ring wants to solve the dead battery problem of smart locks. To prevent you from accidentally being locked out of your home at an inopportune time, the Ring Smart Lock lets you crank the thumbturn a few times to produce the energy needed to power the lock for a few moments. Then, you can let yourself back in.

The Ring Smart Lock supports everything you’d expect out of a smart lock. You can use your fingerprint to unlock it, a touchscreen keypad, or your phone with the Ring app.

There’s a few features the Ring app enables as well, including checking and locking the door remotely, or creating scheduled or time-limited unlocks for family members or other visitors. It also integrates with Amazon Echo and other Ring doorbells and cameras you may own.

It comes in three finishes: black, silver, and brass – and requires no additional wiring. It’ll be available early next year for $249. You can learn more about it here.

New 4K cameras

	

Beyond its first ever smart lock, Ring also has some new 4K cameras that support the new Retinal Vision 4K standard. This means you’ll have great low-light performance with accurate colors. All of these are available to preorder or purchase starting today:

Outdoor Cam 4K Plus: 140° wide-angle view, multiple power options including battery, plug-in, hardwired, and power-over-ethernet – $149.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Floodlight Cam 4K Plus: Powerful floodlight, 24/7 recording and smart detection with a hardwired connection – $219.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Spotlight Cam 4K Plus: 550-lumen spotlight, 140° wide-angle view, comes with battery, plug-in, and solar configs – $199.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Indoor Cam 4K: First ever 4K indoor video camera from Ring, dual-band Wi-Fi 6, 115° field of view – $99.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Ring also has a new Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K for $69.99, which brings its 360° pan coverage to a lower price point. It can follow motion, and also has a privacy shutter. You can learn more about it here.

title: Nous Research confirms it hit $1.5B valuation, launches AI agents for business users
snippet: The developer of Hermes Agent raised a $90 million Series B.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

1:48 PM PDT · October 7, 2026

Image Credits:Nous Research

		

							

											
									

					

	

Nous Research, the startup developing the open source Hermes Agent, has raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation, confirming TechCrunch’s earlier reporting.

The round was led by Robot Ventures, with participation from other backers including Nvidia, Union Square Ventures, Menlo Ventures, Samsung, and 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The new financing brings the three-year-old startup’s total funding to $158 million.

Popular among developers and individuals, the open source Hermes Agent has been cloned more than 24 million times, driving roughly 2.5% of global AI token usage, according to the startup’s estimates.

The capital will fund Nous Research’s push into the enterprise sector with “Hermes for Businesses,” allowing companies to deploy customized AI agents that can handle multi-step workflows while keeping their data private and secure.

Nous was at roughly $36 million in annualized revenue by mid-September 2026 and expects to pass $100 million before the end of 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported.

title: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11
snippet: Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its Surface Laptop Ultra, AI PCs that run on Nvidia chips that are designed to run AI models and agents.
fullText:
Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.

On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra. The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)

Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.

The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.

Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.

Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.”

He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.”

The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.

Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.

Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy, priced at $3,800.

title: Uber and China’s Pony.ai plan to launch robotaxis in London
snippet: The two companies said on Thursday that they would begin testing Pony.ai's Gen-7 robotaxis in London in the coming weeks.
fullText:
Uber and Chinese autonomous vehicle maker Pony.ai plan to launch a robotaxi service in London as part of an expanded partnership to bring driverless cars to Europe. The two companies said on Thursday that they would begin testing Pony.ai’s Gen-7 robotaxis in London in the coming weeks.

The announcement is the latest instance of Uber’s ambitious push into autonomous vehicle technology through a growing web of partnerships and investments. The ride-hailing company has struck deals with more than 30 autonomous vehicle companies, including Pony.ai, over the past few years as it seeks to capture a share of the autonomous delivery and ride-hailing markets.

Uber expects to offer AV trips in as many as 15 cities globally by the end of 2026, roughly split between U.S. and international markets.

Uber and Pony.ai first partnered in May 2025, initially focusing on the Middle East. The relationship has since expanded to Europe, where it plans to deploy 2,000 robotaxis, starting with Croatia’s capital, Zagreb.

In August 2026, the companies launched an autonomous ride-hailing service in Zagreb with a third partner, Verne. Under that arrangement, Pony.ai supplies the autonomous driving system and the Arcfox Alpha T5 robotaxi, developed with Chinese automaker BAIC. Verne, a startup set up by Rimac Group founder and CEO Mate Rimac, owns and operates the fleet, while Uber provides access to its vast ride-hailing network.

The London service will follow a similar model, although the companies have not said who will own and operate the fleet.

Pony.ai won’t be Uber’s only robotaxi partner in London. The company has also partnered with and invested in British self-driving startup Wayve, and plans to launch a robotaxi service in the city.

In February 2026, Wayve raised $1.2 billion in a funding round that saw investments from Microsoft, Nvidia, and Uber. The total funding in that round could reach $1.5 billion thanks to an additional $300 million from Uber, contingent on Wayve deploying robotaxis, starting in London.

Uber has pursued this multi-partner strategy elsewhere. In Dubai, for instance, it has struck separate deals with Baidu and WeRide to launch robotaxi services.

Pony.ai, meanwhile, has launched robotaxi services in four Chinese cities and secured partnerships with local transportation authorities as it works to expand into European and Middle Eastern markets, including Qatar.

title: China’s Manus raises over $500M in first funding round since split with Meta
snippet: Boyu Capital and IDG Capital led the funding round, and existing shareholders Tencent, HSG (formerly known as Sequoia China), ZhenFund, and others also participated.
fullText:
Chinese AI lab Manus’ parent company, Butterfly Effect, said on Thursday in a WeChat post that it has raised more than $500 million, the company’s first funding round since Meta was forced to call off its $2 billion acquisition of the startup.

Boyu Capital and IDG Capital led the funding round, and existing shareholders Tencent, HSG (formerly known as Sequoia China), ZhenFund, and others also participated. The AI company said it will continue hiring both at home and abroad.

Manus did not disclose its valuation, but last month was said to be in talks with investors to raise $500 million at a $4 billion valuation.

Manus, which went viral following a demo of its AI agent last year, relocated its staff to Singapore in mid-2025 before announcing a $2 billion acquisition deal with Meta that December. The startup was said to be pulling in annual recurring revenue of over $100 million at the time.

In April, Chinese authorities ordered the AI startup to unwind the deal amid intensifying worries in China over losing AI talent and researchers to the West. 

Manus in August resumed independent operations following the end of the Meta deal, and said it was required to delete some user data as part of the split. The company is also reported to be considering going public in Hong Kong, according to the report.

Manus did not respond to TechCrunch’s questions about its valuation.

Manus makes AI products and agents similar to what companies like Cursor, Lovable, and Replit offer. It offers a chatbot and vibe-coding tools to let users build apps and websites, create designs and presentations, generate video, and more.

The company recently launched Manus 2.0, which it says brings a new architecture with new products and capabilities built around a new harness. It also introduced Cue, a stand-alone app that gives personal AI agents their own email addresses, phone numbers, digital wallets, and computers. The app lets agents communicate, handle tasks across services, and make payments within limits set by the user.

title: Vesta raises $30M to bring swarms of agents to mortgage lenders
snippet: Vesta, an AI-native software startup that helps lenders originate mortgages, announced a $30 million round led by Conversion Capital.
fullText:
Vesta, an AI-native software startup that helps lenders originate mortgages, announced on Thursday that it raised a $30 million round led by Conversion Capital.

The startup uses AI agents to automate much of the loan origination process, which, the founders say, helps lenders reduce the time and costs of processing mortgages. Three of the company’s customers, including Pennymac and New American Funding, also invested in the round alongside Citi Ventures and Andreessen Horowitz. 

Mike Yu co-founded the company in 2020 with Devon Yang. Yu, the company’s CEO, told TechCrunch that now was the perfect time to raise because demand for the product has “exploded in the last year.” He said revenue is up 12x year over year. The company has raised $85 million in funding to date.

“While the traction is great, we are still under 5% market share and now is the time to staff up, take the market, and invest in new product lines,” Yu said. 

Those new product lines include a personal assistant for mortgage issuers that can help perform tasks and track workflows. It takes around 40 days to close a mortgage in the U.S., costing around $11,000 per loan. “Most of that cost is human labor, and a major bottleneck in the timeline is just waiting for a person to get to reviewing your loan.” 

With Vesta, the idea is to allow humans to deploy a swarm of agents to speed completion of tasks. Customers decide what tasks they want to assign the Vesta agents: “Many of our customers start an AI agent with a person approving its work, then let it handle a share of loans on its own, then expand,” Yu explained, adding that some lenders are even using Vesta AI agents to make mortgage underwriting decisions. 

Companies remain responsible for underwriting decisions, he said, regardless of what software or AI agents they use, and Yu added that all actions and reasoning behind a decision are recorded for compliance and to audit AI decisions. 

This level of autonomy stems from the vast improvements in AI models in the past year, which weren’t good enough, at that time, to build agents for the complex multi-stage tasks involved in mortgage lending. Before, the company was just focused on building the right data architecture to use the most advanced tools to automate the mortgage process. 

“For us, the big breakthrough was [Claude] Sonnet 4.5, which we just found to be much better at adhering to user-configured instructions over the time horizons we need than previous generations,” Yu said. 

Vesta is, in many ways, competing against both traditional mortgage systems like ICE Mortgage Technology and other AI-native companies also trying to automate the mortgage lending process, like Xpanse. 

At least against legacy incumbents, Yu said Vesta’s advantage is that those companies weren’t built for AI agents, and “putting AI agents on top of them is very hard,” he said. As for what’s next, “our priority is earning the business of the rest of the mortgage industry,” Yu said. “Then, we’ll go wherever our customers take us.”

title: Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think
snippet: Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access. more…
fullText:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.

According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.

Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”

There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra. Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.

	

	

Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra

In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”

This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.  

At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.

It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

title: Cal AI’s 19-year-old founder just raised $10M for his new AI startup
snippet: Zach Yadegari, the teen co-founder of popular Cal AI calorie tracking app, has launched a new personal AI agent startup that competes with Instinct, Muse, and Bee.
fullText:
Zach Yadegari, the teen co-founder of calorie tracking app Cal AI, has launched Persona, a new AI agent startup, and already raised $10 million. Vine Ventures led the round, with Z Fellows founder Cory Levy and Collective Global participating.

In March, MyFitnessPal acquired Cal AI for an undisclosed sum after it zoomed ahead of the older calorie app in the app store rankings. The deal was big enough to convince Yadegari and his co-founders to sell the company after it had pulled in over $30 million in annual revenue in under two years, MyFitnessPal told TechCrunch at the time.

Yadegari and his co-founders originally went to work for their new owner, continuing development on Cal AI, but he left the bigger company in June, he tells TechCrunch. He then went right to work on his next idea. (He is working with another co-founder who has yet to be announced.)

That idea is Persona, a personal AI assistant similar to Instinct or Meta’s Muse but with a hardware component that will soon be available: a $179 wearable band.

Persona bandImage Credits:TechCrunch

That makes Persona somewhat more like Bee, the wearable AI device that Amazon acquired in 2025, but Persona’s device differs in several ways, Yadegari tells TechCrunch. For one, it won’t be ambient AI, meaning it won’t always be listening and recording. The band will have a button that activates the assistant, or it can be set up to activate with the flick of one’s wrist.

Yadegari also says that Persona is designed with user privacy in mind. Persona doesn’t run its AI model or store user data on the device. Instead, the model runs in Persona’s cloud, and user data is sent there. The assistant protects privacy by encrypting data in transit and at rest. Users can also delete their data, the company says.

In this way, it is promising that user conversations stay private and cannot be sold to advertisers or data brokers. 

The team is also baking in safeguards to protect the assistant against phishing and prompt-injection attempts, Yadegari says. These are two areas that can plague agents, say AI labs like OpenAI.

Plus, he promises that Persona’s agent can’t see a user’s credit-card details and that purchases will require the user’s approval, with payment handled through external providers such as Stripe Link. Link is Stripe’s secure wallet designed for use by agents.

Although user data won’t be sold to advertisers, the startup’s current business model does rely on ads. Yadegari says the company will show advertised wares during shopping research. But he says that the agent will present unbiased recommendations because the agent won’t know which of the items are advertised. For example, if someone is researching office chairs, he says, “the agent knows their preferences” and will show them chairs that match those preferences, some of them sponsored results.

The bands are expected to be available in December, and an app is in the works. In the meantime, Persona has launched as a free beta product in which users work with the assistant via iMessage text messages. It has attracted “a few thousand beta users,” Yadegari said. The band has also already generated “five figures in preorder revenue.”

Like other consumer AI assistants, he says, Persona can order food or rides, take notes, book travel, answer questions and emails, among other tasks.

“All of the utility apps that you use on your phone day-to-day, whether those are apps for shopping, whether it’s Uber, DoorDash, your email — these are all collapsing and will collapse into a single super app powered by an AI assistant,” Yadegari said.

Eventually, he hopes to make Persona even more proactive. “It can offer help and solve problems before you even know you have a problem, and overall be more seamless with your life, so that you don’t need to stare at a rectangle in your hand all day.”

Come see Zach Yadegari speak at TechCrunch Disrupt on “How to create viral growth and capitalize on it.” Disrupt takes place October 13-15 at the Moscone Center in San Francisco. Before Cal AI, Yadegari built his first business in the ninth grade and sold it for $100,000 when he was 16.

title: Amazon unveils new Alexa tablets with Alexa+ and Google Play Store access
snippet: The lineup includes three models: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, Amazon Alexa Tablet 11, and Amazon Alexa Tablet 8.
fullText:
Amazon on Thursday unveiled a new lineup of Alexa tablets that feature personalized intelligence from its Alexa+ AI assistant and full access to the Google Play Store. The lineup includes three models: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, Amazon Alexa Tablet 11, and Amazon Alexa Tablet 8.

The tech giant says each tablet features an aluminum unibody design, high-resolution displays, and runs on Android. Plus, with access to the Google Play Store at launch, users will be able to download millions of apps, including YouTube, Netflix, Gmail, and more.

Until now, Amazon’s tablets have run Fire OS and ship with its own app store. With these new tablets, however, Amazon is taking a different approach to reach a wider audience. An Amazon spokesperson told TechCrunch that these are an all-new product line with new hardware and a new OS, rather than a rebrand of Fire Tablets.

The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro measures 6.5 mm thick and is engineered for “perfect balance,” Amazon explained in a press release. It houses a 12-inch, 280 PPI display, a 120Hz refresh rate, and a 3:2 aspect ratio for more usable screen space, which the company says is perfect for reading, watching, or working. It comes in two display options: a standard display and a Nanomatte display with anti-glare.

Amazon says the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro delivers nearly three times the processing performance and nine times the graphics performance of any tablet it has shipped before. The company says the tablet can easily handle everything from multi-window multitasking and graphics-intensive gaming to 4K streaming. It features Dolby Atmos speakers, Wi-Fi 6E, and 16 hours of video playback.

Image Credits:Amazon

The company also announced the Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and Pro Keyboard, which Amazon says are designed to turn the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro into a full workstation.

The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $499.99, while the Nanomatte model starts at $549.99. The tablet comes in Graphite.

The new tablets are launching with built-in access to Alexa+. Users will be able to say “Alexa” or tap the “Ask Alexa” button to get answers to questions, control their smart home, and more. With On-Screen Intelligence, users will be able to ask Alexa to look at what’s on screen to receive contextual help. For example, while browsing a list of trails, users can ask Alexa, “Which of these hikes is best for me?”

The Alexa Tablet 11 is an 11-inch device with a 2.5K display at 276 pixels per inch, 90Hz smooth scrolling, and a 16:10 aspect ratio. The tech giant says it’s designed for streaming, gaming, reading, and browsing. It features 15 hours of video playback and dual Dolby Atmos speakers. It starts at $329.99 and comes in Graphite, Amethyst, and Matcha. 

The Alexa Tablet 8 is the smallest and most portable of the three, featuring an 8.7-inch display and an all-aluminum design that weighs 329 grams. It’s designed to be held in one hand and carried anywhere for reading, browsing, and streaming on the go, Amazon says. It starts at $229.99 and comes in Graphite, Rosette, and Teal.

All of the new tablets are launching with a new Kindle reading experience. When users open the Kindle app, notifications are silenced, blue light is reduced, and battery life can last up to 20 hours.

Image Credits:Amazon

The company also announced on Wednesday that it’s launching new Amazon Kids Tablets, with 8.7-inch and 11-inch sizes available. Bundles include a tablet, a kid-proof case, and a year of Amazon Kids+, which provides access to thousands of kid-friendly books, games, videos, and apps in an ad-free environment.

There are separate versions for pre-K kids (ages 3+) and kids 6+, as younger kids get a soft bumper case in designs from franchises like Paw Patrol and Barbie, while older kids get a slim hard case with a built-in kickstand.

All three Amazon Alexa Tablets and the Amazon Kids Tablets will go on sale October 14, 2026, in the U.S., Mexico, and Canada. They’ll launch in the U.K., Germany, France, Italy, and Spain on October 19, while the Amazon Kids Tablets will also be available in Japan starting October 14.

title: Google’s SynthID AI content detector expands globally, will work on Apple’s models ‘soon’
snippet: Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners. more…
fullText:
Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners.

SynthID is a necessary tool as AI content has taken hold of heavy portions of the internet. Models have evolved so much that it’s nearly impossible to tell whether some videos or photos are even real, and it has you second-guessing whether real ones are generated. SynthID takes aim at that problem by introducing invisible watermarks at the generation stage, and when used on an image, it will detect those watermarks.

Of course, that only works if the image generation tool inserts its own footprint to begin with.

Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future. The tool has progressed some, but this is a bigger step for AI content detection. According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility.

	

The new SynthID will work with content generated on Google’s own Gemini, a given, as well as content from more partners. So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple. That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together.

Google notes that images made with Apple Intelligence will carry a SynthID watermark “soon,” which implies it might be a little bit before users can reliably identify AI-generated content from Apple’s models. But the expansion means that more users in total will be able to do some due diligence on photos and videos posted online.

title: Meta rolling out audio upgrades, turn-by-turn navigation for Ray-Ban smart glasses
snippet: Meta’s most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation. more…
fullText:
Meta’s most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation. 

The most recent system update for Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses is version 129. This update brings two main changes, both to audio playback. Users can now balance audio between the two speakers to best suit their hearing, or set both speakers to mono playback instead of stereo.

Meta explains:

Mono Audio: Hear the same sound on both sides. If you have hearing anomalies, Mono Audio combines the left and right channels so nothing gets missed on the side you can’t hear. Applies to sounds your glasses make, like Meta AI and notifications. Turn it on in Device settings › Audio › Accessibility.

Audio Balance: Shift sound toward your left or right ear, one step at a time, until the balance feels right for your hearing. Applies to sounds your glasses make like Meta AI responses. Adjust it in Device settings › Audio › Accessibility.

Beyond that, update version 128 is broadly available after first debuting earlier in September and it brings some key updates including Spatial Audio support, further anti-tampering tweaks to stop the camera from working if the privacy LED has been mesed with, and also new location features.

	

Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses now feature turn-by-turn walking navigation directions. This pulls your location from your phone and you can also share navigation from your mapping app directly to Meta AI to be used on the glasses.

Pedestrian Navigation: Turn-by-turn pedestrian navigation is here! Get walking directions to your favorite places nearby. Just say “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” For further away places, we’ll send a notification with driving directions to your phone.

Share location from phone to glasses: Open your phone’s mapping app and find a location that you’d like to walk to. Tap Share. Select Meta AI from the list of applications. Navigation will start on your connected glasses.

While the new audio changes are still starting to roll out, the navigation upgrades from version 128 are now broadly available as an update in the Meta AI app.

title: Google releases a new local-first Granola competitor
snippet: Google’s new AI Edge Foresight app takes on Granola with an offline meeting note-taker that can transcribe conversations, generate notes, and answer questions using on-device AI.
fullText:
Earlier in April, Google released an AI-powered dictation tool that worked with local models. Now, the same team has released a new competitor to the AI note-taker Granola and others, which it calls Google AI Edge Foresight.

The Mac app can work completely offline, utilizing the on-device EmbeddingGemma 2 model, with 740 million parameters, to capture meeting notes across apps, including those from in-person meetings.

The app is similar to the popular AI note-taker Granola because it has a split-screen view with the ability to write shorthand notes on one side and AI-generated notes on the other side. 

Like Granola, it also lets you take manual notes while transcribing the meeting. Plus, in Google’s app, you can view the transcript of the meeting or chat with the Gemma 4-powered assistant to get answers.

In addition, users can upload documents including PDFs, Google Docs, Microsoft Office formats, plain text, Markdown, and web bookmarks to build a knowledge base. Using your meeting notes and documents, the app can answer questions in real time if a point related to data in the knowledge base comes up.

Image Credits:Google

On its FAQ page, the company specified that Google AI Edge Foresight is optimized for Apple Silicon and can completely work offline. This means you can work with your meeting notes when you are traveling or in a place without an internet connection.

While Google’s earlier dictation app was an experimental one that didn’t make it to mainstream usage, its new meeting note-taker could be just to showcase the ability of its Gemma series of offline models. 

However, Google could very well release a consumer version of meeting note-taker that works across video calling apps through its Gemini apps while relying on its cloud models.

The meeting note-taker space is competitive and crowded. But that hasn’t stopped companies from creating their own tools. In the last few months, dictation company Wispr and scheduling company Calendly released their own note-takers. Meanwhile, productivity startup Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) acquired YC-backed note-taker Fathom last month.

title: The Surface Laptop Ultra Is Here: Microsoft and Nvidia Built a Premium Computer for the AI Age
snippet: With Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip and platform, Microsoft’s newest laptop is ready to compete with AI heavyweights.
fullText:
After months of teasers, Microsoft officially gave the Surface Laptop Ultra the two things it needed: a release date and a price. You’ll like one and hate the other. Let’s get into everything Microsoft announced at its Oct. 7 Windows and Surface event.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is anything but a surprise. Microsoft first unveiled the device this spring at Computex, and since then, it popped up at Microsoft’s Build software conference and IFA. The 15-inch laptop is powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip and platform. This computer is a workhorse, meant for developers, creators and others who need a lot of horsepower to power through their work. It also comes with a magnetic USB-C charging cord, new for Microsoft.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is available for preorder now, and devices will begin shipping on Friday, Oct. 16. 

			

More from CNET

Pricing for the Ultra is going to depend a lot on how much memory you need in your laptop. The base model with 24GB of RAM, a 512GB SSD and a lower-end RTX Spark N1X processor (the version with the 18-core CPU and 5,120-core GPU) starts at $2,600. But upgrade to the 32GB model, with 1TB SSD, and you’ll pay $3,300. The most expensive model, with 128GB of RAM, goes all the way up to $5,900. And that’s before shipping and taxes.

If the pricing didn’t give it away already, this laptop is not an affordable, everyday option. It’s not meant to be: It’s the flagship member of the Surface lineup, aimed at hardcore workers who need or want a device that can handle a lot of AI compute-intensive tasks or a lightweight system that can handle GPU-intensive work.

“We built it for developers and creators pushing the limits of performance, who want portability with exceptional craft,” Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s Windows chief, said at the event on Wednesday.

A big part of Microsoft’s sales pitch is the ability to run AI models and agents locally on device. There are some advantages to using local AI models. You keep all the information more secure within your hardware — no outsourcing to the cloud — and after the initial setup costs, it can be cheaper to run. Both of those points are appealing to businesses that need to keep their data private and avoid hefty bills from “AI tokenmaxxing” employees (people who use a lot of AI).

To truly get the most use out of local AI, you need a device that can handle your generative and agentic tasks without eating more memory than you’ve got or taking forever. That’s where Nvidia comes in with its RTX Spark. It’s a new Arm-based system-on-chip platform that brings Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU architecture — sometimes used in AI data centers — to Windows laptops.

We’ll have to wait and see just how well the Surface Laptop Ultra handles in our full testing. For now, check out CNET’s best laptops of 2026.

title: Report: Apple’s smart home push includes LG-made doorbell, lock, thermostat, more
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plans for smart home products include devices, sensors, and cameras codeveloped in partnership with LG. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plans for smart home products include devices, sensors, and cameras codeveloped in partnership with LG. Here are the details.

Apple and LG working together on domestic connected devices

According to Bloomberg, Apple and LG have been working together to develop a series of connected home products that will complement Apple’s upcoming smart home hub, marking “a formal reboot of HomeKit.”

That includes “a doorbell, thermostat, […] a smart deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera and floodlight camera,” says Bloomberg.

Gurman notes that although Apple and LG “worked together to develop the accessories, the products will carry the LG brand,” adding that “the South Korean firm is handling manufacturing and product support” and has sought regulatory approval in recent weeks.

This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories. Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps.

It is worth noting that although these products are part of Apple’s broader push into the connected home, which is expected to expand next week with the introduction of its new smart home hub, an updated Apple TV, and a new HomePod mini, Bloomberg says that “the products aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.”

Here’s Bloomberg:

In recent weeks, LG has sought regulatory approval for the devices, including with the US Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions, a product certification company. In many cases, the databases for both organizations include filings that reveal product names, specifications, features and drawings of the accessories.

That includes products labeled as the LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Indoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat and LG Temperature Sensor. LG requested that photos and more precise details on the products remain confidential until early next year. The filings don’t mention Apple’s involvement.

	

When it comes to connectivity and standards, the report notes that many devices will support Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Matter. It adds that the smart lock also includes UWB (ultra-wideband), which will enable proximity-based features such as automatic door unlocking.

Finally, the report notes that for both Apple and LG, these products will mark a broader expansion into the smart home market, with Apple looking to give new momentum to its home ecosystem:

[Apple] is also planning its own additional offerings in the future, including a privacy-centric home-monitoring device, a version of its smart home hub that attaches the screen to a robotic arm, and an in-home security monitoring service, Bloomberg News has reported.

It is worth stressing that although today’s report comes on the heels of Apple’s announcement of the long-rumored ‘HomePad’ connected home hub and other products next week, the LG-made accessories aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.

title: Is That Picture AI? Google’s SynthID Detector Launches to Identify AI-Generated Media
snippet: Anyone can now upload a suspicious image to Google’s online tool, but it’s not a foolproof way to check for authenticity.
fullText:
AI slop is getting so good that it’s not always easy to distinguish a photorealistic forgery from a real photo. It’s no longer as easy as looking for the six-fingered renderings of just a year ago. Beyond looking for subtle clues, spotting AI images often comes down to a gut feeling that something simply looks off.

Now there’s another tool to help identify fakes, and it works with AI-edited audio and video, too. Google has opened its SynthID Detector to the public, so anyone with a Google, Apple or ChatGPT account can upload media to determine whether it’s been saved with a SynthID tag indicating manipulation using generative AI.

Google introduced SynthID in 2023 and, in late 2025, made it possible to query Google Gemini about whether images were created using Google’s AI. At the Google I/O annual developer conference this past May, the tool expanded to include detecting video and audio content in Google Chrome and Google Search.

			

More from CNET

The standalone SynthID Detector tool currently detects media generated by Google, OpenAI, Nvidia and Kakao. Not yet named is Apple, which announced it would support SynthID at its recent fall event announcing the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

A spokesperson for Google, in an email to CNET, emphasized that working with other companies is crucial when it comes to identifying AI-generated content because no single company can solve the problem alone. They also said there’s no specific date for Apple support, but that it will be available soon.

Even so, the SynthID Detector seems already wired for Apple’s content. I uploaded a photo shot with an iPhone 18 Pro and edited using Apple’s Reframe tool, and it successfully detected the embedded SynthID tag. For an untouched iPhone-captured photo, the detector correctly did not detect a tag.

The original photo, captured with an iPhone, underwent a slight perspective shift using Apple’s Reframe tool, which then embedded a SynthID tag that was recognized by Google’s SynthID Detector.Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Images generated from prompts using ChatGPT were correctly flagged as including AI-generated content

This photo was entirely AI-generated from a prompt in ChatGPT. Although the SynthID tag was detected, the janky pattern of leaves on the ground gives it away, too.Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

To probe the level of Apple support in the tool, I created an entirely AI-generated image in Apple’s Playground app using ChatGPT’s image generation model, but the SynthID Detector did not identify it as AI-generated. It’s likely the Playground app does not yet have SynthID tagging wired in.

Apple’s Playground app was used to generate this variation, which was created with ChatGPT, but the detector found no SynthID metadata.Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

I also tested some photos captured using a Google Pixel 11 Pro. The company takes a two-pronged approach to image veracity on its own devices: embedding C2PA (or Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) metadata in every image it creates to verify the accuracy of the original capture, and adding a SynthID when an image has been edited using AI.

I edited the original photo with a Pixel 11 Pro XL in Google Photos by asking Gemini to create a night version with an aurora, shown at right. The SynthID Detector correctly noted the SynthID tag in the edited version.

Although Apple is adopting SynthID, it has not signed onto C2PA. Instead, it’s using its own Reference Image technology to store a cryptographically verified original of an image. Those shots must be captured in the Reference mode in the iPhone’s Camera app, though.

It’s also encouraging to see Google handle the media in a sensible way. When you first visit the site, you must agree to terms of service that spell out that media files you upload are processed in real time and then deleted after the results are displayed. A digital signature of the media is mapped to your user identifier and then deleted after 24 hours.

OpenAI has its own verification tool, but it only looks for OpenAI watermarks; the AI-generated samples I tested with Google’s tool came up negative on OpenAI’s site.

Any tool that helps determine genuine content is welcome, but as usual, the responsibility falls on the viewer to make that determination — if not by noticing on sight, then by making the effort of downloading the media, loading the tool and uploading it. The upside is that tracking technology such as SynthID is finally making its way into more media and paving the way for more widespread detection of AI slop.

And if you’re an Amazon Prime subscriber, you can access Alexa Plus for free for more advanced capabilities, better smart home device controls and access to voice-ordering from apps like Uber and Grubhub.

What’s the best choice?

My Prime picks can work in all types of homes, depending on what you need. My personal favorite is probably the Nest thermostat because I watched mine pay for itself across a few years of use, but that’s not an upgrade everyone wants to spend money on. Another favorite is the Tapo smart plug pack, because Tapo is one of the very few smart plug makers that offer energy monitoring, which is also nice for saving energy when you’re using something like a space heater or my Zafro tower fan pick.

Amazon is also having some of the biggest discounts on its own Echo speakers and smart displays, so it’s the best time of the year to pick one of those up if you want a smart home controller and voice assistant music hub.

title: Alexa Plus is better at running my home, but it’s not ready to run my life
snippet: I’ve spent a year living with Alexa Plus, and it both delights and frustrates me, which is the smart home in a nutshell. | Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge Of all the things Alexa Plus can do, I never expected it to make me cry. Since my son left for college, the Echo Show in my office has been making then-and-now photo montages: the toddler with his first tennis racket next to the captain of his varsity team; me hugging him as a tween beside me hugging him as a young man. I've teared up more than once. But then comes the ad, a full-screen photo of a hideous brown leather recliner. I go from nostalgic joy to irritation in an instant. That pretty much sums up my year with Alexa Plus. One minute it will do something seriously impressive; the next, it acts like it doesn't know who I am. I've bee … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Of all the things Alexa Plus can do, I never expected it to make me cry. Since my son left for college, the Echo Show in my office has been making then-and-now photo montages: the toddler with his first tennis racket next to the captain of his varsity team; me hugging him as a tween beside me hugging him as a young man. I’ve teared up more than once. But then comes the ad, a full-screen photo of a hideous brown leather recliner. I go from nostalgic joy to irritation in an instant.

That pretty much sums up my year with Alexa Plus. One minute it will do something seriously impressive; the next, it acts like it doesn’t know who I am.

Alexa Plus’s memories feature pulls images from your Alexa Photos albums. It’s become very good at pairing images from over the years, like these two of my son and me.

I’ve been testing Amazon’s AI-powered Alexa Plus assistant in my home since July 2025, shortly after it launched in early access and ahead of its full launch in February 2026. With Google’s rollout of Gemini for Home earlier this year, and rumors that Apple is finally bringing the full Apple Intelligence experience to Apple Home this month, now felt like a good moment to review Amazon’s progress.

A year in, Alexa Plus is the best smart home assistant I’ve tested: It’s easy to talk to, handles routines and multistep commands, and helps in the kitchen. But Amazon’s attempts to stretch it into a personal assistant are underbaked and frustrating, and the ads on the Echo Show smart displays are out of control.

The Echo Dot Max is the flagship Alexa Plus speaker and your best option if you want to run Alexa without seeing ads every day.

Alexa is more reliable in my smart home

I tested Alexa Plus with an Echo Show 11 in my kitchen, Pops and Dots around my house, and a Show 15 and 8 in my office. I use voice commands to control my smart home devices, help me with timers and recipes, add events to my calendar and groceries to my shopping list, and occasionally order something from Amazon. I use the screen-based devices as photo frames, for viewing camera feeds, and as touchscreen controllers for my smart home.

To get Alexa Plus to work properly for me, I had to rebuild my smart home from scratch

A lot has improved. Smart home control, routines, general queries, calendar management, and shopping are light-years ahead of pre-AI Alexa, mostly because the new Alexa understands me better. The big promise of LLM-powered voice assistants was the ability to say what you want without using stilted, precise nomenclature. In my testing, that’s proven out. My family uses Alexa more now than they used to, and I like being able to give more general instructions, like “Alexa, make it brighter in here” and “Alexa, I’m cold,” and it knows what to do.

The Echo Show’s calendar interface is much better, though it still isn’t as good as the Skylight Calendar for viewing multiple schedules.

It’s also now faster and more reliable. When I started testing the new assistant, I ran into a litany of issues, from misunderstood commands to messed-up routines and very slow responses. Today, questions about the weather or general knowledge and commands like setting a timer execute in three to five seconds, a big change from the 10 to 15 seconds I saw in 2025. When it gets a request wrong the first time, a follow-up now usually fixes it. I can say “Lock the front door, turn off the lights, turn down the thermostat, and tell the robot to clean downstairs,” and it happens promptly, without any back talk.

Alexa is also much better at answering questions, especially in the kitchen. Talking with it is easier now that you can speak conversationally and don’t have to repeat the wake word — but I had to switch to the new Brief personality mode after one too many superlatives about my shopping list ( “Oooh, that will make for one spicy salsa!).

The Show 8 and Show 11 are very good smart displays (ads aside). The Ring security camera integration is impressive — I can ask when I last had a package delivered, and it will show the clip and tell me what’s in the package (if it was from Amazon).

I recently snapped a picture of my friend’s Dutch baby recipe while in England and sent it to Alexa via the app. When I got home, I asked Alexa to help me cook it; the assistant pulled up the reformatted recipe, and we chatted back and forth easily while I cooked. I could ask, “What temperature should I preheat the oven?” and “How many ounces are 160 grams?” and it would remember we were discussing the recipe and give the right answer. Alexa still sometimes forgets what it’s doing, and getting back to the recipe can be tricky, but it’s the best voice-assistant cooking experience I’ve tested.

What is Alexa Plus?

Alexa Plus is Amazon’s revamped digital assistant powered by generative AI. You can access it by voice through Echo smart speakers and displays, Fire TV, and other Alexa-built-in devices. You can also access it in the Alexa app on smartphones and tablets and at Alexa.com.

It is free to use on the web, in the app, and on Fire TV but requires an Amazon Prime membership or a $19.99-a-month subscription (in the US) to access on compatible Echo devices.

Alexa Plus is available in the U.S. and Canada and is in early access in Mexico, the U.K., Italy, Spain, Germany, Austria, France, Brazil, Australia, and India. The original Alexa is still available for free on Echo devices.

I’ve also found Alexa more useful for general knowledge, something it used to be terrible at, and calendar management has become more reliable, too. I can now email and upload documents and photos to Alexa Plus, and it can import events from them into my calendar. I added my daughter’s entire school schedule that way. Shopping is also hugely improved. I uploaded 10 screenshots of sewing supplies from my daughter’s teacher to the Alexa app, and it found all the items and added them to my Amazon cart, saving me a lot of time.

My favorite upgrade is creating Alexa smart home routines by voice. I think of something I want my home to do, tell Alexa, and it does it. I wanted the string lights on the porch to turn on when I walk outside; Alexa set up a routine using the motion sensor on the Ring camera. I can also adapt routines on the fly. One night, my daughter came out of her bathroom complaining, “The lights kept shutting off.” I told Alexa to change the “Hallway bathroom light” routine to shut off after 30 minutes instead of 15, and it fixed it.

But it took a long time to get here. Like many Alexa users, I had a lot of technical debt in my smart home, and as a reviewer, my Alexa app was a graveyard of zombie devices. To get Alexa Plus to work properly for me, I had to rebuild my smart home from scratch, deleting all my old Alexa skills and routines and killing dead and duplicate devices. It took months, literally. I’ve had to re-add 55 Hue devices six times over the past year. And while Alexa has improved, the Alexa app has not. Adding, deleting, and moving multiple devices is still deeply painful, and the app experience is Alexa’s biggest flaw.

What I really want is Alexa Plus to manage all that for me so I never have to touch the app. From setting up gadgets to troubleshooting issues, Alexa should be able to put devices in the right room and, if something isn’t working, figure it out. I want it to manage my smart home for me. That is an assistant I would pay money for.

The ads on the Echo Show smart displays are Alexa Plus’s worst feature.

Agents, accuracy, and ads

While Alexa Plus has made a lot of improvements, there are three big issues, one of which may make you flat-out not want to use the service: ads, inconsistency, and mostly failed attempts at being a personal assistant.

Display ads are out of control. Every Show device is now a rotating billboard in my home for Amazon goods. Even if you turn off all the homescreen content (the rotating screen on the displays), you still get ads interspersed between your photos and the clock. Timing is random; I can see one an hour on the Echo Show 5 in the bedroom and then go a whole day without seeing one on the 11 in my kitchen, but they’re fairly constant on the Show 8 in my office.

Alexa Plus is still inconsistent at executing more complicated requests

Daniel Rausch, VP of Alexa & Echo at Amazon, tells me these ads are curated and designed to be relevant. “When it’s done well, an ad should show up with something useful at just the right moment,” he said. But it hasn’t felt curated to me; among the beauty products, car accessories, snacks, furniture, health supplements, and smart home gear that have assaulted my eyeballs, nothing has been something I wanted to buy. Even worse, Amazon recently added video ads.

There is now a fix, but it will cost you: Amazon’s new Photo Gallery Unlimited feature removes the ads from the homescreen for $2.99 per month per device. If you don’t want to pay monthly to avoid ads, I would stick with the Echo speakers.

Amazon trying to sell my 15-year-old daughter motor oil doesn’t feel “curated.” Though the anti-aging cream ad I saw one morning did hurt.

Alexa Plus is still inconsistent at executing more complicated requests. This was a big issue in my initial testing and has improved, but not gone away. The shift from the reliable but restricted command-and-control architecture of the old Alexa to the LLM-powered generative AI has introduced a lot of uncertainty: Alexa Plus sometimes has to guess at what you want.

Alexa Plus misheard my request for a Coffee Grande and instead generated an image of a coffee grinder.

For example, Alexa still can’t reliably make a cup of coffee. I have an Alexa-capable Bosch 800 Series coffee machine with a special integration that gives Alexa more granular controls, including making a specific drink, such as a coffee grande. This works most of the time — a big improvement over my initial testing. But the other day I asked Alexa to make me a coffee grande, and it replied, “I’d love to, but I’m fresh out of arms and a coffee maker.” I asked again, and it said, “Sure, here’s a coffee grinder,” displaying an AI-generated image of a coffee grinder.

Alexa Plus still struggles with timely information. Asking it when England next played in the soccer World Cup in June almost made me miss kickoff, and last month when I asked what channel an Ohio State–Illinois football game was on, it offered to set up a reminder for a game that had already started.

I’m not against Alexa doing more for me but the assistant has failed to finish several tasks

Getting dates and times wrong is not a trait I want in a personal assistant, which is what Amazon is pushing Alexa Plus as. Instead of a stoic, disembodied voice, I’m now greeted every morning by a perky pair of digital hands proffering a cheery emoji and a line like “Hey Jen, tell me what I can do for you today?” on the Echo Show in my kitchen.

Perkiness aside — I’m English; we don’t do perky — I’m not against Alexa doing more for me. It’s just that the assistant has failed to finish several tasks I’ve given it. Most of these new agentic features, including integrations with Thumbtack, OpenTable, and Ticketmaster, feel underbaked and mostly a waste of my time.

This feature-stuffing is inevitable as Amazon starts charging to use Alexa on Echo devices ($19.99 a month if you aren’t a Prime member) and competes with the AI giants in the agentic space. But nothing is more frustrating than spending time explaining what you want done, only to then have to do it yourself.

Trying to order lunch with Uber Eats using voice and touch on the Show 8 was frustrating and ultimately unsuccessful.

When I tried ordering lunch through Uber Eats on the Echo Show, Alexa confidently told me, “Just tell me what you like, and I’ll find it on the menu as you speak.” That wasn’t the case. Instead, I spent 20 minutes trying to order a Chick-fil-A meal with iced tea, while the Uber Eats interface on the smart display insisted on ordering me a s’mores milkshake I never asked for. Booking an electrician was no better; after 10 minutes dictating my electrical issues to Alexa and going through several Thumbtack sign-up screens, it gave me the electrician’s number to call.

A bigger problem is memory. Alexa has the memory of a goldfish. For a while, it forgot who I was and kept asking me to introduce myself whenever I asked it to do something. Which was frankly rude, since it’s been living in my house for a decade. It’s also supposed to have a feature called Remember This that stores information you tell it, similar to the memory features in ChatGPT or Claude.

I told it what school my daughter went to, asked it to remember this, then asked what the traffic was like getting there. It gave the correct answer. But the next day, when I made the same request, it confidently gave me the traffic conditions and travel time to an entirely different school, and it insisted that was the school I’d asked it to remember.

Remembering details about you, your household, and your home is a crucial skill for a personal assistant. If I hired one that sent my daughter to the wrong school, I’d fire them immediately.

Alexa Plus has deeper integration with this smart Bosch coffee machine, making it better at handling more granular commands — such as “Make me a coffee grande” — but it’s inconsistent.

Amazon already knows a lot about my household, from what I buy to what’s on my shopping list and even what arrives at my front door — that’s a privacy tradeoff you have to grapple with when using Alexa. What it lacks is the personal context a personal assistant needs. This is where Google and Apple have the lead, and where Amazon has a lot of catching up to do to succeed here.

I test all the major smart home assistants, including Google’s Gemini for Home and Siri in Apple Home, and Alexa is the most reliable and functional for controlling my home. But I’ll turn to Siri to send a text message or Google to get me a traffic-free route to my daughter’s school.

With Alexa Plus, Amazon has taken a big step toward the ambient smart home the company has imagined for over a decade. What it needs to do now is avoid the temptation to become a general-purpose AI bot, and instead focus on becoming the brain for your home — potentially one you could integrate with your personal AI assistant of choice (something Google is doing with Google Home). This would require Amazon to rediscover the openness that defined the platform when it launched in 2014 — it increasingly feels closed, with features that work only with Amazon’s brands and curated partners. But Alexa remains the biggest mainstream smart home platform, with broad third-party support, a huge install base, and wide support for protocols — including Matter and Thread.

Where it wins in breadth, however, Alexa lacks in depth. Alexa Plus should be able to control every feature of every device, not just on and off (Amazon recently launched a developer toolkit that could help here). Combined with its Omnisense fusion sensor platform, announced last year, this could bring it much closer to fully learning and understanding your household’s patterns. With that context, it could suggest proactive routines and start taking action for you — beyond random hunches every now and then. That’s the next frontier for the smart home, and today Amazon is best poised to overcome it.

The smart home assistant I want isn’t the one that can book a restaurant or write an email; it’s the one that understands my home, can manage it for me, and knows when I need a cute baby pic to cheer me up.

title: Robot data startup Mecka AI nabs $60M from Sequoia
snippet: Mecka AI collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other kinds of robots. The startup pays people to record everyday tasks.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

4:36 PM PDT · October 7, 2026

Image Credits:J Studios / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Mecka AI, a startup that collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other kinds of robots, announced it has raised a $60 million Series B round led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Microsoft’s venture fund M12, and others. TechCrunch had previously reported that the startup was nearing a new funding round at a $500 million valuation.

Founded in 2024, the startup intends to do for robotics what Scale AI, Mercor, Surge, and other data-labeling companies have done for LLMs. Those companies supply the human-generated data these systems learn from. Mecka pays people to record themselves doing everyday tasks, like making coffee or fixing cars, while wearing body sensors and using smartphones.

Other startups that collect real-world data for robot training include XDOF, which was in talks to raise a Series B round at a $1.2 billion valuation according to TechCrunch’s previous reporting. Human-data platforms that began with LLMs are also expanding into robotics, such as Scale AI and Micro1.

title: ChatGPT is adding new ads
snippet: OpenAI confirmed today that its ChatGPT app will be adding more space for ads starting with a test later this month. more…
fullText:
OpenAI confirmed today that its ChatGPT app will be adding more space for ads starting with a test later this month.

Announced today, OpenAI will be adding a “new visual ad format” to the ChatGPT app that shows when prompts are processing. Specifically, these will start showing during image generation.

OpenAI explains:

Our new visual ad format helps people imagine how products and services could fit into their lives. Through images showing product inspiration, product usage, or the experiences they make possible, people can discover a new brand, understand what makes an offering distinctive, and decide what to buy. For advertisers, this creates new opportunities to tell their story through images.

Initially, we’ll test this new ad format during image generation in ChatGPT. Ads will be clearly labeled, and remain separate from the image being created. As with our other ad formats, advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Previously, OpenAI tested ads that would show up at the bottom of answers with advertisements related to that prompt. An example showed a grocery delivery ad below a recipe response.

	

As for when you might start seeing these new ads in ChatGPT, OpenAI says it will be testing the format in its app for users in the US starting “later this month,” but a broad rollout isn’t confirmed yet.

OpenAI’s post touts that early findings with its ChatGPT ads have found lower cost per acquisition rates and that businesses are finding higher rates of new customers via the ads.

title: The first thing you should do on Googlebook is fix the trackpad
snippet: If you are an early Googlebook buyer, you should know that one of the first changes you should make on one of these new machines is to adjust the trackpad speed, because it’s a bit frustrating out of the box. more…
fullText:
If you are an early Googlebook buyer, you should know that one of the first changes you should make on one of these new machines is to adjust the trackpad speed, because it’s a bit frustrating out of the box.

Every Googlebook in this initial wave comes with a haptic trackpad, but they also seem to have a slight headache out of the box.

The cursor is incredibly slow.

“Touchpad accleration” on Googlebook, at least by default, is considerably slower than other platforms such as Windows and macOS. It’s something that we’ve all noticed here on the 9to5Google team as we’ve started using Googlebook machines this week across multiple models. It’s far from unusable, but it’s very jarring compared to any other laptop you might go buy at the store today.

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Alongside its new collection of Alexa Tablets that run Android with full access to the Google Play store, Amazon is introducing kid versions with similar functionality but the ability for parents to limit what software and content they have access to. The Amazon Kids Tablets also come with two different styles of colorful cases featuring characters from Paw Patrol, Barbie, and SpongeBob: a thicker more protective option for pre-kindergarten children, and a thinner one for kids aged six and up.

The Amazon Kids Tablets are available in two sizes that both feature lightweight aluminum designs and 8-core processors and seem identical to the smaller versions of the new Alexa Tablets, but with added software. The Kids Tablet 8.7-inch starts at $229.99 and comes with 64GB of storage and a battery good for up to 14 hours of video playback. The larger Amazon Kids Tablet 11-inch starts at $329.99 and features a better 2.5K display, 8GB of RAM for improved gaming experiences, and stylus support. Both will be available for preorder soon with shipping starting on October 14th in the US.

All versions of the Kids Tablet comes with a one-year subscription to Amazon Kids Plus which includes a collection of ad-free content including books, TV shows, games, apps, and audiobooks from companies like Disney, Nickelodeon, and Lego. Amazon is also introducing a new feature to Kids Plus called Storybuilder that uses AI to generate picture books and comics from descriptions of characters, worlds, and plot twists provided by kids.

Amazon’s Parent Dashboard comes pre-installed on the new Kids Tablets allowing them to set screen-time limits, monitor usage, and set learning goals that prioritize educational apps and games over entertainment. All of the settings in Parent Dashboard can also be accessed remotely through iOS and Android apps, including approval for every download from the Google Play Store.

In addition to releasing macOS 27.2 Golden Gate public beta 2, Apple is now rolling out the first Release Candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2. Here are the details.

Security updates continue for older macOS versions

As is usually the case for point updates of older macOS versions, Apple today rolled out the first release candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2, without first releasing regular beta versions.

Apple released macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 late last month, both of which saw two RCs before the official rollout.

Apple’s release notes for the first macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 RCs mention only that they “provide[s] important security fixes and [are] recommended for all users.” Last month’s updates contained a single CoreGraphics security fix, with its details reading:

Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.

Apple will likely detail the fixes included in macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 after their official release, which will likely come alongside macOS 27.2 Golden Gate within the next few weeks.

The release build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 RC 1 is 24H219, while the release build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 RC 1 is 25G320.

title: Meta’s Muse launches on iPad just a month after its mobile debut
snippet: Meta’s AI agent Muse is now available on iPad, just a month after its mobile debut, as the company rapidly expands the assistant’s reach and integrations.
fullText:
If there’s any doubt about how seriously Meta is taking AI, here’s a new signal: The company on Wednesday announced that its Muse assistant is now available in a dedicated iPad app. That’s a milestone it took Instagram some 15 years to reach, despite constant user demand.

Muse, meanwhile, hit the iPad just a month after launching on iPhone.

(To be fair, it may not be as difficult to bring something like Muse to iPad, given its text-heavy interface, where image and video resolution and formatting matter less.)

Since launching on iOS and Android on September 8, Muse has topped 6.6 million installs, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. The app, which is now one of dozens of consumer-facing AI agents, lets users connect their accounts to stay on top of email, meetings, bills, and more, and to complete tasks like booking reservations, ordering groceries, setting goals, and making purchases.

To make that work, Meta has been adding partners in the effort, which appear in Muse as “connectors.” Users can add and sign in to them selectively, depending on which parts of their online life they’re comfortable letting an AI agent handle.

With the iPad release, Meta has updated this list with several of its newer additions, including connectors aimed at small businesses, like Asana, Canva, Dropbox, Figma, QuickBooks, GitHub, Klaviyo, and Zoom, as well as connectors for Meta ad accounts. It also added Notion and Granola.

In addition, Meta recently announced more retail partners, like Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. These allow the agent to shop those retailers’ sites and complete transactions on users’ behalf. Because this technology is still new, these experiences can still run into issues as websites mistake agents for bots and block their access.

On Tuesday, Meta announced that it’s working with industry partners on a technological solution to this problem in the form of an open standard that would allow personal AI agents to identify themselves to businesses. That would help businesses sort the good bots from the bad.

title: There’s a clear divide between Galaxy S27 tiers, as the latest leak lists price
snippet: Samsung’s Galaxy S27 launch is getting closer, which means pricing and final details are being finalized and, further, leaked. The latest report lists Galaxy S27 series pricing and one spec that divides the lineup into two distinct tiers. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s Galaxy S27 launch is getting closer, which means pricing and final details are being finalized and, further, leaked. The latest report lists Galaxy S27 series pricing and one spec that divides the lineup into two distinct tiers.

It’s been known that Samsung wants to add another device model to the Galaxy S27 series. It tried last year, but the Galaxy S26 Edge never came to be and was replaced by a rushed S26+. Recent reports specify four different Galaxy S27 models, and none of them seem to be thin. The Galaxy S27 will consist of a base model, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra.

A Twitter/X post by @phonefuturist adds a little more context around pricing in the US and Korea for the Galaxy S27 series (via Android Headlines). The common sentiment has everyone expecting a price increase again. The post pushes back on that, stating that the Galaxy S27 will start at $899 in the US. Here’s the list, according to the leak:

Galaxy S27 – $899

Galaxy S27+ – $1,099

Galaxy S27 Pro – $1,299

Galaxy S27 Ultra – $1,399

Technically, the Galaxy S27 is listed here as cheaper than the current Galaxy S26, because Samsung recently jacked the prices up on an existing phone. But due to an added device in the middle, the structure gets a little wonky and can’t be compared to the previous series 1:1.

	

But going by launch pricing, the Galaxy S27 Pro could cost the same as the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the new version of the Ultra will bring the series to a peak of $1,399. For reference, a good foldable device like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is only $500 higher.

The leak also points out a divide in the group based on display specs. The Galaxy S27 and S27+ could get Samsung’s M14+ OLED panel, while the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra get the M16 OLED panel. The latter could mean a privacy display for both devices, while the two more affordable options are left without. The M16 panel is new this year and is also used on the outer iPhone Duo display.

🇺🇸 US/ 🇰🇷SK | 🌍 Int'l*

Regional pricing varies. Current targets, subject to change. https://t.co/SdwG7g5ac2

Pricing is something that can quickly change, so take this information with a grain of salt. Still, the line between the top-tier premium devices and second-best options is clearer. And now, users get another choice, even though the “Ultra” could cost $100 more.

The AI race is becoming an infrastructure race

Much of the AI conversation has focused on models, chips, and applications. But none of them operate in isolation. Scaling AI depends on an expanding physical stack: power generation, grid connections, data centers, cooling, electrical equipment, and the systems required to keep everything running.

That creates a different kind of challenge. What happens when demand for compute grows faster than power and infrastructure can be delivered? Which shortages are temporary, and which could reshape the market for years? Where does a constraint stop being a problem and start becoming a category of its own? Those are the questions this session will tackle.

Rather than looking at AI solely through the software layer, Bill Thayer and Ben Longmier will examine the infrastructure underneath it — and what those pressures could mean for founders, investors, and companies planning for the next phase of AI growth.

Where do the real opportunities sit?

Infrastructure booms create opportunity, but the benefits are rarely distributed evenly. The challenge is identifying which parts of the stack genuinely need new solutions, where spending is likely to persist, and which emerging categories can support durable businesses rather than short-term demand.

Bringing together leaders across energy, data center solutions, and market intelligence gives the discussion a wider view of that question. For founders, that means looking beyond the obvious AI application. For investors, it means understanding where infrastructure demand could create defensible markets. For tech leaders, it offers a clearer view of the physical systems increasingly shaping where and how AI can scale.

The next AI company may solve a physical-world problem

The next major opportunity created by AI may not look like an AI company at all. It could emerge in energy, data centers, cooling, grid technology, electrical equipment, infrastructure software, or entirely new categories that don’t yet have established names.

The common factor is the same: AI is creating new demands on the physical world, and those demands need solutions. That is what makes this session broader than an infrastructure discussion. It’s about understanding where the next markets could emerge — and who is positioned to build for them.
