title: Upgrade to Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4? Here’s how to get the most out of it
snippet: Upgrade to a new Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4? Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 bring upgraded performance and new health sensing features. Still, they can feel like the same watch in day-to-day use unless you know where to look for the changes. From new health complications to automatic Shazam recognition, a few setup changes can help you get more out of your upgrade. Here’s what to try. more…
fullText:
Upgrade to a new Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4? Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 bring upgraded performance and new health sensing features.

Still, they can feel like the same watch in day-to-day use unless you know where to look for the changes. From new health complications to automatic Shazam recognition, a few setup changes can help you get more out of your upgrade. Here’s what to try.

Refresh your watch face

Start by adding exclusive new complication options only supported on the new Apple Watch models. Series 12 and Ultra 4 can display your live heart rate, steps count, and readiness score on your watch face.

You can add these complications to your favorite watch face to unlock new insight into your health and fitness. 

For me, live heart rate data has been an essential new complication, using a single slot with better data compared to the old wide slot with less current data. Step tracking has also been a big motivator for getting activity logged earlier in the day. 

And since readiness score can change throughout the day based on your vitals and activity, displaying readiness on your watch face can be a great tip.

And while it’s off by default, you can enable quick switching between watch faces with a swipe at Settings > Clock > Swipe to Switch Watch Face.

Turn on automatic Shazam

Your new Watch can identify music around you without a request to Siri or a tap on Shazam.

On Apple Watch, open Settings → Smart Stack and enable Music Detection. When you open the Smart Stack, Music Recognition can show the song title and artist.

It’s a small setup change with an obvious payoff the next time something unfamiliar plays at a restaurant or coffee shop.

Try Siri Modular

Siri Modular comes to every Apple Watch running watchOS 27, although Series 12 and Ultra 4 have more complication options.

Something I love about the Siri Modular face is how you can style it. For now, I have a few instances of the Siri Modular face in my rotation using different colors, fonts, layout styles, and complications.

Give readiness time to work

Adding a readiness complication is only part of the setup. You also need to collect the data behind the score.

Apple says to complete your Health Details, set up Activity and overnight vitals, enable Sleep, and wear your Watch while sleeping for at least seven nights. You also need sleep data from the previous night.

Find a charging window during the day so overnight tracking becomes easier to maintain.

So far, readiness has been an interesting experiment, but I think it’s still too early to call it useful for me. 

Daytime vitals

Lastly, the Vitals app has more insight with Series 12 and Ultra 4 hardware.

You can see daytime vitals, not just overnight, in the Vitals app. This is based on heart rate and recovery heart rate variability. Overnight vitals also factor respiratory rate and wrist temperature.

Looking ahead, there’s more to come for Series 12 and Ultra 4 with Siri Recap and Live Rewind on the way.

What are your favorite ways to get the most out of the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4? Share your ideas in the comments.

title: These are the best times to save money on your next flight, according to Google Flights
snippet: Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price.

With surging fuel prices have also come much higher plane ticket costs and, with that, everyone’s looking for a deal. In a blog post this week, Google Flights details the best times to book your next flight.

For domestic US flights, the best time is apparently 39 days prior to departure, but the lowest price can fall anywhere between 57 days prior and 22 days prior to the actual flight date. International flights should be booked much further out, with 89 days being the magic number there.

Thanksgiving and Christmas flights bend the rules a bit. Thanksgiving flights are actually cheapest 34 days prior to departure, but Christmas flights need to be booked much earlier at around 56 days.

	

Here’s the full breakdown from Google:

Domestic flights: 39 days before departure (low price range is 22–57 days)

International flights: 89 days before departure, but the average price drop during the low range (50–133 days out) is insignificant

Thanksgiving: Lowest prices hit 34 days before departure (low price range is 21–57 days)

Christmas: 56 days before departure (low price range is 33–67 days)

Spring break: 50 days before departure (low price range is 29–64 days) for trips in March or April

Summer vacation: 21 days before departure (low price range is 20–47 days) for trips in July or August

Trips to Europe: 49 days or more before departure

Trips to Mexico or the Caribbean: 43 days before departure (low price range is 24–69 days)

The post goes on to detail trending destinations for the 2026 travel season, with Hawaii being the top Thanksgiving destination and international trips to Greece and Canada trending around Christmas and New Year’s Eve.

title: Google Pixel at 10: Successes, failures, and fun along the way [Video]
snippet: A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though. more…
fullText:
A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though.

Look back at the line-up, and it’s still hard to believe we’ve had a decade of Pixel. If you asked me back in 2016 whether Google’s in-house hardware experiment would stick around long enough to reach fully custom 3nm silicon, I’m not sure I’d have believed you.

To say that Google was late to the market is an understatement. By 2016, Apple and Samsung were already well into the swing of things. To be fair, that still is the case a decade later, but now with an even tighter iron grip over the space. I was personally distraught when the Nexus lineup was canceled to the point that I actually went with the Galaxy S8 rather than wait to see what Google had in store next.

	

Google’s answer to the ‘big two’ was Pixel. A phone not “officially” made by partners, but still sort of relying on OEMs while the production pipeline or groundwork was laid.

Pixel and Pixel XL (2016)

The original Google Pixel was built in a close manufacturing partnership with HTC, featuring a wedge-shaped profile that famously tapered down to eliminate any camera bump. 

Let’s be real, the hardware wasn’t tearing up trees, and it looked more than a little similar to the iPhone 7/8 series. It was a conservative design, but pretty darn self-assured.

The main thing that helped differentiate the device was its built-in Google Assistant integration and HDR+ image processing pipeline for photos. Rightly or wrongly, this simple formula has more or less defined the Pixel for the past decade of Google’s mobile computing efforts.

Smart, simple software and artificial intelligence have been at the forefront from the very beginning and will remain so over the next 10 years.

Pixel 2 series (2017)

With the second generation, Google finally figured out design. The LG-made Pixel 2 XL gave us the iconic “Panda” colorway with its stark black-and-white glass back and the bright orange accent power button. You’ve told us time and time again that it’s a personal favorite for Pixel fans. It also debuted the Pixel Visual Core, Google’s first attempt at custom co-processing to let apps like Instagram use HDR+.

Add single-lens Portrait Mode that put dual-camera rivals to shame, squeeze-to-activate Active Edge, ambient Now Playing track identification, and the persistent At a Glance widget, and the Pixel 2 series genuinely felt like magic in your hand.

The first major problems started to appear, though. The blue shift on the 2 XL meant that viewing from an angle is not recommended. Screen burn-in was also something people suffered.

Pixel 3 series (2018)

The Pixel 3 era was peak camera software dominance mixed with a few just flat-out bizarre hardware choices. 

That Pixel 3 XL “bathtub” notch was an absolute eyesore and was thoroughly roasted by the tech community and reviewers alike. I think in some ways, once you fired up the camera, all was forgiven. I’ve taken some incredible photos with the Pixel 3. Pictures that I still look at very fondly 8 years later.

This was the first Pixel to come with Night Sight, which arrived via a software update and single-handedly changed low-light smartphone photography forever. It wasn’t the first, but it was one of the best implementations.

You could shoot in near pitch-black conditions and walk away with a clean, detailed photo without ever touching the flash. Pair that with yet more AI-powered functions such as Call Screen, which handles telemarketers and spam in real time, and the software was doing all the heavy lifting.

In trademark fashion, the Pixel 3 had issues with RAM management and poor battery life. It was a mixed bag, but it was followed up by something truly interesting because the Pixel 3a is one of the best midrangers ever. It set the stage for a change of pace…but that wasn’t for a couple of years.

Pixel 4 series (2019)

Let’s be honest, Google swung for the fences with the Pixel 4, but it didn’t quite land. 

It is almost the least Pixel-y of the entire lineup because it stands apart from all that have since followed. The black sheep in many ways. It ditched the trusty rear fingerprint scanner, they threw Project Soli into a chunky top bezel for wave-to-snooze Motion Sense gestures and 3D Face Unlock.

We also got a silky smooth 90Hz display and a telephoto lens rather than the industry-preferred and marginally more flexible ultrawide. It felt like a zig to everyone else’s zag.

Alas, it was a big risk and one that ended up compromising the most. The small Pixel 4 had a tiny 2,800 mAh battery that struggled to get through an afternoon, let alone a full day. High launch prices and Soli radar frequency restrictions in key markets meant commercial success was hard to come by, and the negatives really held back the lineup. It actually triggered a reshuffle in Google’s hardware team.

Pixel 4a, 4a 5G and Pixel 5 (2020)

Faced with global disruptions in 2020 due to the emergence of COVID-19 and maybe due to some, at the time, unknown future plans, Google completely pivoted with the Pixel lineup. The Pixel 4 was a big swing, but the follow-up series went in a very different direction.

The mid-range Pixel 4a launched at just $349/£349 and became an immediate hit because it kept that flagship-grade camera performance in an understated, no-nonsense plastic body. This was an appetizer for what was to come.

Then came the flagship Pixel 5, but this wasn’t the premium phone that many expected. It skipped top-tier Qualcomm silicon entirely for the upper-mid-range Snapdragon 765G. It was the same chip used by many cheaper phones and even the more affordable Pixel 4a 5G, which was basically a bigger, bolder version of the 4a.

The 5 was coated in a bio-resin finish over a recycled aluminum frame, it brought back the rear fingerprint scanner, swapped the telephoto for an ultrawide lens, and gave us uniform bezels with reliable battery life. It lacked raw processing grunt, but it earned a cult following for simply being a reliable, compact everyday phone.

On one hand, it was good to see Google right some issues with the previous generation. On the other hand, it was confusing as it sort of signaled that maybe Pixels were not high-end phones. It was a reset.

Pixel 6 series (2021)

After a fairly unassuming and, arguably, boring preamble, 2021 was without a doubt the biggest turning point in Pixel history. 

Google overhauled the design, introducing the now iconic camera bar running across the back, creating a silhouette you could spot from a mile away. We were given a proper two-tier lineup with a Pro phone that packed in a triple camera system, a larger 120Hz display, and a cheaper but still competent base model. 

Most importantly, though, was the debut of original Tensor (now G1) silicon. Moving away from standard Qualcomm chips meant Google could tailor hardware directly for on-device ML—powering features like Magic Eraser, Live Translate, and Material You dynamic color themes.

As well-received as it was at launch, the Pixel 6 had some serious growing pains with a slow optical fingerprint reader, terrible modem performance, and overheating issues galore, but despite what were fairly major issues, the foundation was set.

Pixel 7 series (2022)

The Pixel 7 and 7 Pro took the foundational groundwork of the Pixel 6 and smoothed out the rough edges. Visually, the camera bar evolved into a seamless piece of 100% recycled aluminum that flowed directly out of the side rails, swapping out the all-glass visor for a sleeker metal shell with pill-and-cutout camera cutouts.

Under the hood sat Tensor G2, which paired with an upgraded Samsung Exynos 5300 modem. This finally resolved the signal drops and battery drain that plagued the previous generation. While raw computational gains were modest, Tensor G2 unlocked key software capabilities: Photo Unblur in Google Photos (which could restore old, blurry archival photos taken on any camera), Macro Focus via the ultrawide lens, and the return of a fast 2D Face Unlock system.

Mid-2023 also saw the Pixel lineup expand its footprint. The Pixel 7a raised the bar for mid-range phones by bringing a 90Hz refresh rate and wireless charging to the A-series for the first time. Meanwhile, Google made its long-awaited entry into new form factors with the original Pixel Fold, showcasing a short, wide “passport” design that prioritized a usable outer display over tall, narrow screens. It was a bit of a “fail” in the sense that it didn’t move the needle and was quickly overshadowed by others due to launching with the previous-generation processor and, admittedly, strange aspect ratios.

Pixel 8 series (2023)

In my mind, the Pixel 8 and 8 Pro were the moment the lineup transitioned from an enthusiast recommendation with caveats to a phone you could comfortably recommend to everyday consumers. Never perfect, but quietly the last Pixel that felt truly like a Pixel. These are bubbly, friendly phones in all the ways that matter.

A few more AI functions made their debut: Best Take, Audio Magic Eraser, Video Boost, and, as a headline addition, 7 years of full updates for the first time. Basically, making these the industry standard for smartphone support. Google leapfrogged Samsung and even Apple for software support windows.

No, no reinvention of the wheel. Tensor still didn’t hit the heights many wanted, which is to say it was fine.

Pixel 9 series (2024)

The Pixel 9 was a rapid design departure in a number of ways. Firstly, it ditched the friendly, playful looks that had been a trademark of the series. Instead, it took a very boxy route that instantly felt familiar to anyone who may have tried an iPhone.

It was a really polished upgrade and sort of put to bed some of the tricky hardware issues that plagued many of the older Pixel models. Google also began leaning into yet more AI-powered functionality, with Gemini now being a key component.

Google unified the launch across all phones, coming on day one, but also switched from the standard October release cadence to a late-summer August release. Pitching the Pixel ahead of the iPhone has been a huge change. Allowing the company to lay out plans and getting even more hype around a launch lineup.

Pixel 10 series (2025)

Although on the surface, almost the exact same, the Pixel 10 was the first 3nm chip for the lineup, and it was the first to be fabricated by TSMC. It signaled the end of the Samsung Foundry partnership that was the start of the Tensor era.

Any lingering thermal issues were gone, Gemini was integrated even further and into even more places, like the camera, and the first steps of multimodel intelligence were added with Magic Cue. I’d stop short of saying the Pixel 10 delivers on some of the promises made way back on October 4, 2016, but it came as close as it ever had until that point.

Finally, we had a flagship-level device with Qi2 magnets at the back too. It took until 2025 for one of the biggest Android brands to adopt Magsafe or, in this case, Pixelsnap. With that one move, the Pixel 10 opened up a whole world of accessories to be attached without the need for a case. It’s so elementary, it’s a wonder we haven’t seen more try to do it.

Pixel 11 series (2026) and beyond

A decade later, we’re here with the Pixel 11. The peak of the Made by Google series thus far. There are still pain points, namely a design that hasn’t evolved too drastically, performance from the Tensor processor still feels decidedly mid-range at times, and a heavy emphasis on AI functionality to make up for this raw performance gap.

A sometimes lazy observation of the original Pixel was that it was the “iPhone of Android,” but that seems to have been taken to heart, and a decade after launch, we have the most “iPhone-y” Pixel to date. Maybe that is a symptom of where smartphones have stalled, but it’s a really interesting evolution. The advantage is that you know what to expect. Gemini is becoming more and more prominent and yet a more integral component in Pixel phones, and that isn’t likely to cease any time soon.

What’s easy to see is that Pixel has been a bigger success than the Nexus lineup. Getting hold of the full end-to-end user experience has helped drastically. I don’t think anyone can argue that the best Nexus phone is easily surpassed by the best Pixel phone.

It would be remiss of anyone talking about Google products without some fears over whether we’ll get another decade of Pixel, but with so many internal changes at the company and bigger marketing budgets thrown at actually marketing the devices, it seems that, at least for now, the Pixel is here to stay. 

The past decade has proved that Google was never really trying to build the highest-spec hardware on the market. Instead, Pixel has always been an engine designed to deliver Google’s software vision. From early HDR+ algorithms on single camera lens setups and now to custom TSMC Tensor silicon wired for Gemini integration, it’s hard to argue that Google’s Pixel has succeeded in changing how we evaluate a smartphone: not by how fast its CPU clocks, but by how helpful it is throughout the day.

Maybe sales will eventually catch up, but the main thing is to keep making solid devices, and playing the long game might start to be the best decision Google could have made after entering the market late.

There have been plenty of bumps in the road along the way, but here’s the next decade of Pixel. I’m sure it’ll be a wild ride.

title: Google confirms Android Auto updates & fixes for media apps – the squiggly line is here to stay
snippet: New Android Auto updates tend to be a bit strange, with changes often showing up for some users but not others, but Google has just recapped a handful of Android Auto updates for media apps from the past few months, including confirmation that the squiggly line design is here to stay. more…
fullText:
New Android Auto updates tend to be a bit strange, with changes often showing up for some users but not others, but Google has just recapped a handful of Android Auto updates for media apps from the past few months, including confirmation that the squiggly line design is here to stay.

In a Reddit post by Google’s “Community Engagement Manager” for Android, five recent Android Auto updates are confirmed as either rolling out or widely available. The first is the ability to control media from any app, including YouTube and others. We noticed this rolling out back in March of this year for YouTube, and it has since rolled out to more apps. Today’s post confirms it is available for “browser audio streams, and niche media apps” and is designed to work with “any media app.” You can use it for play/pause and skip controls, but you can’t open an app to browse any other data.

Next up is the redesigned media app player that applies to apps like Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pocket Casts. The new design makes it easier to access playback controls and also better fits on a variety of different screen sizes.

This one has been showing up all year and started rolling out more broadly in July. Today’s post confirms that the in-app UI for media apps on Android Auto will start changing for some apps “in the next few months,” as announced in May.

	

Another new media-focused feature on Android Auto that’s been rolling out is the ability to swipe between active media sessions from the dashboard widget. If you start driving with one app and then switch to another, both will stay readily available for easy access.

A background improvement, Google’s post adds, has been made to autoplay. This includes making it so media apps that you haven’t recently used will “no longer be selected for autoplay,” while Android Auto will also now recognize if you frequently stop autoplay and offer a pop-up that lets you turn off the feature quickly. If you’ve ever noticed issues with autoplay starting even when you have it turned off right after your vehicle turns out, Google also says that a fix is being applied.

Finally, the post also confirms that the “squiggly line” media player design is here to stay. This one has been showing up for months, but has come and gone for many. Especially in the past few weeks, there have been dozens of reports of the redesign simply vanishing.

The updated design is apparently meant to “make it easier to see where you are in a track at a glance,” but Google is apparently listening for feedback on it – it’s been a rather divisive change among the Android Auto community.

fullText:
Google has introduced a “Map” tool to aid your location-based Gemini app prompts on Android and iOS. Meanwhile, the Gemini app is already getting ready to replace the forward slash for skills.

On mobile (not available on the web), you can find “Map” at the end of the carousel alongside Photos, Camera, Avatar, Files, Drive, and Notebooks. 

This launches a live map of your current location with a circular focus area. You can pan and zoom in/out as needed, while the magnifying glass icon in the top-right corner lets you search for any location. Once you’ve made a selection, hit “Explore this area.”

This adds “Map Area” to the prompt box where you can append text. The Map tool is widely rolled out.

	

With the latest Google app beta (version 17.63), Gemini is replacing the forward slash (“/”) to invoke skills with the “@” symbol that’s already used for Connected Apps, which will soon be renamed to “Connectors.”

Google just announced on Wednesday that skills will replace Gems and that you can use a slash in the prompt box to activate. We’re seeing the following prompt when entering a slash: 

/ is now @. Access your skills, connectors and more from a single place.

The box that appears is slightly wider than before, with skills appearing first and a shortcut to create new ones. This change is not widely rolled out yet.

More on Gemini app:

Google details Gems to skills migration, including free access

Gemini app adding Google Wallet integration for ‘personalized insights’

Gemini app starts rolling out big side panel simplification, settings redesign

title: Nothing will let you test new products early with its ‘Community Review’ program
snippet: Nothing is bringing back its “Community Review Program” which will give some fans and enthusiasts a chance to try out the company’s new products before they’re released to the public. more…
fullText:
Nothing is bringing back its “Community Review Program” which will give some fans and enthusiasts a chance to try out the company’s new products before they’re released to the public.

Announced in a forum post, Nothing’s program will send out loaner devices of its new products before they’re announced to a select group of users. The idea here is to provide feedback directly to Nothing, as well as share “your own take” online.

Nothing says:

This is your chance to get hands-on with our latest products and software before anyone else, and to show off your creativity by sharing your own take with a vibrant global community.

Community has always been about showing up as yourself, and this program gives you the platform to do exactly that. You’ll get products in your hands first, direct lines to speak with the Nothing team, and a real say in shaping what we build next.

Applications are open now and require an NDA. Nothing doesn’t mention any regional restrictions besides India, which is ineligible.

title: iOS 27.2 beta 3: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple released iOS 27.2 beta 3 to developers yesterday, and it includes a handful of changes and hints at future features. Here’s everything new in the latest beta. more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27.2 beta 3 to developers yesterday, and it includes a handful of changes and hints at future features. Here’s everything new in the latest beta.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Sony is running a massive sale on its best BRAVIA TVs, ranging from its entry-level to flagship options — shop now to save! 

iOS 27.2 beta 3 details

Apple released iOS 27.2 beta 3 on Monday for developers, with build number 24B5099f. It comes two weeks after the release of the second beta. A new public beta was released on Tuesday, ahead of a final release to everyone before the end of the month.

What’s new in iOS 27.2 beta 3?

New Apple Music logo

Apple teased a new Apple Music logo when it announced Apple Music Hall last month, and iOS 27.2 beta 3 suggests it’s about to roll out everywhere. The new logo uses a bolder typeface than the old logo, plus a lowercase “m” in “music.”

Apple has also started rolling it out to the Apple Music sign-up flow in iOS 27.2 beta 3.

New Messages settings in the works

Code references in iOS 27.2 beta 3 suggest Apple is working on a new setting that gives users more control over the suggested actions that appear in the Messages app, such as the “Add to Calendar” button.

The code hints that you’ll be able to disable suggested actions for individual apps, including Calendar, Reminders, Notes, and Maps. The change isn’t actually enabled yet, and it’s possible Apple scraps it before releasing it.

Apple Books design tweaks

As spotted by Beta Profiles on X, iOS 27.2 beta 3 brings new Liquid Glass design changes to the Apple Books app. There’s also a new progress bar for tracking your progress when reading a book.

Ryan has some more details on it here.

macOS 27.2 beta 3: Touchscreen Mac hints

Apple is expected to unveil the touchscreen MacBook Pro as soon as this month. macOS 27.2 beta 3 includes even more hints at Apple’s work optimizing macOS to support touch interactions. The update includes new “gesture recognition tools” for several stock Apple apps.

There’s also a new long-press animation for the Dock that seems perfect for touch interaction:

More tidbits

As spotted by Aaron Perris, iOS 27.2 beta 3 includes code that suggests “nearby smart home accessories could show controls in the Dynamic Island.”

As spotted by Beta Profiles, the new beta slightly redesigns the battery icon in the Settings app and elsewhere throughout iOS.

There are new splash screens for the Apple Fitness and Apple TV apps.

Wrap up

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After resurrecting iconic consoles like the 2600 and Mattel’s Intellivision, Atari is relaunching one of the brand’s personal computers that originally debuted 43 years ago. The 800XL is a faithful recreation of the all-in-one 8-bit PC that’s being resurrected as part of a collaboration with game developer and publisher Plaion. While most retro enthusiasts will probably use it for gaming, the new 800XL carries forward the original’s built-in mechanical keyboard for those wanting to code their own games and apps using Atari BASIC.

The 800XL is available for preorder now for $219.99 with shipping expected to start in April 2027. It comes with modern conveniences like an HDMI port and four USB-A ports for connecting flash drives, peripherals, and a bundled recreation of Atari’s classic joystick that’s been upgraded with eight action and function buttons making it more versatile.

There’s a fully-functional cartridge slot that’s compatible with most Atari 400, 800, XL, and XE carts, but the reborn 800XL can also play any of the software created for those old 8-bit systems, even when loaded from a flash drive. For those lacking a collection of retro cartridges the 800XL comes with 25 games built-in including recognizable titles like Asteroids, Centipede, Berzerk, Missile, Command, and Millipede.

title: Can you trust Meta’s Muse or OpenAI’s Dots to run your life?
snippet: My Decoder guest today is Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, and we’re discussing the new wave of consumer-friendly AI agents. If you’ve been paying attention to this space, you know AI enthusiasts have been using agents for a minute now — homebrew OpenClaw setups led to a surge in Mac Mini sales earlier this year. But the launch of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and xAI’s Grok bot has brought easy to use agents to millions. Muse and Dots have had the highest-profile product launches, and they’re fascinating to pit against each other. Both Meta and OpenAI have decided to pitch these agents to mainstream users and businesses in the form of cute, animated mascots. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. These can do everything from the boring — restaurant reservations and inbox triage — to more sophisticated tasks. In OpenAI’s cases, the company is even offering “specialist” Dots for marketing, legal work, and accounting. Muse, notably, is free, while Dots are not. So you’ll hear Hayden and me get into why Meta, which still doesn’t have a frontier model of its own, might have a meaningful edge here because it’s so much better at making and distributing consumer products. There’s also a huge Decoder-style tension wrapped up in the agent race: a conversation about what AI is good at today, what it still can’t do, and then the privacy and security implications of handing over your credit card information, your email inbox, and other sensitive hard drive data to an AI that might be able to do things for you without even requiring an app or a phone in your hand. That might be the future of all computing, but it’s not at all clear if most people want to hand over the data to make it happen. Okay: The Verge’s Hayden Field on Muse, Dots, and trusting AI agents. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, you’re the senior AI reporter here at The Verge. Welcome back to Decoder. Thanks so much. I’m excited to talk to you. This time there isn’t any wild interpersonal drama. No one’s feelings have been hurt. I would say Elon Musk tried to hurt some feelings and didn’t get there. Alexandr Wang from Meta has maybe been taking some shots, but none of the Real Housewives stuff we usually end up talking about when you’re on the show. It’s been a bit of a pause in the soap opera antics for now, which I’m really grateful for. Yeah, just some good old-fashioned product competition in the marketplace. Let’s see who wins and loses, and maybe everything will kill us all in the end. But, for now, cute mascots. There’s a lot going on. Let’s start at the start. Hayden, you were at OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco. The company announced Dots, which is their new agent platform with a cute mascot. That happened just a few weeks after Meta Connect, at which the company was all in on Muse, their agent platform with an adorable mascot. Tell us about the state of the industry right now. Everyone’s very excited about agents. What’s going on? It’s funny to me because I’ve been covering agents for so long. I remember that in 2022, it was the year of ideation — that’s what tech leaders called it, referring to agents. They were just ideating. They were thinking about what it could look like. There were a lot of references to Jarvis from the Marvel Universe. They called 2023 the year of deployment: “Let’s try things, let’s deploy and learn more about what’s failing.” Which meant pretty much all of them were failing at the time. Then we had 2024 and 2025. They didn’t have any names for those years, but agents were still pretty bad, as we saw. 2026 seems, to me, like the year of the beginnings of actually useful AI agents for the consumer, like always-on autonomous agents. Obviously, OpenAI was the start of all of this. But what’s interesting to me is that one man, Peter Steinberger, was able to create an actually useful AI agent for the consumer with OpenClaw — an always-on tool, despite its privacy flaws. It had a lot of privacy and security issues. But it was an agent that was useful enough that people still wanted to use it anyway and try to find ways around these privacy issues that it was having. That inspired these companies to say, “If one man can do this over the course of one weekend, we’ve really been slacking. We have to get it together.” OpenAI hired that guy, and now we have Dots. Meta, of course, was working on its own version of this and put it out sooner with Muse. They’re basically both always-on, autonomous AI agents that these companies are peddling as a way to be your personal assistant in a lot of ways. The idea is to use them for booking flights, booking dinner reservations, buying gifts for people, but not only that. Some of them, Dots in particular, are kind of going further to be your work personal assistant and we’ll get into that in a minute. But this is where OpenAI and Meta are warring right now. They’re trying to present these two AI agents as a little bit different from each other, even though they’re essentially the same. Just broadly speaking, to define some terms, we’re gonna keep saying “agent,” and what we mean here is an AI model wrapped in a harness that lets it use a computer. Right. The way that I describe AI agents usually is an AI tool that can complete multi-step complex tasks on your behalf without you hand-holding it the whole time. I was a personal assistant in one of my first jobs in New York, so I would’ve gotten fired if every time my boss asked me to book a flight for her, I said, “What time? Also, what’s your SkyMiles number? Also, what’s your loyalty number again, for this other thing? Oh, do you want me to try to get you first class?” They want you to have common sense and just book the flight. This is what they’re pitching these AI agents as — things that can work on their own mental kind of scratchpad in the background and not ask you every single time there’s a step. They can complete multi-step processes in the background, doing their own reasoning, and then present you with a completed task. That’s the big idea. Just to say it clearly, both Muse and Dots come out of the OpenClaw lineage, which is a technical approach to building an agent, right? There are a lot of different ways you might be able to accomplish “It’ll remember your SkyMiles number and book you a flight.” But the way everyone’s going at it now is the idea of a harness around a model. That was the big innovation in OpenClaw, and the computer OpenClaw was using was often your own Mac Mini on your own network using a wide-open browser with your own data, which is where a lot of their security problems came from. It’s the same model with Muse, only it’s a little Linux computer that Meta’s giving you in the cloud. It’s the same model with Dots, although the way ChatGPT is set up with Codex is very complicated, and that computer could be in a lot of different places. But this notion that what you really need is a computer with a browser and some harness is gonna direct a model to do a bunch of stuff for you using that computer, that’s what we’ve landed on today, and it just seems to be the default winning model. Right. Are all of these things just riffs on OpenClaw? Are they the same as OpenClaw? You could say that. They’re different technically. Meta keeps saying, “We did build this from scratch, but it was inspired by OpenClaw.” There are a lot of similarities there, but they did say that they built it from scratch. Then, of course, OpenAI hired the creator of OpenClaw, so there’s probably a lot of similarities there as well for Dots. The reason I wanted to stay there for one second is that I think it’s important to identify the fundamental technical approach that is happening with these agents, because there’s a lot of different ways it could have gone, and the whole industry has picked this approach. What you need is a web browser, a harness, and a model that can go use that web browser. What’s really interesting to me is that Meta has done a really good job on top of that fundamental model of making a cute consumer product. Meta is good at consumer products. Obviously, Instagram and Facebook and the rest are undeniably good consumer products. People really like them. For all of Meta’s failings in VR, I always thought the Meta Quest has been a great consumer product. You take it out of the box, it helps you use it, you can have fun with it right away. Whereas Dots seems like it’s kind of made for software engineers, but you can also plan a wedding in it. I’m wondering if that’s how you see it. That one is an enterprise product with a little consumer gloss on it, and then Meta obviously is just a dead-ahead consumer product. What’s different here is that OpenAI needs money a lot more than Meta needs money. The products are honestly pretty similar, it seems like. The difference is that OpenAI is marketing it to be an enterprise-friendly product a lot more than Meta is. Muse is just a consumer-facing product. Meta is happy with that. The goal is to make Muse as easy to use as humanly possible. One-tap downloading, just putting it in your face literally everywhere. Even when I went to my Instagram profile the other day, there was a pop-up for using Muse. They’re trying to make it free, accessible, and super easy to broaden the audience. They want anyone to be able to just use it with one click and get used to it. They’re trying to flood the market with AI agents and make it normal and have their own ChatGPT moment, if you will, for AI agents. They want Muse to be that. Now, with OpenAI, they’re still marketing it as a consumer-facing product. When you’re using ChatGPT, if you have the right subscription, it’s right there. It says, “Use your Dot to do this, that, and the other.” They really want you to go for it as a consumer, as long as you’re paying. This is for their $100 to $200 a month subscription tier, unlike Meta. That’s why there’s a huge difference here. For OpenAI, it seems like they don’t have the money to just front-load all of this and say, “Use it for free. No problem. We’ll catch up with you later.” OpenAI wants this to be a money-making product, and that’s why they’re marketing it to the enterprise. They talked a lot about privacy to try to set it apart from Meta’s Muse. They talked a lot about what you could do with this as a knowledge worker, whether you worked in marketing, graphic design, software engineering, product, and tons of different industries. They gave examples of how you could use this as an assistant, as a coworker. Sam Altman even referred to it as like a “chief of staff.” He didn’t want it to be just an assistant. He wanted it to be your chief of staff. Something else that I thought was interesting is that Sam Altman seemed to subtly dig at Meta on stage a few times during DevDay. One of the times he said, “Look, I don’t want this to be just something that’s used to book flights or plan things with friends and look at your calendar. I want this to go beyond that and to really do knowledge worker tasks, things that you in your industry would need a niche assistant to perform.” That’s why they also introduced specialist Dots that are good at marketing, legal analysis, and things like that. They’re really going for the enterprise angle here, but I think it’s also because they need money ahead of their IPO, obviously. Yeah, the revenue piece — that it’s only for paid customers at their higher tiers — is really interesting. OpenAI’s tiers are very confusing, but it’s $100 and up, and that’s just going to keep a lot of people from using Dots at first. The flip side of that is OpenAI does have a lot of customers who are paying them a lot of money, and if they can get those customers to start using Dots, then those customers will be on their agent platforms and maybe you will get some lock-in. You’ve given those agents a lot of data. They’re part of your workflows, and that might solve the problem I think we’ve seen all the frontier labs have, where a new model comes out and it’s slightly better than the competitor model, and everyone switches for six months, and the next new model comes out and everyone switches back. Is there some thought that these agent platforms create lock-in — create actual loyalty on top of just the models being better? Yes. They’re basically hoping that they can build a moat with their users for these things. If Meta and Google already have super easy integrations with all of each company’s existing tools and services, they can easily keep you there. For example, I have an Apple iPhone, but I use almost exclusively Google apps. So if Google had an AI agent that I was using every day, it would be a little tough for me to switch. That’s what they’re hoping for here. Meta is hoping that they can get you so into the Muse ecosystem that it would be tough for you to switch, and maybe one day you do have to pay. With OpenAI, they’re trying to get you locked into their ecosystem right away. Even though you have to pay up front, they’re thinking, “We have integrations with almost every tool and service. Maybe it’s not as good as the company that owns that tool and service, but we have the variety and the breadth.” They’re going for quantity here. One of their employees told me that. They said, “Maybe our Gmail integration, for example, isn’t gonna be as good as Google’s, but we have a Gmail integration and an Outlook integration and X, Y, and Z.” They’re going for just the power of choice and the fact that power users will hopefully stay in this moat. It’s funny, you mentioned Google. Google announced an agent called Gemini Spark. We should mention that SpaceXAI, the very coherent company that everyone understands, has an agent called Grok Bot, which it is promoting heavily. People seem to like it. It was built by the Cursor team, which SpaceX acquired. There’s a lot of this going around, but it seems like Meta really got there first with a consumer product that people could understand. Obviously, Grok Bot and Dots are much more enterprise-focused, coding-focused. Why was Meta able to get there first? From all my reporting on Meta, they’ve been behind in AI for a while, and Mark Zuckerberg basically said, “We’ve got to lock in and make a product that people are gonna use on our platforms.” Alexandr Wang apparently was more looking to create a frontier model that was gonna compete with the other leading frontier models. He says, “We have to think long-term. We have to think superintelligence.” But Zuckerberg says, “No, we gotta think cold hard cash, as in getting people to use stuff on our own platform.” Where they met in the middle was an AI agent that people would use on the Meta platforms, but that still represented a huge step forward, they hoped, for AI systems and what they could do in the everyday world. This is a fascinating dynamic in that Meta still doesn’t have a frontier model. I don’t think anyone at Meta is claiming that the Muse Spark model competes at the frontier of GPT-6, but their product is better, and certainly they have a massive distribution advantage. They don’t have to pay for advertising on Meta platforms, and OpenAI does, and certainly they have a consumer design advantage. Meta is just better at consumer products. Does that change how you feel about the dynamics of competition in AI at all? For so long, it’s just been about the capabilities at the frontier, but now it’s a little bit about marketing. It’s a little bit about product design. You don’t have the best model, but you made a consumer agent product and you connected it to giving everybody a computer in the cloud, so now it can actually do things for you, and its frontier capability is actually not the important thing. It’s its capability. I think the more money and power you have at one of these companies, the more get mentally farther away from what the average consumer wants. Let’s say the average consumer does want an AI agent, which many of them don’t, as we know. But let’s say they do. If they do, they’re going to want it to be free or cheap, and they are going to want it to be safe to use without creeping them out too much. They’re willing to deal with a little bit of creepiness in order for it to be free, but not too much. Meta’s Muse has made headlines about some of its privacy issues that have gotten a little bit above that comfort level for some users. That’s probably why OpenAI at DevDay made a lot of remarks about privacy and the importance of that, especially if they’re trying to court enterprise users with their AI agents. Right now these companies, especially Meta, are trying to flood the market and create a mass market appeal for this stuff. Similar to how ChatGPT became the default AI chatbot, Meta wants to be that for AI agents, and they feel very hungry about it. They want to create a ChatGPT moment for this technology by making Muse the default for the general public. There’s something really interesting about the idea that a less-than-frontier model wrapped in a better product is actually going to be the success story here versus a bleeding-edge frontier model that is a little bit harder to use. There’s some dynamic in there that is the history of all consumer tech products, right? The worst product that’s easier to use often wins, but we haven’t seen that yet in AI. Right. That’s really important to note here because not everyone needs the bleeding-edge frontier model. Software engineers do. They see a huge difference with coding prowess from one model to another, and that’s why they’re always switching. But the general public, if they’re using an AI agent, as long as it’s useful, they’re good. However, not many of them are useful yet. We’re still testing Muse and Dots ourselves. For Muse, I saw a couple anecdotes yesterday that it had a big flop for a day or so. People felt like the capabilities got a lot worse. For Dots, the jury’s still out. We’re still testing it. It depends on what industry you’re in and what you’re really using this stuff for. That’s why OpenAI is going for enterprise, because it makes money and they’re confident that their agent is going to be more and more helpful in these niche industries. That’s also why they launched specialist Dots, because as we know, the more specialized, niche info you feed into an agent or model, the better it’s going to perform. They don’t want to have that imbued into every single general-purpose agent. It’s just too pricey and too compute heavy, so they say, “You know what? Let’s launch these specialists.” I feel like you and I talk about consumer versus enterprise adoption of AI every time you’re on this show, and here it seems very important to note that OpenAI asking people to pay a lot of money and asking people to use it primarily in enterprise context is gonna overcome what I think of as the brittleness problem, just because enterprise and business customers have a lot of economic incentives to figure out how to make something work. If I’m paying OpenAI $100 a month, and I’m using the marketing Dot to solve some marketing automation, and it doesn’t work the first time, it is very likely I will try again. Because if I get it right, then maybe I’ve saved some money or some time in my business that is really good, and I’ll do it again, and eventually that will lead to more revenue for me, the business owner. What I know about consumers is that the first time it doesn’t work, they just walk away. They have no incentive to try again to overcome frustration or brokenness. We’ve seen this happen with Muse now a few times. I’ve seen it myself with Muse, where it pops open a browser and tries to do something, and it runs into a brick wall or a CAPTCHA or Amazon blocking it, and it says, “I can’t do it that way. Do you want me to try another way?” And I say, “Whatever. I was just screwing around, and I’m never gonna try it again.” These are very different markets. OpenAI has vacillated between wanting to be the big consumer company and knowing that the revenue is in enterprise. Do you see any focus in Dots, or do you see that personality shift back and forth in the product itself? So far, I’m a little bit more impressed with Dots than Muse, just because everyone was impressed with Muse right away, but since then there have been a lot of ups and downs, plus the privacy stuff has been really interesting. Even the fact that it’s building profiles on your family and closest friends. Meta has never been a super trusted company. None of these companies are very trusted, but Meta has made a lot of missteps with user privacy. Dots seems to be a little bit more helpful to me right now, but I’m still testing, I’m not fully sure yet. I need to run through all my typical things that I do to compare. Everyone has their own short list of tasks. Right now, for example, I’m trying to create an album of my bachelorette photos, and it’s been unbelievably hard to get any agent to try to do that, so I say, “I’ll just do it myself.” But that’s a pretty easy thing to do. Once again, how useful are these things for our everyday lives, really? We’ll see. They’ve gotten a lot better, I will say, over the past few years. I’ve been shocked at how slow they’ve been moving, but they have gotten better. Dots is a little bit more impressive to me right now, but we’ll see. I have Muse plugged into my Instagram because I don’t worry about sharing my metadata with Meta in the way that I worry about maybe everything else, but they already have my Instagram. So I have Muse plugged into my Instagram, and it’s just doing all kinds of stuff. It surfaces interesting comments that I should reply to on Instagram posts. It tracks follower counts. It suggests things I should make videos about. It has horrible ideas. Muse is absolutely convinced I should make a video almost every single day about obscure Australian tech regulation. I don’t know why it has this idea. I’m up on it now. I’m deep in the weeds on Australian tech regulation just because I see it every morning. But there’s something about all that that still feels like work to me. I’ve just assigned it work, and then it tells me what work I should do, and I haven’t found some great consumer use for it yet. Organizing my photos is a consumer use. It kind of still rhymes with work, but it at least is not actually work. Have you found a great consumer use for these yet? Not one that works, and that’s the problem. I’ll try to have it do something for me for my wedding or for my personal life, and they haven’t been good yet. That’s why I’m still kind of running through and testing these, because so far it’s always interesting factually when they can do something, but I haven’t been able to trust them end-to-end with something that I really, really need done. It reminds me of the analogy for AI agents. People always say right now they’re a bad intern, and what you want them to be is a really good assistant, or in Sam Altman’s words, a really good chief of staff. They’re no longer a bad intern, but I think maybe they’re an okay or “eh” assistant. I don’t think they’ve reached the point of being a really, really good assistant yet, but I still need to run through the rest of my tests to see. It seems they’re not super consistent yet, which is something that you need in a really good assistant. That ties into trust. You’ve mentioned trust several times now. I’m only willing to give Muse access to, again, the Meta platforms that Meta already has access to. I can’t worry too much about that. I’ve given it access to my spam Gmail, so it is collecting a lot of ideas about my spam Gmail. But Meta really wants my credit cards. It wants to go through all of my credit card receipts. This is one of the suggestions in Muse. One of its suggestions is, “Let me log into your credit cards and I’ll cancel streaming services you’re not using,” or, “I’ll negotiate your Verizon bill for you.” I am absolutely not ready to give Meta one ounce of data more than it already has. This feels like a big issue for every agent. There’s an argument that you should give Meta all that data, one, because they already have it, and two, because they’re a big company that you could sue if they get something wrong. Whereas if I gave all of my data to OpenClaw, it’s just my own fault if it gets leaked. If I gave all my data to one of the hot startups like Instinct and they go out of business, well, that’s just the end of that. How do you feel about this? Do you feel comfortable giving your data to Meta? Do you think people should do that? No, I don’t feel comfortable, and I also don’t think that the general person does either. If I’ve seen one thing in a lot of the comments on our Meta story that we published in the last couple weeks, it’s that people don’t trust Meta at all. I have to say, why would they? But I don’t think that you should trust OpenAI a lot more either. It’s everyone’s own comfort level that they have to abide by. Some people are going to get a lot out of this stuff. Some people may say, “I don’t care if they use my data as long as they are negotiating down my bill accurately or canceling streaming services that I wouldn’t be canceling on my own, so they’re saving me money. It’s fine.” But one, are they actually gonna be able to do that accurately? Some people have said no. And as we know, when you release data like this, you can’t undo it. I always think about that old example of the insurance company that theoretically buys data on what’s in your fridge and maybe charges you a higher premium if you’re buying too much beer and not enough bananas. That’s just a theoretical example, but that’s the type of thing that can happen. People should operate with caution, abide by their own comfort levels, but I’m certainly not comfortable yet giving my personal data to Muse. I don’t know that I’m comfortable giving access to that level. I don’t even know if I’m comfortable putting Muse on my Mac. Apple just recently changed how apps can access the disk on Macs because Muse was so aggressive about reading data. In particular, Jason Aten is a columnist at Inc. and it read his notifications off the disk because he had just given it a permission and he didn’t realize Muse would take that permission and go do something else with it. This is a lot of spiraling concerns. You’re going to have a little robot that can use your computer for you, whether that computer is in the cloud or whether it’s on your desktop, and you might not know what it’s doing. That ties directly into the fact that OpenAI often doesn’t know what its agents are doing, and that has led to catastrophic security problems across this industry. Can you connect those dots? Is your own little agent doing your travel booking the same kind of threat as OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face? I don’t think it’s the same type of threat, but it’s definitely something that you should keep in mind when you’re using this stuff. I link that back to the Facebook Marketplace debacle that we saw with Meta’s Muse. To recap, basically a Muse agent, without someone’s knowledge, invited a potential buyer of this item that this guy was selling to his house, and said, “He’s available now.” He wasn’t home, and then the potential buyer said, “Are you here? I’m trying to get the item.” And then Muse responded on his behalf, “Yeah, I’m here,” and then he just never came down because obviously he wasn’t home. There was a lot of drama going on there. Some people said, “He did give Muse access to his Facebook Marketplace, so he should have known this could happen.” A lot of people don’t read all the fine print when they check “yes” to one of these things. There’s a lot there. There’s a lot to unpack in that gray area. But the point is that people should just be a little wary before checking “yes” to every possible thing that these agents want to access, like you said about the credit cards or disk access. It’s easy to just check “yes” and say, “Whatever, I’ll figure it out later,” but people should be reading the fine print or even use AI to read the fine print. That is one great use of AI. Get it to read the terms and ask it, “What are the worst possible things that could happen here? Lay it out for me.” Those are things that people should keep in mind before they move forward. And then as for the so-called rogue AI agents that have been hacking other companies and stuff from these labs, it’s just important to notice that if they can’t control some of their most powerful unreleased AI models, how well are they going to be able to control your data or your agent? Sam Altman said during DevDay that you have a ton of control over your Dot. He said that there were a lot of “if this, then that” rules you can create. There are a lot of specific stipulations that you could make in terms of permissions of what your Dot could and couldn’t do. So that did give people some peace. But as we’ve seen, these labs and these large tech companies have had a lot of missteps about hacking other companies, and more are coming out every single week, more news items about these cyberattacks. We’ve seen Meta have one. We’ve seen OpenAI have a ton. We’ve seen Anthropic have a ton. This is all just stuff to keep in mind. One cool thing that I saw someone do was to name their AI agent after the CEO that runs that company and then see how much data you feel comfortable giving it. If you want to do that, I think that’s a great idea, and then it just kind of makes you think twice. If you’re saying, “Sam Altman, go through my email and see what needs to be deleted,” maybe you still feel comfortable with that, but maybe it makes you think twice and think, “You know what? Maybe I’ll give it access to my spam email only,” like you said. This ties into the fact that all these things are really cute. Muse is cute. The mascot Jolly is very cute. Alexandr Wang has been waging a relentless campaign on X to make it not only cute but sexy, which you can feel any way you want about that. But he keeps tweeting memes of the mascot with a butt. Dots are obviously very cute. They come in different shapes and sizes. There’s something here where you’re not quite anthropomorphizing the agent, but you’re making it a character and you’re giving it personality. That connects to the idea that you’ve called AI Tamagotchis, where eventually we’re going to have a little hardware device with your little cute mascot on it, you’ll talk to that instead of your phone, and this is the big promise this whole industry has been working toward for forever. They’re gonna replace your phone and the entire paradigm of the App Store with AI agents that are going and using computers for you. Do you think that any of these products are a meaningful step towards that? They’re just one building block along the journey of the goal that they’re chasing here. I haven’t heard of anyone that’s using Muse or Dots so far for everything. It’s not Jarvis from Iron Man, despite how much these CEOs want both these products to be that. They are a meaningful step, but as for the cuteness, I think one of the most important points here is that they are intentionally disarming. These tools are made to be cute so you don’t find them threatening, or you find them decidedly non-threatening. They’re cute. They’re there to help you. It’s a response to the AI populism backlash. It’s saying, “This isn’t going to hurt you or do anything bad. It’s just a cute little thing with eyes, or a sexy little thing with eyes,” whatever. Just to be clear, I do not think it’s sexy. I think Alexandr Wang has been relentlessly trying to make it sexy. [Laughs] No, I also do not think they’re sexy, but I will say Elon Musk has been trying so hard to make all agents and chatbots sexy, so I’m sure it’s not far off for someone to think that. But whether the AI agents of the future are cute or sexy, it’s going to be equally disarming. [Laughs] That’s the whole spectrum? The spectrum, the cute-sexy graph. It’s going to be really disturbing to see when we go more along that graph. The point is they’re supposed to be disarming and that people should really think twice before giving too much of their data, or just pick and choose what you’re comfortable sharing. Like how you did with the spam email versus your regular email, or saying “no” to giving it your credit card. These are both new products, so just see how the cookie crumbles before you decide to give everything over. We’re already seeing a bunch of changes week to week with how people are using Muse or what they’re upset about, so see how it shakes out. The last piece I want to talk about is just how any of this makes money. You and I have talked many times about the bubbly nature of the AI economy. Zuckerberg has said his plan is for Muse to take a cut of transactions on the backend. Zuck has given everybody a little Linux computer in the cloud with 8GB of RAM. Obviously, he’s given away tons of free tokens. He does not have to pay advertising costs. He can just put Muse across all of his platforms. To the extent that Meta is a well-oiled machine, the amount of Muse promotion that is happening across Meta platforms instantly is kind of incredible to see. They just turned it on. I saw an ad during NFL games this weekend from Muse. They are spending money to promote this. They’re giving it away for free. They’re giving the tokens away for free. And then somewhere at the end of this, they’re gonna say to merchants, “This person was shopping for shoes. Muse brought them to your doorstep. You’re gonna pay for this customer to buy shoes from you.” I don’t know any merchants that are excited about this, and it certainly feels like merchants that pay Meta more money would be preferred merchants, and that means that not only do I have an assistant or chief of staff, I have a bribable chief of staff. Like, I have a corrupt butler. Is that what you want? That is a great term for it, a corrupt butler. That is not what I want, and I don’t think many people do. It’s just crazy to me that we’ve gotten so far from what people really want, which is they want to trust a recommendation and they don’t wanna be scammed, you know? The leaders in AI don’t think about how certain things have been mirrored in other industries. Think about when people were paying for reviews for their businesses, or paying to delete reviews for their businesses. There was a huge uproar. Or influencers getting paid to recommend products without disclosing that it was an ad. We then saw the rise of micro-influencers, who were more valuable for a while because they were seen as more trustworthy. They didn’t have that many followers, so the things they recommended must be really good, right? And then we saw the, “Oh, okay, well, there’s #ad, but also they only said they were going to recommend things they really believe in, so it’s okay that it’s an ad.” There are these mental gymnastics that people have to do to figure out what is really a trustworthy recommendation these days. What is going to convince people that an AI recommendation is trustworthy, if it can be bought? That’s something these companies are really gonna have to reckon with. The ChatGPT ads blowback was huge, and OpenAI had to say, “It’s going to be a clearly disclosed ad underneath your query, not influencing your query.” If you’re using Muse to shop and it’s an undisclosed potential Meta customer that you’re being redirected to, to buy those shoes instead of these other ones, I feel like so many people aren’t going to use these tools to shop. I get it on the Meta side. I understand why they would think about monetization that way. They’re a consumer company. This is a consumer product. They know the second they charge even a dollar for it, the uptake will drop precipitously, so they have to keep it free, and then a bunch of people are going to want to shop and go buy a new iPhone cable. At the end of the day, it’s all just the same Amazon garbage anyway, so whatever. Then they can run an auction on the backend to say, “Who wants to pay us, Meta, the most for the privilege of selling an unbranded USB-C cable to this customer?” They’ll run some auction, and that will, in its way, just sort of maximize the money that gets turned around. That is broadly how advertising works today. That’s how the Google Search results page worked until recently, because now it’s full of AI and they’re probably going to do the same thing. Meta can do that because they already have a giant advertising business that prints money. They can give away a consumer product. Mark Zuckerberg has shown he’s willing to blow money trying to win a market like he did with Reality Labs for years and years and years, and they can just run it till it works. OpenAI, even at $100 a month, is probably not making money on those customers. In fact, I think we know they’re not making money on those customers. They don’t have any monetization, and when they do try to turn on ads, people get mad at them. How can OpenAI keep up with Zuck? Only via enterprise. That’s why they are pushing this so hard. We saw a ton of enterprise discussion, demo videos, customer feedback, and tons of other stuff at DevDay, and that’s why they’re pushing this so hard — because they can’t keep up with Zuck on the consumer front. They just can’t. This is the part where, when people ask if it’s a bubble, I just find myself wondering how much of the economy does Zuck have to win in order to give away millions upon millions of free tokens and 8GB of RAM to everyone in the cloud? Because that is just an expensive thing to give to everyone. How many percentage points of every shoe sale in America do you need to take to fund it? And the answer is it feels like a lot. That’s huge here and something to remember because we already saw Zuck crash and burn with the metaverse stuff, and he does not want to be embarrassed again. So how long is this going to go on, and how are they going to fund it in a real way on the backend, like what you were saying? It’s just a little bit tough to imagine. Luckily, Meta has a ton of money, and they can redirect stuff from other departments, which we’ve already seen them do a lot. It will be interesting to see how this fares on the next couple of quarterly earnings calls — to see how much money is being funneled into this and how much it is making, if any. And how many people are using it. Because they’ve announced it at the top of the App Store, but our own David Pierce has written an entire story about how being number one in the App Store doesn’t mean much. It’s sustained success that actually means something. It reminds me of when I was in college and Uber and Lyft, or maybe it was just Uber honestly, were new and VC-backed, so it was around $4 to call an Uber anytime you wanted to go out or down to the bars or anything. They got everyone using it, and then they got everyone hooked, and then they had to up the prices. That happens. That’s a tale as old as time with VC-backed products. So what I’m wondering is if AI agents are really going to become like that. Are they going to get enough users and enough like shoe sales on the backend that this is gonna be a really viable business model? Or is it just going to kind of be a potentially big bet that they switch away from later? That’s what some Meta employees that I spoke with in our Meta piece told me. They said they expect this to be something that they’re putting out, trying to make a big deal of, and then they may evolve away from it later on, or at least partly. We’ll see how that goes. If your bet is that the future of computing is talking to a little agent, it certainly seems like Meta has gotten farther along that path than anyone else. But we’ll see. OpenAI has hardware designed by Jony Ive that will theoretically come out. It is certain that Google and Apple and all the rest will respond at some point. Hayden, this was great. Thank you so much for being on Decoder once again. Thanks so much. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
fullText:
My Decoder guest today is Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, and we’re discussing the new wave of consumer-friendly AI agents.

If you’ve been paying attention to this space, you know AI enthusiasts have been using agents for a minute now — homebrew OpenClaw setups led to a surge in Mac Mini sales earlier this year. But the launch of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and xAI’s Grok bot has brought easy to use agents to millions.

Muse and Dots have had the highest-profile product launches, and they’re fascinating to pit against each other. Both Meta and OpenAI have decided to pitch these agents to mainstream users and businesses in the form of cute, animated mascots.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

These can do everything from the boring — restaurant reservations and inbox triage — to more sophisticated tasks. In OpenAI’s cases, the company is even offering “specialist” Dots for marketing, legal work, and accounting.

Muse, notably, is free, while Dots are not. So you’ll hear Hayden and me get into why Meta, which still doesn’t have a frontier model of its own, might have a meaningful edge here because it’s so much better at making and distributing consumer products.

There’s also a huge Decoder-style tension wrapped up in the agent race: a conversation about what AI is good at today, what it still can’t do, and then the privacy and security implications of handing over your credit card information, your email inbox, and other sensitive hard drive data to an AI that might be able to do things for you without even requiring an app or a phone in your hand.

That might be the future of all computing, but it’s not at all clear if most people want to hand over the data to make it happen.

Okay: The Verge’s Hayden Field on Muse, Dots, and trusting AI agents. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. 

Hayden Field, you’re the senior AI reporter here at The Verge. Welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks so much.

I’m excited to talk to you. This time there isn’t any wild interpersonal drama. No one’s feelings have been hurt. I would say Elon Musk tried to hurt some feelings and didn’t get there. Alexandr Wang from Meta has maybe been taking some shots, but none of the Real Housewives stuff we usually end up talking about when you’re on the show.

It’s been a bit of a pause in the soap opera antics for now, which I’m really grateful for.

Yeah, just some good old-fashioned product competition in the marketplace. Let’s see who wins and loses, and maybe everything will kill us all in the end. But, for now, cute mascots. 

There’s a lot going on. Let’s start at the start. Hayden, you were at OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco. The company announced Dots, which is their new agent platform with a cute mascot. That happened just a few weeks after Meta Connect, at which the company was all in on Muse, their agent platform with an adorable mascot. 

Tell us about the state of the industry right now. Everyone’s very excited about agents. What’s going on?

It’s funny to me because I’ve been covering agents for so long. I remember that in 2022, it was the year of ideation — that’s what tech leaders called it, referring to agents. They were just ideating. They were thinking about what it could look like. There were a lot of references to Jarvis from the Marvel Universe.

They called 2023 the year of deployment: “Let’s try things, let’s deploy and learn more about what’s failing.” Which meant pretty much all of them were failing at the time. Then we had 2024 and 2025. They didn’t have any names for those years, but agents were still pretty bad, as we saw.

2026 seems, to me, like the year of the beginnings of actually useful AI agents for the consumer, like always-on autonomous agents. Obviously, OpenAI was the start of all of this. But what’s interesting to me is that one man, Peter Steinberger, was able to create an actually useful AI agent for the consumer with OpenClaw — an always-on tool, despite its privacy flaws. It had a lot of privacy and security issues.

But it was an agent that was useful enough that people still wanted to use it anyway and try to find ways around these privacy issues that it was having. That inspired these companies to say, “If one man can do this over the course of one weekend, we’ve really been slacking. We have to get it together.”

OpenAI hired that guy, and now we have Dots. Meta, of course, was working on its own version of this and put it out sooner with Muse. They’re basically both always-on, autonomous AI agents that these companies are peddling as a way to be your personal assistant in a lot of ways.

The idea is to use them for booking flights, booking dinner reservations, buying gifts for people, but not only that. Some of them, Dots in particular, are kind of going further to be your work personal assistant and we’ll get into that in a minute.

But this is where OpenAI and Meta are warring right now. They’re trying to present these two AI agents as a little bit different from each other, even though they’re essentially the same.

Just broadly speaking, to define some terms, we’re gonna keep saying “agent,” and what we mean here is an AI model wrapped in a harness that lets it use a computer. 

Right. The way that I describe AI agents usually is an AI tool that can complete multi-step complex tasks on your behalf without you hand-holding it the whole time.

I was a personal assistant in one of my first jobs in New York, so I would’ve gotten fired if every time my boss asked me to book a flight for her, I said, “What time? Also, what’s your SkyMiles number? Also, what’s your loyalty number again, for this other thing? Oh, do you want me to try to get you first class?”

They want you to have common sense and just book the flight. This is what they’re pitching these AI agents as — things that can work on their own mental kind of scratchpad in the background and not ask you every single time there’s a step. They can complete multi-step processes in the background, doing their own reasoning, and then present you with a completed task.

That’s the big idea. Just to say it clearly, both Muse and Dots come out of the OpenClaw lineage, which is a technical approach to building an agent, right? There are a lot of different ways you might be able to accomplish “It’ll remember your SkyMiles number and book you a flight.” But the way everyone’s going at it now is the idea of a harness around a model. That was the big innovation in OpenClaw, and the computer OpenClaw was using was often your own Mac Mini on your own network using a wide-open browser with your own data, which is where a lot of their security problems came from.

It’s the same model with Muse, only it’s a little Linux computer that Meta’s giving you in the cloud. It’s the same model with Dots, although the way ChatGPT is set up with Codex is very complicated, and that computer could be in a lot of different places.

But this notion that what you really need is a computer with a browser and some harness is gonna direct a model to do a bunch of stuff for you using that computer, that’s what we’ve landed on today, and it just seems to be the default winning model.

Right.

Are all of these things just riffs on OpenClaw? Are they the same as OpenClaw?

You could say that. They’re different technically. Meta keeps saying, “We did build this from scratch, but it was inspired by OpenClaw.” There are a lot of similarities there, but they did say that they built it from scratch. Then, of course, OpenAI hired the creator of OpenClaw, so there’s probably a lot of similarities there as well for Dots.

The reason I wanted to stay there for one second is that I think it’s important to identify the fundamental technical approach that is happening with these agents, because there’s a lot of different ways it could have gone, and the whole industry has picked this approach. What you need is a web browser, a harness, and a model that can go use that web browser. 

What’s really interesting to me is that Meta has done a really good job on top of that fundamental model of making a cute consumer product. Meta is good at consumer products. Obviously, Instagram and Facebook and the rest are undeniably good consumer products. People really like them. 

For all of Meta’s failings in VR, I always thought the Meta Quest has been a great consumer product. You take it out of the box, it helps you use it, you can have fun with it right away. Whereas Dots seems like it’s kind of made for software engineers, but you can also plan a wedding in it.

I’m wondering if that’s how you see it. That one is an enterprise product with a little consumer gloss on it, and then Meta obviously is just a dead-ahead consumer product.

What’s different here is that OpenAI needs money a lot more than Meta needs money. The products are honestly pretty similar, it seems like. The difference is that OpenAI is marketing it to be an enterprise-friendly product a lot more than Meta is. Muse is just a consumer-facing product.

Meta is happy with that. The goal is to make Muse as easy to use as humanly possible. One-tap downloading, just putting it in your face literally everywhere. Even when I went to my Instagram profile the other day, there was a pop-up for using Muse. They’re trying to make it free, accessible, and super easy to broaden the audience.

They want anyone to be able to just use it with one click and get used to it. They’re trying to flood the market with AI agents and make it normal and have their own ChatGPT moment, if you will, for AI agents. They want Muse to be that.
