Now, with OpenAI, they’re still marketing it as a consumer-facing product. When you’re using ChatGPT, if you have the right subscription, it’s right there.

It says, “Use your Dot to do this, that, and the other.” They really want you to go for it as a consumer, as long as you’re paying. This is for their $100 to $200 a month subscription tier, unlike Meta. That’s why there’s a huge difference here. For OpenAI, it seems like they don’t have the money to just front-load all of this and say, “Use it for free. No problem. We’ll catch up with you later.”

OpenAI wants this to be a money-making product, and that’s why they’re marketing it to the enterprise. They talked a lot about privacy to try to set it apart from Meta’s Muse. They talked a lot about what you could do with this as a knowledge worker, whether you worked in marketing, graphic design, software engineering, product, and tons of different industries. They gave examples of how you could use this as an assistant, as a coworker. Sam Altman even referred to it as like a “chief of staff.” He didn’t want it to be just an assistant. He wanted it to be your chief of staff.

Something else that I thought was interesting is that Sam Altman seemed to subtly dig at Meta on stage a few times during DevDay. One of the times he said, “Look, I don’t want this to be just something that’s used to book flights or plan things with friends and look at your calendar. I want this to go beyond that and to really do knowledge worker tasks, things that you in your industry would need a niche assistant to perform.”

That’s why they also introduced specialist Dots that are good at marketing, legal analysis, and things like that. They’re really going for the enterprise angle here, but I think it’s also because they need money ahead of their IPO, obviously.

Yeah, the revenue piece — that it’s only for paid customers at their higher tiers — is really interesting. OpenAI’s tiers are very confusing, but it’s $100 and up, and that’s just going to keep a lot of people from using Dots at first.

The flip side of that is OpenAI does have a lot of customers who are paying them a lot of money, and if they can get those customers to start using Dots, then those customers will be on their agent platforms and maybe you will get some lock-in.

You’ve given those agents a lot of data. They’re part of your workflows, and that might solve the problem I think we’ve seen all the frontier labs have, where a new model comes out and it’s slightly better than the competitor model, and everyone switches for six months, and the next new model comes out and everyone switches back.

Is there some thought that these agent platforms create lock-in — create actual loyalty on top of just the models being better?

Yes. They’re basically hoping that they can build a moat with their users for these things. If Meta and Google already have super easy integrations with all of each company’s existing tools and services, they can easily keep you there.

For example, I have an Apple iPhone, but I use almost exclusively Google apps. So if Google had an AI agent that I was using every day, it would be a little tough for me to switch. That’s what they’re hoping for here.

Meta is hoping that they can get you so into the Muse ecosystem that it would be tough for you to switch, and maybe one day you do have to pay. With OpenAI, they’re trying to get you locked into their ecosystem right away. Even though you have to pay up front, they’re thinking, “We have integrations with almost every tool and service. Maybe it’s not as good as the company that owns that tool and service, but we have the variety and the breadth.”

They’re going for quantity here. One of their employees told me that. They said, “Maybe our Gmail integration, for example, isn’t gonna be as good as Google’s, but we have a Gmail integration and an Outlook integration and X, Y, and Z.” They’re going for just the power of choice and the fact that power users will hopefully stay in this moat.

It’s funny, you mentioned Google. Google announced an agent called Gemini Spark. We should mention that SpaceXAI, the very coherent company that everyone understands, has an agent called Grok Bot, which it is promoting heavily. People seem to like it. It was built by the Cursor team, which SpaceX acquired. 

There’s a lot of this going around, but it seems like Meta really got there first with a consumer product that people could understand.

Obviously, Grok Bot and Dots are much more enterprise-focused, coding-focused. Why was Meta able to get there first?

From all my reporting on Meta, they’ve been behind in AI for a while, and Mark Zuckerberg basically said, “We’ve got to lock in and make a product that people are gonna use on our platforms.” Alexandr Wang apparently was more looking to create a frontier model that was gonna compete with the other leading frontier models.

He says, “We have to think long-term. We have to think superintelligence.” But Zuckerberg says, “No, we gotta think cold hard cash, as in getting people to use stuff on our own platform.” Where they met in the middle was an AI agent that people would use on the Meta platforms, but that still represented a huge step forward, they hoped, for AI systems and what they could do in the everyday world.

This is a fascinating dynamic in that Meta still doesn’t have a frontier model. I don’t think anyone at Meta is claiming that the Muse Spark model competes at the frontier of GPT-6, but their product is better, and certainly they have a massive distribution advantage. They don’t have to pay for advertising on Meta platforms, and OpenAI does, and certainly they have a consumer design advantage. Meta is just better at consumer products.

Does that change how you feel about the dynamics of competition in AI at all? For so long, it’s just been about the capabilities at the frontier, but now it’s a little bit about marketing. It’s a little bit about product design. 

You don’t have the best model, but you made a consumer agent product and you connected it to giving everybody a computer in the cloud, so now it can actually do things for you, and its frontier capability is actually not the important thing. It’s its capability.

I think the more money and power you have at one of these companies, the more get mentally farther away from what the average consumer wants. Let’s say the average consumer does want an AI agent, which many of them don’t, as we know.

But let’s say they do. If they do, they’re going to want it to be free or cheap, and they are going to want it to be safe to use without creeping them out too much. They’re willing to deal with a little bit of creepiness in order for it to be free, but not too much. Meta’s Muse has made headlines about some of its privacy issues that have gotten a little bit above that comfort level for some users.

That’s probably why OpenAI at DevDay made a lot of remarks about privacy and the importance of that, especially if they’re trying to court enterprise users with their AI agents. Right now these companies, especially Meta, are trying to flood the market and create a mass market appeal for this stuff. Similar to how ChatGPT became the default AI chatbot, Meta wants to be that for AI agents, and they feel very hungry about it. They want to create a ChatGPT moment for this technology by making Muse the default for the general public.

There’s something really interesting about the idea that a less-than-frontier model wrapped in a better product is actually going to be the success story here versus a bleeding-edge frontier model that is a little bit harder to use.

There’s some dynamic in there that is the history of all consumer tech products, right? The worst product that’s easier to use often wins, but we haven’t seen that yet in AI.

Right. That’s really important to note here because not everyone needs the bleeding-edge frontier model. Software engineers do. They see a huge difference with coding prowess from one model to another, and that’s why they’re always switching. But the general public, if they’re using an AI agent, as long as it’s useful, they’re good.

However, not many of them are useful yet. We’re still testing Muse and Dots ourselves. For Muse, I saw a couple anecdotes yesterday that it had a big flop for a day or so. People felt like the capabilities got a lot worse. For Dots, the jury’s still out. We’re still testing it.

It depends on what industry you’re in and what you’re really using this stuff for. That’s why OpenAI is going for enterprise, because it makes money and they’re confident that their agent is going to be more and more helpful in these niche industries.

That’s also why they launched specialist Dots, because as we know, the more specialized, niche info you feed into an agent or model, the better it’s going to perform. They don’t want to have that imbued into every single general-purpose agent. It’s just too pricey and too compute heavy, so they say, “You know what? Let’s launch these specialists.”

I feel like you and I talk about consumer versus enterprise adoption of AI every time you’re on this show, and here it seems very important to note that OpenAI asking people to pay a lot of money and asking people to use it primarily in enterprise context is gonna overcome what I think of as the brittleness problem, just because enterprise and business customers have a lot of economic incentives to figure out how to make something work. 

If I’m paying OpenAI $100 a month, and I’m using the marketing Dot to solve some marketing automation, and it doesn’t work the first time, it is very likely I will try again. Because if I get it right, then maybe I’ve saved some money or some time in my business that is really good, and I’ll do it again, and eventually that will lead to more revenue for me, the business owner. What I know about consumers is that the first time it doesn’t work, they just walk away. They have no incentive to try again to overcome frustration or brokenness.

We’ve seen this happen with Muse now a few times. I’ve seen it myself with Muse, where it pops open a browser and tries to do something, and it runs into a brick wall or a CAPTCHA or Amazon blocking it, and it says, “I can’t do it that way. Do you want me to try another way?” And I say, “Whatever. I was just screwing around, and I’m never gonna try it again.”

These are very different markets. OpenAI has vacillated between wanting to be the big consumer company and knowing that the revenue is in enterprise. Do you see any focus in Dots, or do you see that personality shift back and forth in the product itself?

So far, I’m a little bit more impressed with Dots than Muse, just because everyone was impressed with Muse right away, but since then there have been a lot of ups and downs, plus the privacy stuff has been really interesting. Even the fact that it’s building profiles on your family and closest friends.

Meta has never been a super trusted company. None of these companies are very trusted, but Meta has made a lot of missteps with user privacy. Dots seems to be a little bit more helpful to me right now, but I’m still testing, I’m not fully sure yet.

I need to run through all my typical things that I do to compare. Everyone has their own short list of tasks. Right now, for example, I’m trying to create an album of my bachelorette photos, and it’s been unbelievably hard to get any agent to try to do that, so I say, “I’ll just do it myself.”

But that’s a pretty easy thing to do. Once again, how useful are these things for our everyday lives, really? We’ll see. They’ve gotten a lot better, I will say, over the past few years. I’ve been shocked at how slow they’ve been moving, but they have gotten better. Dots is a little bit more impressive to me right now, but we’ll see.

I have Muse plugged into my Instagram because I don’t worry about sharing my metadata with Meta in the way that I worry about maybe everything else, but they already have my Instagram. So I have Muse plugged into my Instagram, and it’s just doing all kinds of stuff. It surfaces interesting comments that I should reply to on Instagram posts. It tracks follower counts. It suggests things I should make videos about. 

It has horrible ideas. Muse is absolutely convinced I should make a video almost every single day about obscure Australian tech regulation. I don’t know why it has this idea. I’m up on it now. I’m deep in the weeds on Australian tech regulation just because I see it every morning.

But there’s something about all that that still feels like work to me. I’ve just assigned it work, and then it tells me what work I should do, and I haven’t found some great consumer use for it yet. Organizing my photos is a consumer use. It kind of still rhymes with work, but it at least is not actually work.

Have you found a great consumer use for these yet?

Not one that works, and that’s the problem. I’ll try to have it do something for me for my wedding or for my personal life, and they haven’t been good yet. That’s why I’m still kind of running through and testing these, because so far it’s always interesting factually when they can do something, but I haven’t been able to trust them end-to-end with something that I really, really need done.

It reminds me of the analogy for AI agents. People always say right now they’re a bad intern, and what you want them to be is a really good assistant, or in Sam Altman’s words, a really good chief of staff. They’re no longer a bad intern, but I think maybe they’re an okay or “eh” assistant.

I don’t think they’ve reached the point of being a really, really good assistant yet, but I still need to run through the rest of my tests to see. It seems they’re not super consistent yet, which is something that you need in a really good assistant.

That ties into trust. You’ve mentioned trust several times now. I’m only willing to give Muse access to, again, the Meta platforms that Meta already has access to. I can’t worry too much about that. I’ve given it access to my spam Gmail, so it is collecting a lot of ideas about my spam Gmail. 

But Meta really wants my credit cards. It wants to go through all of my credit card receipts. This is one of the suggestions in Muse. One of its suggestions is, “Let me log into your credit cards and I’ll cancel streaming services you’re not using,” or, “I’ll negotiate your Verizon bill for you.” I am absolutely not ready to give Meta one ounce of data more than it already has.

This feels like a big issue for every agent. There’s an argument that you should give Meta all that data, one, because they already have it, and two, because they’re a big company that you could sue if they get something wrong. Whereas if I gave all of my data to OpenClaw, it’s just my own fault if it gets leaked.

If I gave all my data to one of the hot startups like Instinct and they go out of business, well, that’s just the end of that. How do you feel about this? Do you feel comfortable giving your data to Meta? Do you think people should do that?

No, I don’t feel comfortable, and I also don’t think that the general person does either. If I’ve seen one thing in a lot of the comments on our Meta story that we published in the last couple weeks, it’s that people don’t trust Meta at all. I have to say, why would they?

But I don’t think that you should trust OpenAI a lot more either. It’s everyone’s own comfort level that they have to abide by. Some people are going to get a lot out of this stuff. Some people may say, “I don’t care if they use my data as long as they are negotiating down my bill accurately or canceling streaming services that I wouldn’t be canceling on my own, so they’re saving me money. It’s fine.”

But one, are they actually gonna be able to do that accurately? Some people have said no. And as we know, when you release data like this, you can’t undo it. I always think about that old example of the insurance company that theoretically buys data on what’s in your fridge and maybe charges you a higher premium if you’re buying too much beer and not enough bananas.

That’s just a theoretical example, but that’s the type of thing that can happen. People should operate with caution, abide by their own comfort levels, but I’m certainly not comfortable yet giving my personal data to Muse.

I don’t know that I’m comfortable giving access to that level. I don’t even know if I’m comfortable putting Muse on my Mac. Apple just recently changed how apps can access the disk on Macs because Muse was so aggressive about reading data. In particular, Jason Aten is a columnist at Inc. and it read his notifications off the disk because he had just given it a permission and he didn’t realize Muse would take that permission and go do something else with it.

This is a lot of spiraling concerns. You’re going to have a little robot that can use your computer for you, whether that computer is in the cloud or whether it’s on your desktop, and you might not know what it’s doing. That ties directly into the fact that OpenAI often doesn’t know what its agents are doing, and that has led to catastrophic security problems across this industry.

Can you connect those dots? Is your own little agent doing your travel booking the same kind of threat as OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face?

I don’t think it’s the same type of threat, but it’s definitely something that you should keep in mind when you’re using this stuff. I link that back to the Facebook Marketplace debacle that we saw with Meta’s Muse. To recap, basically a Muse agent, without someone’s knowledge, invited a potential buyer of this item that this guy was selling to his house, and said, “He’s available now.”

He wasn’t home, and then the potential buyer said, “Are you here? I’m trying to get the item.” And then Muse responded on his behalf, “Yeah, I’m here,” and then he just never came down because obviously he wasn’t home. There was a lot of drama going on there. Some people said, “He did give Muse access to his Facebook Marketplace, so he should have known this could happen.”

A lot of people don’t read all the fine print when they check “yes” to one of these things. There’s a lot there. There’s a lot to unpack in that gray area. But the point is that people should just be a little wary before checking “yes” to every possible thing that these agents want to access, like you said about the credit cards or disk access.

It’s easy to just check “yes” and say, “Whatever, I’ll figure it out later,” but people should be reading the fine print or even use AI to read the fine print. That is one great use of AI. Get it to read the terms and ask it, “What are the worst possible things that could happen here? Lay it out for me.”

Those are things that people should keep in mind before they move forward. And then as for the so-called rogue AI agents that have been hacking other companies and stuff from these labs, it’s just important to notice that if they can’t control some of their most powerful unreleased AI models, how well are they going to be able to control your data or your agent?

Sam Altman said during DevDay that you have a ton of control over your Dot. He said that there were a lot of “if this, then that” rules you can create. There are a lot of specific stipulations that you could make in terms of permissions of what your Dot could and couldn’t do. So that did give people some peace.

But as we’ve seen, these labs and these large tech companies have had a lot of missteps about hacking other companies, and more are coming out every single week, more news items about these cyberattacks. We’ve seen Meta have one. We’ve seen OpenAI have a ton. We’ve seen Anthropic have a ton.

This is all just stuff to keep in mind. One cool thing that I saw someone do was to name their AI agent after the CEO that runs that company and then see how much data you feel comfortable giving it. If you want to do that, I think that’s a great idea, and then it just kind of makes you think twice.

If you’re saying, “Sam Altman, go through my email and see what needs to be deleted,” maybe you still feel comfortable with that, but maybe it makes you think twice and think, “You know what? Maybe I’ll give it access to my spam email only,” like you said.

This ties into the fact that all these things are really cute. Muse is cute. The mascot Jolly is very cute. Alexandr Wang has been waging a relentless campaign on X to make it not only cute but sexy, which you can feel any way you want about that. But he keeps tweeting memes of the mascot with a butt.

Dots are obviously very cute. They come in different shapes and sizes. There’s something here where you’re not quite anthropomorphizing the agent, but you’re making it a character and you’re giving it personality. 

That connects to the idea that you’ve called AI Tamagotchis, where eventually we’re going to have a little hardware device with your little cute mascot on it, you’ll talk to that instead of your phone, and this is the big promise this whole industry has been working toward for forever. They’re gonna replace your phone and the entire paradigm of the App Store with AI agents that are going and using computers for you.

Do you think that any of these products are a meaningful step towards that?

They’re just one building block along the journey of the goal that they’re chasing here. I haven’t heard of anyone that’s using Muse or Dots so far for everything. It’s not Jarvis from Iron Man, despite how much these CEOs want both these products to be that. They are a meaningful step, but as for the cuteness, I think one of the most important points here is that they are intentionally disarming.

These tools are made to be cute so you don’t find them threatening, or you find them decidedly non-threatening. They’re cute. They’re there to help you. It’s a response to the AI populism backlash. It’s saying, “This isn’t going to hurt you or do anything bad. It’s just a cute little thing with eyes, or a sexy little thing with eyes,” whatever.

Just to be clear, I do not think it’s sexy. I think Alexandr Wang has been relentlessly trying to make it sexy. 

[Laughs] No, I also do not think they’re sexy, but I will say Elon Musk has been trying so hard to make all agents and chatbots sexy, so I’m sure it’s not far off for someone to think that.

But whether the AI agents of the future are cute or sexy, it’s going to be equally disarming.

[Laughs] That’s the whole spectrum?

The spectrum, the cute-sexy graph. It’s going to be really disturbing to see when we go more along that graph.

The point is they’re supposed to be disarming and that people should really think twice before giving too much of their data, or just pick and choose what you’re comfortable sharing. Like how you did with the spam email versus your regular email, or saying “no” to giving it your credit card. These are both new products, so just see how the cookie crumbles before you decide to give everything over. We’re already seeing a bunch of changes week to week with how people are using Muse or what they’re upset about, so see how it shakes out.

The last piece I want to talk about is just how any of this makes money. You and I have talked many times about the bubbly nature of the AI economy. Zuckerberg has said his plan is for Muse to take a cut of transactions on the backend. 

Zuck has given everybody a little Linux computer in the cloud with 8GB of RAM. Obviously, he’s given away tons of free tokens. He does not have to pay advertising costs. He can just put Muse across all of his platforms. To the extent that Meta is a well-oiled machine, the amount of Muse promotion that is happening across Meta platforms instantly is kind of incredible to see. They just turned it on.

I saw an ad during NFL games this weekend from Muse. They are spending money to promote this. They’re giving it away for free. They’re giving the tokens away for free. And then somewhere at the end of this, they’re gonna say to merchants, “This person was shopping for shoes. Muse brought them to your doorstep. You’re gonna pay for this customer to buy shoes from you.”

I don’t know any merchants that are excited about this, and it certainly feels like merchants that pay Meta more money would be preferred merchants, and that means that not only do I have an assistant or chief of staff, I have a bribable chief of staff. Like, I have a corrupt butler. Is that what you want?

That is a great term for it, a corrupt butler. That is not what I want, and I don’t think many people do. It’s just crazy to me that we’ve gotten so far from what people really want, which is they want to trust a recommendation and they don’t wanna be scammed, you know?

The leaders in AI don’t think about how certain things have been mirrored in other industries. Think about when people were paying for reviews for their businesses, or paying to delete reviews for their businesses. There was a huge uproar.

Or influencers getting paid to recommend products without disclosing that it was an ad. We then saw the rise of micro-influencers, who were more valuable for a while because they were seen as more trustworthy. They didn’t have that many followers, so the things they recommended must be really good, right? And then we saw the, “Oh, okay, well, there’s #ad, but also they only said they were going to recommend things they really believe in, so it’s okay that it’s an ad.”

There are these mental gymnastics that people have to do to figure out what is really a trustworthy recommendation these days. What is going to convince people that an AI recommendation is trustworthy, if it can be bought?

That’s something these companies are really gonna have to reckon with. The ChatGPT ads blowback was huge, and OpenAI had to say, “It’s going to be a clearly disclosed ad underneath your query, not influencing your query.” If you’re using Muse to shop and it’s an undisclosed potential Meta customer that you’re being redirected to, to buy those shoes instead of these other ones, I feel like so many people aren’t going to use these tools to shop.

I get it on the Meta side. I understand why they would think about monetization that way. They’re a consumer company. This is a consumer product. They know the second they charge even a dollar for it, the uptake will drop precipitously, so they have to keep it free, and then a bunch of people are going to want to shop and go buy a new iPhone cable. At the end of the day, it’s all just the same Amazon garbage anyway, so whatever. 

Then they can run an auction on the backend to say, “Who wants to pay us, Meta, the most for the privilege of selling an unbranded USB-C cable to this customer?” They’ll run some auction, and that will, in its way, just sort of maximize the money that gets turned around.

That is broadly how advertising works today. That’s how the Google Search results page worked until recently, because now it’s full of AI and they’re probably going to do the same thing. Meta can do that because they already have a giant advertising business that prints money. They can give away a consumer product.

Mark Zuckerberg has shown he’s willing to blow money trying to win a market like he did with Reality Labs for years and years and years, and they can just run it till it works. OpenAI, even at $100 a month, is probably not making money on those customers. In fact, I think we know they’re not making money on those customers.

They don’t have any monetization, and when they do try to turn on ads, people get mad at them. How can OpenAI keep up with Zuck?

Only via enterprise. That’s why they are pushing this so hard. We saw a ton of enterprise discussion, demo videos, customer feedback, and tons of other stuff at DevDay, and that’s why they’re pushing this so hard — because they can’t keep up with Zuck on the consumer front. They just can’t.

This is the part where, when people ask if it’s a bubble, I just find myself wondering how much of the economy does Zuck have to win in order to give away millions upon millions of free tokens and 8GB of RAM to everyone in the cloud?

Because that is just an expensive thing to give to everyone. How many percentage points of every shoe sale in America do you need to take to fund it? And the answer is it feels like a lot. 

That’s huge here and something to remember because we already saw Zuck crash and burn with the metaverse stuff, and he does not want to be embarrassed again. So how long is this going to go on, and how are they going to fund it in a real way on the backend, like what you were saying?

It’s just a little bit tough to imagine. Luckily, Meta has a ton of money, and they can redirect stuff from other departments, which we’ve already seen them do a lot. It will be interesting to see how this fares on the next couple of quarterly earnings calls — to see how much money is being funneled into this and how much it is making, if any.

And how many people are using it. Because they’ve announced it at the top of the App Store, but our own David Pierce has written an entire story about how being number one in the App Store doesn’t mean much. It’s sustained success that actually means something. 

It reminds me of when I was in college and Uber and Lyft, or maybe it was just Uber honestly, were new and VC-backed, so it was around $4 to call an Uber anytime you wanted to go out or down to the bars or anything. They got everyone using it, and then they got everyone hooked, and then they had to up the prices.

That happens. That’s a tale as old as time with VC-backed products. So what I’m wondering is if AI agents are really going to become like that. Are they going to get enough users and enough like shoe sales on the backend that this is gonna be a really viable business model? Or is it just going to kind of be a potentially big bet that they switch away from later?

That’s what some Meta employees that I spoke with in our Meta piece told me. They said they expect this to be something that they’re putting out, trying to make a big deal of, and then they may evolve away from it later on, or at least partly. We’ll see how that goes.

If your bet is that the future of computing is talking to a little agent, it certainly seems like Meta has gotten farther along that path than anyone else. But we’ll see. OpenAI has hardware designed by Jony Ive that will theoretically come out. It is certain that Google and Apple and all the rest will respond at some point.

Hayden, this was great. Thank you so much for being on Decoder once again.

Thanks so much.

Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

title: Apple may soon track when Google promotes Chrome inside Safari
snippet: Apple may be preparing to track when Google promotes Chrome or the Google app to users browsing in Safari, and how users react to those promotions. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple may be preparing to track when Google promotes Chrome or the Google app to users browsing in Safari, and how users react to those promotions. Here are the details.

Since iOS 27.2 beta 2, Apple has been testing code in Safari that can detect when Google shows banners promoting Chrome or the Google app on its search pages, as well as whether users interact with those promotions.

While this does not mean that Apple will ship this telemetry feature when iOS 27.2 officially launches, it does suggest that Apple is at least experimenting with a way to measure how often Google promotes its own apps to Safari users and how those users respond.

It is currently unclear why Apple is testing the feature. However, the new code comes amid heightened regulatory scrutiny of competition between Safari and rival browsers, including how users are steered toward alternatives such as Chrome.

In the UK, for instance, Google has specifically cited its efforts to promote Chrome to iPhone users as evidence that it continues to compete with Safari, while regulators have examined whether the companies’ search agreement reduces their incentives to compete in browsers.

In the European Union, in turn, Apple is also subject to Digital Markets Act requirements around browser choice and defaults, with the European Commission previously investigating whether its Safari choice screen complied with those rules.

	

So whether Apple intends to collect and use this data for its own benefit or as part of an effort to address growing regulatory scrutiny over browser competition remains to be seen.

What the code does establish is that Apple has built Safari to detect and log those interactions, and the system works like this: Safari injects a .js script into certain Google home and search results pages, which looks for visible promotional banners or other Google page elements intended to encourage users to open or install Chrome or the Google app.

Safari then looks for links associated with either app, including their custom URL schemes and App Store IDs. If it detects a promotion, it can log certain events, including whether the banner was shown, whether the user appears to be signed in to a Google account, and whether the user interacted with the promotion. This allows Apple to categorize the interaction as either accepted or dismissed and log that result.

As of iOS 27.2 beta 3 and Safari 27.2 beta release notes, Apple has yet to publicly document the feature.

title: iCloud+ just rolled out an improved perk for subscribers
snippet: iCloud+ includes a lot more than additional storage, and one of the service’s perks for subscribers—custom email domains—just got even better. more…
fullText:
iCloud+ includes a lot more than additional storage, and one of the service’s perks for subscribers—custom email domains—just got even better.

iCloud+ subscribers can now create up to 10 personalized email addresses with custom domains

When creating a new email account, you can always go with a standard @gmail.com or @icloud.com domain. But there’s also a more personalized option.

Third-party services offer custom email addresses at a monthly cost. But unbeknownst to many, iCloud+ lets you create custom email addresses at no extra cost when you own the domain.

With iCloud+, you can set up email addresses that end in something personal to you or your business. It’s one of the service’s most underrated perks, and it just got better.

As detailed by pdfu on X, Apple has now increased the number of email addresses you can create per custom domain.

iCloud+ now lets you use up to 10 personalized email addresses per custom domain.

Previously, you were limited to just 3 personalized addresses per domain. The higher limit of 10 addresses is a big expansion that business owners in particular should appreciate. I’ve also seen plenty of families set up custom domains for their family members, and the higher limit will come in handy for that use case too.

Custom email domains with iCloud+ are available for all subscribers, and you can learn how to set them up here.

Do you use custom email addresses with your iCloud+ subscription? Let us know in the comments.

title: Acclaimed British comedy series ‘Small Prophets’ now available on Apple TV
snippet: The first two episodes of “Small Prophets” are now available to stream on Apple TV, following a wave of glowing reviews for the British comedy series. Watch the trailer below. more…
fullText:
The first two episodes of “Small Prophets” are now available to stream on Apple TV, following a wave of glowing reviews for the British comedy series. Watch the trailer below.

’Small Prophets’ now streaming on Apple TV

Earlier today, my colleague Ryan covered the raving reviews for “Small Prophets,” a British comedy series Apple TV acquired for international distribution earlier this year.

The move marked a first for Apple TV, as the streamer had never previously acquired an existing English-language series that had already aired elsewhere.

“Small Prophets” premiered on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two in the U.K. earlier this year, before Apple picked it up for international distribution in August.

It is now available to Apple TV subscribers globally, except in the U.K., where it will arrive on the service in 2027.

“Small Prophets” was created, written, and directed by Mackenzie Crook (Detectorists), who also stars alongside Pearce Quigley (The Way Back), Lauren Patel (The Effects of Lying), Sir Michael Palin (Monty Python), Sophie Willan (Ludwig), Jon Pointing (Big Boys), and Paul Kaye (Game of Thrones), among others.

Following the two-episode premiere, the show will run every Wednesday through November 4.

Here’s Apple TV’s synopsis of “Small Prophets”:

“Small Prophets” is a comic tale of the eccentric Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley) who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has lived a very ordinary life. He works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian (Sir Michael Palin) and hopes for Clea to return. One day Brian shares an old recipe involving rainwater, horse manure and more than a little alchemy. With recipe in hand, Michael sets out (albeit with some skepticism) to create homunculi — magical spirits that can predict the future — in the hope they have the answer to his burning question: “will I ever see Clea again?”

Michael gets help from his young coworker Kacey (Lauren Patel), an unlikely friendship that blossoms partly (but not wholly) through their mutual dislike of store manager Gordon (Mackenzie Crook). Their friendship adds to the frustration and intrigue of his nosy neighbors (Sophie Willan, Jon Pointing) who are obsessed with trying to find out what the hell is going on in the garden shed.

fullText:
I’m in the middle of testing Dell’s 32-inch UltraSharp U3226Q, and my thoughts so far are extremely positive. The picture quality of this OLED panel is impressive, especially when HDR is enabled in macOS. I’ll have a full hands-on review of the UltraSharp on our YouTube channel.

Meanwhile, I wanted to note a key improvement Apple introduced in macOS 27 regarding HDR support. A drawback of using an HDR-ready third-party monitor on macOS 26 Tahoe was the inability to activate High Dynamic Range at the common 2560 x 1440 scaled resolution. Fortunately, the newest macOS release resolves this problem.

The problem

If you’re using an HDR10-capable third-party display with macOS Tahoe, you’ll see a High Dynamic Range toggle in Settings → Displays. When that switch is flipped, HDR content will be viewable. You can see an example of this in the screenshot below.

macOS Tahoe with High Dynamic Range enabled at 1920×1080

But notice in that same screenshot that I’m running the display at a resolution of 1920 x 1080, which is exactly 2x the pixel-doubled resolution of this 4K UHD display’s native 3840 x 2160.

Most users probably don’t want to run at 1920 x 1080 because it makes content appear too large on a 4K display. The Dell Ultrasharp U3226Q is a 32-inch display, and running at 1920×1080 greatly reduces the available screen real estate.

Fixing this issue in macOS is easy; simply select a scaled resolution, such as the popular 2560 x 1440, which is the default setting for Apple’s 5K Studio Display. The problem is that when you select a scaled resolution on macOS Tahoe, HDR is disabled. Notice the screenshot below:

The HDR option is disabled when using 2560×1440 scaled resolution on macOS Tahoe

As you can see, the High Dynamic Range toggle is no longer available, and macOS automatically switches back to Standard Dynamic Range. This means that when running macOS Tahoe with an HDR display, you have to choose between HDR and running the preferred scaled resolution.

Thankfully, this issue has been fixed in macOS 27 Golden Gate. In the screenshot below, you can see that you can have both a scaled resolution selected and HDR enabled simultaneously. This is a native option, and no third-party software is involved.

macOS Golden Gate fixes the ability to run HDR with a 2560×1440 scaled resolution

So if you’re running a third-party HDR display, this feature alone makes upgrading from macOS Tahoe to macOS Golden Gate worth it, in my opinion. Granted, this is on my M4 MacBook Pro. I tried the same thing on my M1 Max MacBook Pro, but I couldn’t select both settings at the same time, even though I was running macOS 27, so there are apparently hardware requirements as well.

macOS Golden Gate includes a range of new features, which I outlined in my Siri AI overview, my macOS Top Features video, and my final review of macOS 27. One such feature related to HDR displays is that macOS 27 offers much more native HDR support across the OS.

EDR/HDR support in macOS Golden Gate

You’ll notice super-bright spectral highlights, cursors, and an overall more contrasty appearance compared to macOS Tahoe. It all results in a fantastic look for both Apple Studio Display XDR users, Pro Display XDR users, and third-party OLED display users.

What are your thoughts? Do you run a third-party external display with your Mac, and if so, would you consider using an HDR-capable display?

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

When Google bought Fitbit back in 2019, it wasn’t clear that the brand had a future. 

As many companies are wont to do, Google had good reason to ingest the accessory maker’s IP and set fire to the rest — but that didn’t happen. After a few fallow years, Fitbit became the software powering the Pixel Watch’s health capabilities, and is now shifting once again to working as a standalone hardware brand within Google.

	

After the monumental success of the Fitbit Air in May, the company is poised to release a Charge follow-up called the Edge. The Charge series hasn’t seen a refresh since 2023, and it appears that Google is updating its design and adding a number of app-like features that should bridge the proverbial gap between tracker and smartwatch.

Of course, Google may not have known Fitbit’s true trajectory back in 2019, but it’s arrived at a place that makes sense: Fitbit’s software is now tightly integrated into all of Google’s health-related endeavors, so the brand is pivoting back to hardware where it made its mark originally.

So the question is whether the Edge, or something like it, is the right move. The Air’s success came from its accessible price ($100) and the growing trend of screenless trackers. I wear a Fitbit Air alongside either a smartwatch or a regular one, and that’s its biggest appeal. And people are going to great lengths to hide the diminutive tracker in places most wearables can’t go. 

The Edge, on the other hand, is a traditional fitness tracker with a few tricks up its sleeve. Judging from the leaks, it will offer notifications, Google Maps, music controls, along with Find My Device support. And of course health tracking that, with a Google Health Premium account, includes an AI-powered fitness coach that’s proven its mettle over the past few months.

I doubt the Edge will have the same cultural impact as the Air, but I also see its existence as proof that Google understands why it bought Fitbit in the first place. Now that it’s plumbed the company for all of its wares, Fitbit rises once again where it all started: with cheap hardware that does just enough well to keep users happy.

title: Amazon Knows You Have a Goldfish Named Ziggy, Even if You Don’t
snippet: Flat buttocks? Own a snail? Here’s how to find out what Amazon’s About You page knows — or thinks it knows — about you as a person.
fullText:
Websites have long kept personalized information about their customers, and it can be useful. Bath & Body Works might alert you to a sale on its three-wick candles, or your local theater can tell you when the musical Six comes to town. 

Few shopping sites have more information about customers than Amazon — currently on day two of its October Prime Day sales — which knows your book preferences, your shoe size and even which cereals you might buy at Whole Foods. But there’s something unnerving about seeing your Amazon personal purchase history distilled into a dossier of factoids — especially when some of them are wrong.

The Amazon About You page, a list of facts the company gathered from your purchases, made the news Tuesday after a post by Threads user fangirlinmegan was picked up by TechCrunch. In the Threads post, the user points out that, in addition to Amazon knowing that she “prepared for a Bluey-themed 2nd birthday celebration” and “consistently repurchases cat hairball treatment,” the giant shopping site has declared, under product preferences, that she “has flat buttocks.”

			

More from CNET

“I mean it ain’t wrong, but damn did you have to call me out like that?” she wrote on Threads.

How to find out what Amazon knows about you

Naturally, that sent other Amazon customers running to check out what personal data Amazon’s About You page keeps about them. It’s easy to find.

On your phone, log in to Amazon, tap the icon that looks like a little person (or chess pawn) in the bottom menu bar, then tap “shopping preferences,” then “about you.”

On a laptop or desktop, log in and hover over where it says “Hello” and shows your name in the upper-right corner of the page. Click on “account” under the “your account” heading, and then look far down under “ordering and shopping preferences,” and click on “your shopping preferences.” Once there, scroll down to “manage your information” to see your Amazon About You page.

An ‘established coffee routine’

My personal Amazon dossier was pretty boring. It knows that I “consistently replenish household essentials,” which was probably gleaned from my recurring Subscribe and Save orders for Bounty paper towels and Charmin. It knows what city I live in and that I have one child, though it underestimated said child’s age by almost a decade.

It knows my family is “invested in the Apple ecosystem.” (Yes, and ouch.) Actually, my little summary makes me sound pretty classy. I did not know that my devotion to coffee and reading meant that I had an “established coffee routine” or that I “value classic and literary fiction.”

I also apparently “maintain a comprehensive beauty routine.” If “comprehensive beauty routine” means slapping on lipstick when I remember, and occasionally trying out a free foundation sample from Sephora… nailed it!

A fish called Ziggy

I may be boring, but other people have fairly hilarious Amazon dossiers. CNET Editor-in-Chief David Katzmaier shared a screenshot of what Amazon knows about him, and hoo, boy, did it really dig deep into his aquarium situation. The e-commerce behemoth knows he has a fish tank with a waterfall and a pond with goldfish that eat only algae, owns a snail, has a fully grown blue crayfish and even has a betta fish with bent fins.

It’s intriguing to track how Amazon garnered this information. If you buy fish accessories, just like I buy coffee and books, it’s not a huge leap to figure out you own fish. But the specificity (bent fins? the color of the crayfish?) is a bit shocking to see.

Most entertaining on Katzmaier’s list is Amazon’s confident declaration that he “owns a goldfish named Ziggy.” How exactly would it know the name of a goldfish? I can see how it might know the name of a cat or dog, as people do order ID tags, personalized beds or even Christmas stockings for their furry friends. But for a fish? And to make it more intriguing, he says the goldfish is not named Ziggy. But he knows where Amazon might have picked up that idea.

“We don’t actually have any fish named Ziggy, but my kid changed one of our Alexa smart speakers’ wake words to ‘Ziggy’ so I think that explains it,” he said. “The rest of this list is largely accurate, and may also be based on his Alexa searches.”

Amazon isn’t exactly hiding that it collects and curates this info. An Amazon representative pointed me to an article published in May on the company’s Amazon News site that shows and explains the preferences page.

And if you don’t want Amazon thinking about the shape of your butt, or are seeking privacy for Ziggy the goldfish, you can make those changes. I found it easy to delete or update some of the information Amazon had on me that I didn’t want used for personalization. Once you’re on your preferences page, clicking a specific statement lets you delete it.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Gael Cooper

title: These US states just said ‘no’ to Apple Wallet driver’s licenses
snippet: Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps expanding to more US states, but two states recently indicated they won’t launch support anytime soon—if at all. more…
fullText:
Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps expanding to more US states, but two states recently indicated they won’t launch support anytime soon—if at all.

Florida and Rhode Island won’t be getting Apple Wallet driver’s licenses anytime soon, per key leaders

The number of US states offering Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps growing, and we even have a good idea of three states launching support soon.

Plenty of states likely intend to support digital driver’s licenses at some point, and haven’t gotten around to it. But there are two who recently indicated they have no plans to launch support.

Those two states are:

Florida

Rhode Island

Last week, Florida rolled out a brand new driver’s license and ID card. Many states take such occasions to launch digital versions too, but the state made zero announcements around digital ID.

That’s no coincidence, as Governor Ron DeSantis actively opposes the idea of digital driver’s licenses. He posted the following on X last November:

The convenience of a digital drivers license is outweighed by the potential for government to abuse it.  

Not gonna happen in FL.  

No digital ID. https://t.co/YD7J6PtBgR

— Ron DeSantis (@RonDeSantis) November 28, 2025

Florida previously did offer a digital ID but abruptly ended support in 2024. Perhaps the next governor will take a different stance.

In Rhode Island, Walter “Bud” Craddock was on a podcast last week discussing mobile driver’s licenses (“MDL”). Craddock is currently Chair of the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators (AAMVA) International Board of Directors.

Here’s what he said:

“I want to see more universal adoption or need for an MDL. I had one of my senators approach and try to talk me into doing it. I had to give him the old Heisman move and push him back…the main user right now is TSA. Up until recently, there was no airport in New England area that could accept an MDL. So why would I spend the money in the development of it? And also, I’m looking to do a solution that is across all platforms. Instead of just doing one for Apple or the Google Wallets, I don’t want to replicate and duplicate efforts.”

Like DeSantis, Craddock’s position of leadership is slated to end in the next few months. So depending on his successor’s stance, perhaps Rhode Island could get Apple Wallet driver’s licenses sometime in 2027.

Here’s the full list of US states currently offering Apple Wallet driver’s licenses, and three expected to launch next.

Do you use a digital driver’s license or are you still waiting for your state to launch support? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google Maps now lets you turn your car into a McLaren F1
snippet: A new Google Maps update lets you change your car’s driving avatar into a McLaren F1. more…
fullText:
A new Google Maps update lets you change your car’s driving avatar into a McLaren F1.

Available for a limited time, Google Maps has added a McLaren F1 driving avatar to its selection. You can change your car’s icon from the default blue arrow or other 3D cars to the Google-sponsored McLaren F1 racing car. 

The temporary avatar is available through late November and celebrates the US Grand Prix that takes place in Las Vegas from October 22-25.

Google says:

	

Celebrate the United States Grand Prix with the official team avatar, available until November 23, 2026.

The avatar is visible on both your smartphone as well as your car’s display via Android Auto or Apple CarPlay. You can adjust your driving avatar via Google Maps > Settings > Your vehicles > Driving avatar.

This is a server-side update that’s still rolling out.

title: Is It Even Worth Buying Tech During Early Holiday Sales? Here’s What We Recommend
snippet: US adults are juggling higher tech prices with smaller budgets this year. Can the sales help them afford more?
fullText:
Early holiday sales are here, but so are bills. 

The holidays have never been merciful when it comes to balancing everyday expenses, so juggling your necessities during a busy (and expensive) shopping season can be tough. There’s a glimpse of that in CNET’s latest holiday survey. This time last year, holiday spending for tech products and services was higher, with the average US adult spending $931. Now, that budget has shrunk to $808, a $123 dip from last year’s survey findings. 

But there have been so many new releases this year, like Apple’s AirPods 5, the highly anticipated Legend of Zelda-themed Switch 2 console, and even Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. We can’t all comfortably fit new devices into smaller holiday budgets. The real question is, who’s to blame for me saying, “Bah humbug!” when I start my holiday shopping — the economy or tech brands? 

			

More from CNET

What’s causing lower holiday tech budgets this year?

Let’s be real, we’re juggling a lot financially. There are higher prices on everything from everyday goods to gas and utilities. Covering necessary expenses doesn’t leave much room to pay for new personal tech that costs hundreds, even thousands, for some devices like the iPhone Duo or the iPhone 18 Pro Max. 

But why are US adults spending less on tech when so many new devices were released this year? CNET Senior Editor Adam Oram, an expert deal hunter, says tech is becoming unaffordable, and we’re dealing with higher everyday living costs. We’re having to be more mindful about how we spend our money — and some new tech simply isn’t worth it. 

Think about the rising cost of tech products, but the lack of innovation. For example, if you have the iPhone 17 Pro, there aren’t many differences from the iPhone 18 Pro that justify the cost to upgrade. What’s more, even if you’re considering existing tech products, you’re seeing price increases due to the RAM shortage, which has driven up hardware and service costs around the world.

“That means people are perhaps keeping their phone for an extra year or persevering with a laptop for a little longer, rather than jumping on the next shiny thing,” Oram says. It also could mean nonessential tech purchases fall into the luxury bucket, which may have less cash in it than before. And since many paychecks aren’t stretching as far, that doesn’t leave much discretionary money to splurge on nonessential items, such as upgrading your smartphone. 

Is it still worth shopping for tech right now?

The answer depends. If your holiday budget is tighter this year, you may be hoping that sales can help you buy the tech you want. However, don’t expect retailers to slash tech prices as much this year, Oram says. For all the reasons listed above, don’t expect big savings, like half off the original price, during early holiday sales, especially for newer device models. 

“In previous years, holiday sales have made for a great time to upgrade big-ticket tech items, but with rising component costs, these deals might not be as staggering this year as in the past,” he says. “That said, if you have a busted TV, laptop or tablet that needs replacing, those items should still top your list as they rarely go on sale for less than around the holidays.”

You may still be able to find deals at different retailers throughout the month of October, depending on the brand, retailer and model of the device you’re looking for. Oram adds that you can expect plenty of deals on items that will likely fall into most people’s “nice-to-have” list, such as smart home and kitchen gadgets. It’s also a good time to stock up on presents and spread the overall cost over the next few months rather than shopping at the last minute. 

On the other hand, if you don’t need to replace a device right away, it may be worthwhile to just wait a few more months. 

“Waiting for the hype around new product launches to die down can lead to scoring a better deal,” Oram says, “especially for things like phones, where carriers begin incentivizing upgrades by offering solid discounts after the initial buzz.”

For now, Oram doesn’t expect prices to drop significantly on tech, so think about whether you need to upgrade versus just wanting to. If you’re planning to upgrade, cover the needs first, and the wants after, if you can afford to.

title: Review: Rhinoshield’s iPhone 18 Pro bumper case is minimalist but surprisingly protective
snippet: iPhone bumper cases have been a fan-favorite since the iPhone 4 bumpers, but options these days are few and far between. Rhinoshield offers a decent option for those wanting a minimal case. more…
fullText:
iPhone bumper cases have been a fan-favorite since the iPhone 4 bumpers, but options these days are few and far between. Rhinoshield offers a decent option for those wanting a minimal case.

Apple finally got back into the bumper business with the iPhone Air last year. I was hoping Apple would expand their bumper case to the iPhone 18 Pro (like they did with the clear case and iPhone 11), but unfortunately they did not. In my search for another option, I came across Rhinoshield’s Minimalist Impact Bumper case. 

Key Details

The Impact Bumper Case has a fit similar to most other bumpers, where the lip on the screen is fairly minor, while the lip on the back is a little larger. A unique feature of this case, and one that I quite like, is that it has special supports that keep the camera plateau and lenses off of wherever your phone is resting, which I particularly appreciate considering the aluminum 17 Pro and 18 Pro. This results in a far more protective case than your typical bumper would be. It also eliminates the annoying wobble when using your phone on a flat surface.

The case’s fit, however, is not quite what I was hoping for. It’s somewhat loose, and you can easily bend the edges outward, and I do wonder if over time they may end up getting stretched out. I don’t think the phone flying out of the case when dropped will be an issue though (and I have unintentionally tested that). That said, the material of the entire case is a hard plastic rather than rubber, so hopefully it will be fine in the long run. Rhinoshield says that it is made entirely of just one material, and is therefore 100% recyclable.

The case comes in three colors, which are matched to the iPhone 18 Pro colors: white, blue, and black (sorry Burgundy fans). The blue, which is what I have, is close to Glacier but not perfect. 

Downsides

There are some downsides, however. My primary gripe with the case is that the buttons can be hard to press. For some reason they went with a nearly flush design, and the way that the buttons are designed makes them mushy. 

The material choice as a whole may be a downside. To me, it feels cheaper than the likes of Apple’s iPhone Air bumper, but some may end up preferring it. I certainly prefer it to the materials of a typical TPU/rubber clear case. The material and loose design also seem to attract pocket dust.

If you use Apple’s Wrist Strap or Crossbody Strap, be aware that this case does not have the required loop connection points. 

Conclusion

The Rhinoshield bumper is definitely not perfect, and I still hope that Apple will extend their bumpers to other iPhones. In the end though, I have decided to keep the case, for one primary reason: it lets me have a near-caseless experience without worry of the fragile aluminum getting chipped or dented. As far as I can tell, the bumper case is usually only available from their own website, so the price of about $30 matches the price of Apple’s ($39) after shipping. You can get the Rhinoshield Minimalist Impact Bumper case here. (Occasionally, an Amazon listing will pop up, so you can give that a try as well.)

title: Googlebooks don’t have the same web app or Linux app support as Chromebooks
snippet: Googlebooks don’t have the same level of web app support as Chromebooks, as only “compliant” apps can be installed, and that’s not the only regression from ChromeOS, as Linux apps don’t work in the same way either. more…
fullText:
Googlebooks don’t have the same level of web app support as Chromebooks, as only “compliant” apps can be installed, and that’s not the only regression from ChromeOS, as Linux apps don’t work in the same way either.

Googlebooks rely on Android apps and web apps for virtually all core functionality, with the Play Store actively directing users to which app is the most ideal on the platform. 

As it turns out, though, support for Progressive Web Apps on Googlebook isn’t quite at the same level as Chromebook. While most PWAs we’ve tried so far are easily installed, we ran into an issue installing the Slack PWA. Google, in a statement today, confirmed this is because Slack is not a “compliant” PWA, with Chromebooks instead relying on “manual installation.” It’s unclear what differs regarding Slack’s PWA — it functions just fine on other platforms such as Windows and ChromeOS — but it can’t be installed on Googlebook or Android devices.

Google says:

	

Installing PWAs is fully supported on Googlebooks. But, the Slack web app isn’t a compliant PWA. Chrome on ChromeOS allows manual installation even though it’s not a PWA. This capability will also be coming to Chrome on Googlebooks soon.

This mirrors another regression in app support compared to Chromebooks.

Googlebooks also, at least for now, lack the same level of Linux app support.

Chromebooks started adding support for installing Linux apps way back in 2018 and, after a few years in development, it became a secret super power of Google’s platform. Linux app support on Chromebook allowed users to bridge the app gap with the ability to install full desktop apps via Linux ports and, while it wasn’t the easiest process, it got the job done.

Googlebooks are in a very different state.

There’s little to no documentation around Linux apps on Googlebook right now, with Google’s only page on the matter describing how you can use the Terminal app to access a Debian command line interface. Google says:

You can use the Terminal app to access a powerful Debian Linux command-line environment directly on your Googlebook. You can install and run developer tools, code environments, and access other Linux applications. It expands your device’s capabilities for advanced tasks and software development.

But installing apps via this portal doesn’t put them within easy reach of the end user. It’s a far cry from Chromebook’s support, which placed most apps within the app drawer once they were installed. 

	

Google says that it’s possible to run apps, but that GUI apps “aren’t the main focus” of the Linux environment on Googlebook:

Just wanted to confirm that yes, there will be a Terminal app available on Googlebook out of the box, and yes it lets you run a Debian Linux environment on your device.

Also yes, you CAN run Linux GUI apps in this environment, but note that for this initial release of Googlebook, GUI apps aren’t the main focus. We’ll have more to share soon on the Terminal app!

One Linux user far more experienced than myself who dug into how Googlebook supports Linux apps, detailing that they show up in a single Terminal display window without their own Android windows or taskbar items. Another user saw the same behavior and noted reliability issues with GIMP, a popular photo editing app for Linux.

As mentioned, there’s no documentation yet on how to get Linux GUI apps running on Googlebook, so this is not functionality for the “average Joe” — not to say Linux apps on Chromebook were either, but it’s certainly odd to see that this has regressed in functionality rather than expanded.

title: Pixel 11 series still not on Android 17 QPR1 with October update
snippet: With yesterday’s October 2026 update, the Pixel 11 series is not yet running Android 17 QPR1. more…
fullText:
With yesterday’s October 2026 update, the Pixel 11 series is not yet running Android 17 QPR1.

The Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold launched in August with the base Android 17 release. In September, the Pixel 11 series received two early updates that presumably addressed issues that emerged since launch. 

	

Later in the month, Google rolled out QPR1 to all other devices. Visual changes in the quarterly release include system blur for the volume slider and power menu, while there’s an updated system media player that gets narrower when other apps are available. The Mobile Data Quick Settings Tile gets a time-saving “Don’t ask me again” toggle, while there’s now a Keyboard QS Tile.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 series did not get the initial Android 17 QPR2 Beta 6 release and had to wait a few days for Beta 6.1, which introduced HiLight support for message notifications. It did get the 17 QPR3 Beta without issue a few days later. 

	

This week’s October release does contain fixes for the Pixel 11:

Fix for issue causing the virtual keyboard to occasionally not appear when interacting with search input fields*[1]

Fix for issue occasionally causing captured photos or recorded videos to save in the incorrect orientation*[3]

It’s unlikely that we’ll get a second October release, with all eyes on November. With QPR2 just a month away at that point, Google might wait for December to align all the devices.

title: iPhone Duo shows what the future of smartphones could look like
snippet: Since the unveiling of iPhone Duo, the idea of all major interface navigation elements being accessible from your thumb has been really interesting. Apple re-invented the idea of smartphone navigation with the outer display on iPhone Duo, and now it feels quite wrong that every smartphone puts things at the top. more…
fullText:
Since the unveiling of iPhone Duo, the idea of all major interface navigation elements being accessible from your thumb has been really interesting. Apple re-invented the idea of smartphone navigation with the outer display on iPhone Duo, and now it feels quite wrong that every smartphone puts things at the top.

Everyone yearns for the days of when phones were smaller, largely because things were more reachable. The downside to that is that, well, your screen is quite small, and the content landscape has evolved from that.

iPhone Duo solves both of these problems by still offering a reasonably large rectangular viewing area to the left of the dock and navigation area on the right. You still get a large viewing area, and you still have everything within a thumbs reach.

Ever since Apple showed this off, many enthusiasts have brought up the idea of an “iPhone Solo,” ie an iPhone Duo sized display, except it isn’t a foldable.

While I doubt Apple would offer this, I do think it’s quite an interesting idea, and maybe one day it could make sense depending on how well the iPhone Duo does. If you think about it, the current form factor of smartphones is a matter of happenstance. We had 16:9 displays, then we decided to axe all the bezels and the home button, which turned phones into this oddly tall device where things aren’t really reachable.

iPhone Duo rethought what a smartphone’s form factor should be. Apple didn’t merely slap normal iOS on the outside display and call it a day. They rethought it to make it optimal, and now I envy the fact that my phone is so tall.

	

We’ll see what happens. An iPhone Solo could easily happen if people receive the Duo’s outer screen well.

title: Call Screening has made a big difference to my iPhone experience
snippet: iOS 27 has brought a lot of new features to the iPhone, but one of the things that has made the biggest difference to my experience of the device as a phone actually dates back a year earlier. Apple introduced Call Screening to the Phone app in iOS 26, but I only started using it a few months ago – and the feature has protected me from a growing number of spam and spam calls … more…
fullText:
iOS 27 has brought a lot of new features to the iPhone, but one of the things that has made the biggest difference to my experience of the device as a phone actually dates back a year earlier.

Apple introduced Call Screening to the Phone app in iOS 26, but I only started using it a few months ago – and the feature has protected me from a growing number of spam and spam calls …

I’ve tried to be reasonably protective of my phone number, only providing it when it is not only demanded by an organization, but where I accept that it will be useful for them to have it. In many cases where a web form insists on it, I’ve used a fictitious number.

The UK’s telecoms regulator actually provides a range of 1,000 mobile numbers that have never been allocated so I can be sure my fake number won’t lead to someone else being spammed.

However, I’ve owned my mobile number for literally decades now, so it’s unavoidable that it has made its way onto some marketing lists, and there are also companies that use robocallers to dial random numbers. I haven’t been bothered by many of these historically, but for some reason there was a significant uptick earlier this year.

When Apple introduced the call screening feature last year, I was concerned about missing genuine calls, so didn’t immediately enable it. However, I did so earlier this year, selecting the Ask Reason for Calling option, and I have to say I highly recommend it.

The main spam/scam calls I received were from companies pretending to be my mobile carrier. I think some are likely third-party resellers hoping to trick me into switching network, while others are either trying to obtain payment details or carry out more general data harvesting. I’ve never let any of these calls get far enough to find out, but it reached the point where I was getting at least one of these calls every week. I’d also been getting a growing number of job scam calls.

Since switching on the feature, not a single one of these has got through to me. I think in the vast majority of cases, they immediately hang up when they get the automated response, while a few of them have bothered to give me their claimed reason for the call, and it’s been immediately obvious that I should reject it.

I also haven’t seen any indication of anyone genuine failing to reach me. I’ve had a number of genuine calls get filtered by the screening feature, but all of these have explained who they are and the reason for the call, and I’ve then been able to answer it.

If you don’t currently have Call Screening enabled, I highly recommend it. Open the Settings app, scroll down to the App section, select Phone, and then scroll down to Screen Unknown Callers.

title: Apple may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU in a tax compromise
snippet: Apple and other tech giants may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU under a modified version of a digital services tax plan. The EU hopes a revised version of earlier proposals will enable it to raise tax revenues without incurring the wrath of the White House … more…
fullText:
Apple and other tech giants may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU under a modified version of a digital services tax plan.

The EU hopes a revised version of earlier proposals will enable it to raise tax revenues without incurring the wrath of the White House …

There has long been debate within EU countries about taxes on digital services, with Apple examples including iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Creator Studio, and more.

Some point to the significant revenues earned from selling subscription services to EU citizens without necessarily paying any tax in Europe on these receipts. Others are concerned that a digital tax could disproportionately hit European companies, while yet others are concerned about threatened retaliation by the White House for additional taxes on US companies.

The Financial Times reports that the European Commission has now come up with a compromise it hopes will keep everybody happy – other than the companies like Apple, Google and Meta who would be paying the new taxes, of course.

Brussels was considering changes to an existing proposal that would require all companies operating in the EU with revenue of more than €100mn a year to pay an annual lump-sum tax contribution, the officials said […] 

Adjusting the thresholds and contributions under the Core proposal to cover only very large corporates would both increase the amount raised from tech groups and defuse criticism in Europe that Core would hit many medium-sized European companies, officials argued.

The revised version of the plan would not single out companies selling digital services, but would apply to all large corporations. Since it was the former proposal that led the White House to threaten retaliatory tariffs, the EU hopes that the new version won’t provoke a new trade war with the US.

	

The amount that would be levied on each company has not yet been decided. The plan is to seek agreement on the principle across the 27 EU countries before setting a rate for the tax.

9to5Mac’s Take

This whole mess was supposed to have been resolved by a global agreement, brokered by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). This would have ensured that all companies worldwide pay at least some taxes in each of the countries in which they operate, and the plan had Apple’s support.

However, Donald Trump withdrew the US from this agreement, leading to calls for an EU-specific version. The idea that Trump won’t object to the revised plan seems to me rather optimistic.
