title: Pixel 11 Pro vs. iPhone 18 Pro: Copy-copy-paste or just copy-paste [Video]
snippet: There’s a new phone in town, and like the Pixel 11 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro looks eerily similar to what we saw last year. What can we glean from this duo? Here’s what you need to know. more…
fullText:
There’s a new phone in town, and like the Pixel 11 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro looks eerily similar to what we saw last year. What can we glean from this duo? Here’s what you need to know.

Same, same, and same again

If you wanted to critique the smartphone industry in Western markets, there are no two devices more obvious to use as the basis for your argument. There is something very familiar about the Pixel 11 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro – two phones that are almost the same as their predecessors.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Hardware progress has almost ground to a halt, which is both a fair criticism and maybe an admission that there really isn’t much left to do on those ubiquitous products we carry each and every day.

	

A smartphone is a tool. It’s your wallet, your mobile shopping card, your digital camera; it’s more than something you want, it’s an essential.

Maybe that is why we haven’t seen the two of the world’s biggest tech companies try to veer away from the “safe” designs they’ve peddled for a couple of years. It could be that we, the buyers of these products, similarly don’t care now.

Realistically, you could just read our deeper dive comparing the iPhone 17 Pro to the Pixel 11 Pro, and you’d get 95% of the way there. However, there are a few changes worth noting, given that Apple is still the top dog in the US market and dominates global sales in the “premium” segment. Google has been using Apple’s playbook, following a tried-and-tested path to some relative success as of late.

And so, we have two phones that look identical to the previous generation. Barely any visual cues save the colors to differentiate. It’s an indictment of where phones are today in some ways.

Camera goods and gimmicks

As far as I can tell, there are only two major changes to the iPhone 18 Pro. A smaller Dynamic Island and a variable aperture for the main lens. The camera aperture has been lauded somewhat, and it’s an interesting addition for a number of reasons.

Samsung experimented with the concept years ago when mobile sensors were significantly smaller, but the implementation here is different. Because modern smartphone sensors have such small pixels, you typically avoid ‘stopping down’ to prevent diffraction. 

However, since Apple widened the base aperture to f/1.4 to improve low-light intake by 50%, the variable aperture now serves as a necessary ‘stop’ to balance image sharpness and exposure control in brighter conditions. Ultimately, this provides more flexibility for videographers, though you’ll probably notice zero difference in daily photography.

The only changes to depth of field are when you get super close to a subject when shooting wide open. I found there were no visual changes to speak of. I’m not even sure it would help for videos, but I will give credit to Apple because the company is trying to give photographers and videographers more manual controls. Right now, it isn’t exactly doing much, but it could be something bigger, better, and more impressive with future updates – despite not really doing as much right now.

I still vastly prefer images from my own Pixel 11 Pro. It’s a vastly more flexible camera experience, bolstered tremendously with the addition of Camera Looks. Having those sensor-level controls makes for a very powerful piece of the Pixel camera system. Without going too deep into the video modes, yes, the iPhone 18 Pro feels like it’s catered to amateurs and professionals more readily than the Pixel 11 Pro.

HiLight is the only other differentiation, and it is, well, there if you care about soft LED lights on the back of your phone.

I talked about a bit of a gap, and you don’t need me to tell you that the A20 chip runs rings around the Tensor G6. Yes, it’s more powerful. It does more, it is more efficient, it’s not exactly a fair comparison.

Obviously, each chip is tuned to its respective OS, so it’s not really one-to-one, but yes, the iPhone 18 Pro is just more powerful without requiring cloud-based or AI functionality to plug some gaps. I think this is where the Pixel can flex some muscle.

Gemini and the functions it enables are more sensibly enabled because they’re passive. Not something you have to seek out. It’s one of the ways in which the Pixel and Proactive Assistance can feel futuristic, as it is doing everything with so little effort.

Apple teased something like this a few years ago, but there’s not enough there yet with Siri to meaningfully move the needle compared to what Google is doing with Gemini. That said, the two experiences outside of AI are just not all that different today. Android and iOS aren’t separated by much. Use apps, play games, send messages, take calls, browse the web. Which you prefer is ultimately up to what you prioritize.

Does the Pixel 11 Pro come up short against the iPhone 18 Pro?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

There isn’t much to really talk about on either device because there is so much similar to last year. If you wanted to save some money, the most sensible thing would be to look back a year. Get either the Pixel 10 Pro or the iPhone 17 Pro. Save your money, get a new case, replace the battery, just make do and mend.

We’re here to discuss the merits, though, and while the gap at times feels quite large, I do think that Google has been diligently working on the Pixel lineup to the stage that most people will be very happy with their purchase. I hoped more would change, but there feels like some artificial brakes have been pumped this time on the Pixel 11 Pro. The iPhone 18 Pro is playing backup to the Duo this year, so it was always less of a priority for the company, even if it will be the biggest seller. 

Google doesn’t really have that excuse to lean on. All of the Pixel 11 phones are basically identical to the previous gen.

Then again, if we are being 100% honest with ourselves, does Apple deserve more criticism than Google for not moving the needle, given that the current crop of Pixel devices lacks a little more in certain key areas? It’s really frustrating to admit that, yes, there are more compromises on a Pixel 11 Pro than an iPhone 18 Pro across almost every area. The Pixel edges the iPhone in AI functionality and maybe stills photography, but the scoresheet isn’t exactly flattering.

To be blunt, this is not glazing the iPhone. It’s important to be objective, and objectively, you just get more for your money with the iPhone this year (again). No, I won’t be switching any time soon, and I likely won’t even keep hold of an iOS device this year, but in some ways, Apple deserves some plaudits as even without much change, the overall package still surpasses a similarly priced and similarly unchanged Pixel 11 Pro.

title: You can unlock a Googlebook’s bootloader, Magisk support in the works
snippet: Googlebook is an Android-based platform and, with that, comes the potential to do a bit more with it. Google has confirmed you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook, and now Magisk root support is already in the works. more…
fullText:
Googlebook is an Android-based platform and, with that, comes the potential to do a bit more with it. Google has confirmed you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook, and now Magisk root support is already in the works.

On a support page, Google details how you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook. Google says that a “developer or advanced user can unlock their device’s bootloader to install a custom version of the operating system or test an app,” but stresses that “most users don’t need to unlock their Googlebook’s bootloader.”

Like on a Pixel or other Android phone that easily supports bootloader unlock, you’ll need to enable OEM unlocking via the Settings menu and Developer options, then press and hold Esc + F2 and press the power button, releasing all keys when the screen lights up. From there, bootloader unlock is located under “advanced options.”

And, with that, root support is also coming.

	

Magisk developer John Wu confirmed on Twitter/X that support for Magisk is in the works for Googlebook. In a separate post, Wu called Googlebook “the ideal platform for Android modding” since modern Android smartphones suffer from broken apps including banking apps when they are rooted. Wu says that there are some tweaks needed to bring Magisk and, in turn, all of the benefits that come with a rooted device to Googlebook, but it’s coming.

title: Apple’s MacBook Pro overhaul is coming soon, here’s what to expect
snippet: Apple just released a MacBook Pro update in March, but there’s more coming soon. Apple is expected to debut one of its biggest MacBook Pro updates ever as soon as later this year. Here’s everything we know so far … including details on a surprising recent twist. more…
fullText:
Apple just released a MacBook Pro update in March, but there’s more coming soon. Apple is expected to debut one of its biggest MacBook Pro updates ever as soon as later this year. Here’s everything we know so far … including details on a surprising recent twist. 

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Sony is running a massive sale on its best BRAVIA TVs, ranging from its entry-level to flagship options — shop now to save! 

New MacBook Pro features

OLED display

The new MacBook Pro will switch from mini-LED to OLED display technology. This will mark the first time Apple has used OLED in a Mac, having previously used it on the iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. This has been reported by sources including Ming-Chi Kuo and Bloomberg.

The MacBook Pro’s rumored OLED display would offer true blacks, higher contrast, and potentially more vibrant colors compared to today’s mini-LED screens. That’s because OLED can turn individual pixels completely off, while mini-LED still relies on a backlight system.

Touchscreen

OLED isn’t the only big display change coming with the refreshed MacBook Pro, though. It will also be Apple’s first-ever touchscreen Mac.

As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is optimizing macOS to take advantage of the MacBook Pro’s touchscreen. For example, when you touch a button or a control, macOS will dynamically adjust to show you relevant touch controls. If you tap on the menu bar, controls will automatically enlarge to make it easier to navigate with your finger.

It will also support common touch interface interaction methods, like pinching and zooming, and faster scrolling.

So, it’s a lot more than Apple simply adding a touchscreen to a Mac. It’s a rethink of macOS to make touch navigation feel fluid and natural.

Dynamic Island

Currently, the MacBook Pro features a notch cutout that houses the FaceTime camera. With this year’s MacBook Pro, however, Apple will reportedly ditch the notch in favor of a hole-punch cutout for the camera.

Additionally, Apple is planning to bring the Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. This will likely work like the iPhone, where the Dynamic Island masks the cutout for the FaceTime camera and displays software interface elements such as Live Activities and notifications.

Thinner and lighter design

With the 2021 MacBook Pro, Apple reversed course and made it thicker than its predecessor. It also added back ports, including MagSafe, HDMI, and an SD card slot. The 2016-2020 MacBook Pro’s industrial design famously had only four USB-C ports.

This year, however, Apple is reportedly planning to make the MacBook Pro thinner once again. We don’t have any specifics on this just yet, and it’s unclear whether Apple will remove any ports to accommodate this change.

One key difference nowadays is Apple Silicon. The 2016-2020 MacBook Pro models used Intel chips that were less efficient than Apple’s own M-series chips. Apple Silicon should mean Apple can make the MacBook Pro thinner without compromising on those things.

The new MacBook Pro will also be “significantly” lighter than its predecessor, according to Mark Gurman: 

But there is one other major difference, I’m told: The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior, miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry.

M5

It was widely expected that the new MacBook Pro models would be powered by the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips. 

In a new twist, however, it sounds like this update will actually use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the current MacBook Pro models. 

The decision comes as Apple is reportedly skipping higher-end chips in the forthcoming M6 generation. Instead, the M6 will be available only in its base configuration, with no M6 Pro, M6 Max, or M6 Ultra variants. 

Apple is shifting its focus to the M7 generation, including the M7 Pro and M7 Max chips. These will reportedly focus on significant improvements to AI performance. 

MacBook Ultra?

Finally, it wouldn’t be an Apple rumor cycle without speculation about naming.

Mark Gurman has speculated that Apple might brand these laptops as MacBook Ultra. This name would “more clearly signal their position at the top of the lineup,” he reasoned.

The latest development that the new MacBook models will use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips adds a new wrinkle to the marketing decisions Apple will have to make. 

New MacBook Pro release date

Apple is expected to debut the new MacBook Pro lineup in October or November. It may seem weird that Apple would update the MacBook Pro twice this year, but it’s not unprecedented.

Wrap up

title: John Ternus and Tim Cook took opposite approaches to design, and both were right
snippet: One of the most famous and successful partnerships in the history of technology has been that of Steve Jobs and Jony Ive. When Tim Cook took over as CEO, he did not play the same role in working with Ive on hardware design – and that was the right decision. John Ternus is apparently taking a much more Steve-like approach to working with Apple’s design lab, and I think that too is the right call … more…
fullText:
One of the most famous and successful partnerships in the history of technology has been that of Steve Jobs and Jony Ive. When Tim Cook took over as CEO, he did not play the same role in working with Ive on hardware design – and that was the right decision.

John Ternus is apparently taking a much more Steve-like approach to working with Apple’s design lab, and I think that too is the right call …

Many of Apple’s most iconic designs were the product of the unique partnership between Steve Jobs and Jony Ive. The two worked incredibly closely together, usually meeting at least once a day, and what emerged was something far better than could have been achieved by either of them alone.

Both wanted to push the boundaries of what was possible in hardware design, and both shared an extremely thoughtful approach. However, each of them had a different primary focus. Ive was obsessed with making the hardware as slim and minimalist as possible, while Steve was equally obsessed with delivering the best possible user experience.

While Ive talked a lot about design being much more than appearance, he still had a reputation for a tendency to prioritize form over function, resulting in issues like the notoriously problematic butterfly keyboard design, and the prevailing view is that Steve had played a crucial role in reining in this tendency during his time.

When Cook took over as CEO, he reportedly took a significantly more hands-off approach with the company’s design team, only visiting the lab around once a month. That makes perfect sense, given that Cook’s expertise was in operations and people management.

That’s not to say Cook didn’t have useful contributions to make, but it would probably have been counterproductive for him to get too involved in design decisions, especially at an earlier stage. In particular, his obsession with cost might have inhibited the team’s ambitions.

	

Ternus, in contrast, is a hardware guy through and through. He effectively took over Ive’s former role as head of hardware engineering prior to becoming CEO, and was credited by Apple as playing a key role in the development of both the iPad and AirPods product lines even before Ive left the company.

Like Steve, Ternus is said to have reversed some of the cases where sleek design had been prioritized over product usability. While the current design partnership of Molly Anderson and Steve Lemay is clearly an extremely effective one, one of the ingredients of that recipe for success appears to be oversight by Ternus. 

Personally, I’m extremely glad to hear that Ternus continues to prioritize this work even now that he has so many more demands on his time. Team Anderson-Lemay-Ternus works, and long may it continue.

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

The Retro Song Bird may look similar to devices like Epilogue’s GB Operator with a slot on top for Game Boy cartridges, but it’s not designed for playing retro games. The featureless box is instead a media player designed to play through all the music and sound effect files on Game Boy cartridges using a basic set of play controls on board for skipping tracks and adjusting the volume of its built-in speaker. It’s like a reimagined Sony Walkman that trades cassette tapes for your childhood game carts you refused to get rid of.

Created by a talented builder simply known as BJ, the Retro Song Bird includes additional functionality. While the built-in speaker reproduces the tunes close to how they sounded through the original Game Boy, there’s also a stereo line out connection for connecting it to better speakers or for recording and sampling purposes. Each of the Game Boy’s four sound channels are available as separate USB audio streams, and the Retro Song Bird can be used to back up ROMs and save game data, or export music files as WAV files to a PC.

Only a few prototypes of the Retro Song Bird have been created so far and they’re not for sale, according to Retro Dodo, but BJ plans to potentially crowdfund or sell the music player directly once its hardware and design is finalized.

title: The Pixel 5 doesn’t get enough credit for making the best of a bad situation
snippet: In 2020, Google Pixel was in a remarkably tough spot. A flailing flagship with one of its central features effectively ruined by a global pandemic combined with massive supply shortages meant that grand plans for the future were on hold. It was always going to be a tough year to release a smartphone but, looking back, the Pixel 5 maybe doesn’t get enough credit for making the best of it. more…
fullText:
In 2020, Google Pixel was in a remarkably tough spot. A flailing flagship with one of its central features effectively ruined by a global pandemic combined with massive supply shortages meant that grand plans for the future were on hold. It was always going to be a tough year to release a smartphone but, looking back, the Pixel 5 maybe doesn’t get enough credit for making the best of it.

Our Damien Wilde reviewed the Pixel 5 and called it an “exercise in compromise,” and I think that sums up this device quite nicely, perhaps even better than we thought at the time. 

On the surface level, the Pixel 5 felt like a weird step forward after the Pixel 4 series. A much less powerful chipset wrapped up in a plastic “bio-resin” that replaced metal and glass was completely out of the ordinary for a flagship smartphone. Yet, it also addressed some of the Pixel 4’s failings by going back to a fingerprint sensor, by packing in a much larger battery, and by feeling a bit more familiar to what had come before after the prior year’s big swing on design.

The Pixel 4 is my favorite Google smartphone hardware to date, and it still holds up

And, looking back on it today, this thing aged quite well!

	
	

It’s still odd to think of this as a “flagship” as, across the board, it was a better fit in the mid-range category. Yet, through and through, it managed to nail down the fundamentals of the hardware. It feels good in a way that’s unique. Where the plastic Pixel 4a had virtually the same design, the Pixel 5’s resin material added some extra grip while managing to feel just a bit more premium. I’m not sure I ever appreciated it enough at the time, but with virtually everything going all-in on shatterable glass and heavy metal in 2026, a durable material like this is so refreshing.

Ultimately, Google’s Pixel 5 was a device that didn’t fit in. We’ll probably never know all of the details around its development, but it’s been said that, at some point, Google apparently wanted Tensor to debut in this time frame rather than ultimately launching a year later on the Pixel 6. We found evidence that suggested the switch wasn’t as last-minute as suggested, but even without such a radical change on deck, the Pixel 5 was absolutely born out of a rough series of circumstances and, looking back, it wasn’t half bad.

title: Apple accuses OpenAI of improperly adding new arguments to trade secrets case
snippet: A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly adding new evidence to its trade secrets case. Today, Apple fired back with its own accusation that OpenAI went beyond what court rules permit in its response. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly adding new evidence to its trade secrets case. Today, Apple fired back with its own accusation that OpenAI went beyond what court rules permit in its response. Here are the details.

Apple says OpenAI went beyond objecting to new evidence

One of the many aspects of the lawsuit in which Apple accuses two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products of trade secret misappropriation involves a request for a preliminary injunction.

In a nutshell, Apple has asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction, arguing that it would prevent its trade secrets from becoming further embedded in OpenAI’s hardware development while the case plays out.

As part of the legal back-and-forth over that request, Apple filed a reply brief supported by five expert declarations. That, in turn, led the defendants to accuse Apple of improperly introducing new evidence and ask the court to disregard some of the material.

In their objection filing, which accused Apple of presenting new evidence, OpenAI and the other defendants also submitted several documents countering Apple’s claims.

Today, Apple filed its response to those objections, arguing that the defendants went beyond simply objecting to new evidence, introducing new arguments and testimony of their own:

Rule 7-3(d)(1) permits a party to object to new evidence in a reply brief, but cautions that the filing “may not include further argument on the motion.” Defendants did not comply with this restriction and used their filing to relitigate the merits of Apple’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction.

For example, Defendants dispute whether Dr. Runge has a “basis to offer any analysis, adequately responds to “contrary evidence,” and demonstrates that certain Apple information is not public. […] Such arguments are not objections to new evidence. […] (“[A]rgument regarding how certain of Plaintiff’s positions are unsupported by evidence or contradicted by other testimony” is “not an objection to evidence.”).

Apple also takes exception to a new declaration from Liu, which it calls “the most egregious overreach” in the defendants’ filing:

The most egregious overreach is a new declaration from Mr. Liu, comprising eight paragraphs of new testimony. Defendants rely on this new testimony to offer excuses for why Mr. Liu “wiped” (i.e., erased) all the data from his iMac before returning it to Apple, […] argue about the meaning of certain text messages with one of Apple’s suppliers, […] and try to explain away his use of one of Apple’s confidential computer files, […] Such testimony violates the prohibition against “further argument on the motion.” Together, the filing and the declaration run 9 pages, which also violates the limitation that the objections “may not exceed 5 pages of text.” […]

It is worth noting that when the defendants filed Liu’s declaration, they argued that the court should consider it only if it also decided to consider the Apple evidence they were challenging.

That said, Apple argues that because the defendants have now presented new arguments of their own, the court should consider the full record rather than strike any of Apple’s reply evidence:

Defendants’ new arguments and evidence are more in the nature of a “sur-reply” rather than an objection. But, Defendants did not seek leave to file a sur-reply. Nonetheless, as Defendants have now adequately answered any “new” evidence from Apple’s Reply in its current filing, the Court should deny Defendants’ request to strike any of Apple’s Reply evidence, and should decide the Preliminary Injunction motion on a full record, including both the arguments and evidence in Apple’s Reply as well as the new arguments and evidence improperly submitted with Defendants’ filing.

The court is scheduled to hear arguments on Apple’s preliminary injunction request on October 14.

fullText:
After testing got underway in January, Google Messages is finally widely rolling out a new long-press menu in conversations.

Update 10/1: Google announced yesterday that the “new long-press redesign for Google Messages has officially launched.”

This update introduces a more intuitive way to interact with your conversations, featuring a tap-activated menu that puts your most-used actions front and center.

There’s also “full support” for light and dark themes, while the experience is now “optimized for landscape mode, ensuring the menu remains accessible and easy to navigate on wider screens.”

The company noted how the “ability to copy only a portion of a text message” was “one of the most requested features.” To do so:

	

Long press any message to bring up the new action menu.

Long press again directly on the text within that message.

Drag the selection handles to highlight the exact part of the message you want to select.

A second dialogue box will appear with options to Copy, Translate, or Select All.

Related: Google Messages rolls out new swipe for timestamps & reply gesture

Original 9/24: This new design replaces the top toolbar that housed various actions. Google only surfaced three actions with everything else in an overflow menu.

	

Upon long-pressing on a chat message or image, Google will show a floating menu with Remix (photos), Reply, Forward, Copy (text), Star, Delete, Select more, Info, and Save (photos).

Each action is accompanied by an icon at the front for quick scanning, while Copy lets you highlight a specific part of the message by pressing down and dragging the bubble. Previously, you could only copy the entire message.

If you’ve selected the newest message in a thread, Google will somewhat center it with a bouncy animation and haptic feedback. Messages prominently blurs the background layer when this menu is active. The row of emoji and “Create” Photomoji shortcuts is unchanged.

As of today, we’re seeing the new Google Messages long-press menu widely rolled out with stable version 20260910_03_RC02. There is a server-side component, so be sure to Force stop from the App info menu if it’s not yet live.

title: This is my biggest AirPods complaint, and it’s not necessarily about the hardware
snippet: AirPods are one of Apple’s most interesting products. The demand for them was largely invented by the fact that the company removed the headphone jack 10 years ago, and now most of us carry this almost magical pair of earbuds that do so much more than just play audio. AirPods offer best-in-class noise cancellation, and also serve as a hearing aid. They get better and better almost every year. fullText:
AirPods are one of Apple’s most interesting products. The demand for them was largely invented by the fact that the company removed the headphone jack 10 years ago, and now most of us carry this almost magical pair of earbuds that do so much more than just play audio. AirPods offer best-in-class noise cancellation, and also serve as a hearing aid. They get better and better almost every year.

Despite everything that AirPods do so well, I have one annoyance with them, and it’s particularly annoying because it could be such an easy software fix.

Right now, if your AirPods need to charge and you plug your iPhone in, you’ll get a notification to also charge your AirPods. This is because Apple figures that it’d probably be no hassle to charge your AirPods while you’re charging your iPhone, and that reminder has saved me from unknowingly having dead AirPods many times.

AirPods often end up dead in the case

If you’ve owned AirPods for a while, you might be quite familiar with this problem: something got in between the pins of your charging case and one of your AirPods, and you pull them out of the case with one of them dead. This can often ruin your walk, commute, or so on.

At least to me, it seems obvious to add a notification to tell users that one of their AirPods isn’t charging. If one of the AirPods is in the case, and the other isn’t detected in-ear, it’s likely safe to assume it’s in the case but not charging, and Apple could then alert the user to adjust the AirPod or make sure theres no obstruction in the case.

	

It’d be such a simple fix to such a major annoyance, and it’d be yet another instance of Apple magic letting you know that one of your AirPods isn’t charging, before it’s too late.

Hopefully, Apple can implement such a feature in a later iOS update. Right now, the latest-generation AirPods Pro 3 are on sale for $179, in case you don’t own a pair.

title: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store
snippet: Amazon has an all-new lineup of tablets ready to tempt you this holiday season, and for once, you might actually want to buy them. While the company has tried in previous years to make an upmarket play for relevancy in the tablet space, these new Alexa Tablets — RIP “Fire” — have the one thing everyone’s wanted for years: actual Play Store support. more…
fullText:
Amazon has an all-new lineup of tablets ready to tempt you this holiday season, and for once, you might actually want to buy them. While the company has tried in previous years to make an upmarket play for relevancy in the tablet space, these new Alexa Tablets — RIP “Fire” — have the one thing everyone’s wanted for years: actual Play Store support.

Yes, a decade after ditching the “Kindle” branding in its tablet lineup, Amazon is ditching the Fire brand entirely for its new lineup of iPad competitors. That’s not me trying to write off its Android-powered rivals; rather, the sizes and designs all make for devices that, frankly, look like iPad knock-offs. Alexa Tablets come in three sizes: an 8-inch entry-level iPad Mini competitor, an 11-inch base iPad-esque slate, and a 12-inch “Pro” model that looks to be the most unique of the bunch. They’re all designed with aluminum bodies and, despite being much more expensive than the Fire tablets they’re replacing, still manage to undercut most of the market.

The 8.7-inch 60Hz Alexa Tablet 8 features 4GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and comes in graphite, rosette, and teal, while the 90Hz 11-inch Alexa Tablet 11 features 8GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and adds matcha and amethyst to the mix. Both run on a MediaTek 8189 8-core processor, a relatively recent chipset that appeared in a handful of seemingly-unreleased ChromeOS devices over the past year or so, before landing in these budget tablets. While I wouldn’t say there’s much to write home here about the specs — and again, the design is just absolutely a blatant copy of the iPad — it certainly sounds like a big upgrade over their predecessors.

And really, that comes down to the software. Despite Amazon’s current Android-less strategy on its Fire TV devices, the company seems to be doubling down on Android with its tablets. While it does have a unique launcher designed to push Alexa+, these things run proper Android, complete with the Play Store front and center on the device. YouTube is one of the highlighted apps on their store listings, and as someone who maintained Play Store sideloading guides at two different tech websites over the past decade, I can certainly say I never saw it coming. I have no idea how the actual software experience will feel day-to-day, but in terms of app support, it’s one problem that’s finally solved.

	

The star of the show, of course, is the 12-inch Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. This is, bar none, the most premium tablet Amazon has ever shipped, with a price that matches. It combines a 2.8K 3:2 120Hz display with quad speakers, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, and a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor. That’s a real processor, and while I wouldn’t say it’s worthy of being called a flagship chipset, it’s undoubtedly the most powerful chip Amazon’s ever used. It’s a good sign when you’re using the same processor that a budget gaming-focused brand like Poco used just a year or two ago.

The 12-inch model also comes in an optional “nanomatte” version for an anti-glare experience, which also allows you to upgrade your RAM and storage to 16GB and 256GB, respectively. 16GB of RAM in an Amazon tablet — it’s a new day after all. And like its last attempt to go full-premium, the company does offer optional stylus and keyboard accessories for road warriors on a budget.

The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $230 for the base 64GB model with lockscreen ads, or $250 without, while the Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $330 for its base model, or $350 for the ad-free version. Both feature a 128GB upgrade for $50 more. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $500 for the base 128GB model; the nanomatte upgrade will run you $50 more. Meanwhile, that high-end 16/256 variant costs a whopping $680, and while that might sound pretty expensive on paper, it comes in well under Samsung’s latest 12-inch tablet for anyone who doesn’t need that level of processing power. Oh, and absolutely no ads on any of the 12 Pro models — the price you see is the price you pay, no upgrades necessary.

snippet: Apple released AirPods Pro 3 last year, bringing several big updates to its in-ear headphones. If you’re currently using AirPods Pro 2, there are three key reasons to consider upgrading, based on my experience using them over the past year. Buy AirPods Pro 3: $179 (Reg. $249) more…
fullText:
Apple released AirPods Pro 3 last year, bringing several big updates to its in-ear headphones. If you’re currently using AirPods Pro 2, there are three key reasons to consider upgrading, based on my experience using them over the past year.

Buy AirPods Pro 3: $179 (Reg. $249) 

Improved ANC

One of the best things about AirPods Pro is Active Noise Cancellation, or ANC. They offer stellar noise cancellation capabilities, blocking out the world around you and creating an immersive listening experience.

Apple says that AirPods Pro 3 offer ANC that is up to 2x more effective than AirPods Pro 2. It’s hard to quantify that claim, but in my review of AirPods Pro 3 last year, I called out the “definitive improvement” in ANC in the real world.

Heart rate monitoring

The other flagship change for AirPods Pro 3 is the addition of a heart rate monitor. During a workout, AirPods Pro 3 can monitor your heart rate and display additional metrics in the Fitness app on your iPhone. You can start more than 50 workout types in the Fitness app, and a Live Activity pops up to help you track that workout.

From a hardware perspective, AirPods Pro 3 feature a heart rate sensor in each earbud. It shines invisible infrared light, pulsed 256 times per second.

This feature improved further in iOS 27, which brought GymKit to the iPhone for the first time. This means you can use your iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 to get an Apple Watch-style workout experience, without actually wearing a watch.

And if you do wear an Apple Watch, AirPods Pro 3 work alongside it to give you the most accurate data possible. For instance, if your Apple Watch shifts into an awkward position on your wrist while lifting weights, the AirPods Pro 3 can step in to ensure your data remains accurate.

Battery life

AirPods Pro 3 offer a notable improvement in battery life over AirPods Pro 2, with up to eight hours of music playback with ANC enabled instead of six.

However, there is an asterisk. AirPods Pro 3 actually offer less overall battery life than AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 2, 30 hours total: : 24 hours from the case + 6 hours from the buds

AirPods Pro 3, 24 hours total: 16 hours from the case + 8 hours from the buds

So, you get more battery life on a single charge from the buds themselves, but you’ll have to recharge the case more often.

One warning though …

If you’re buying AirPods Pro 3, however, it’s important to note that the shape of the earbuds has changed. For me, they are more comfortable than AirPods Pro 2. Some people, however, have found them to be less comfortable:

AirPods Pro 3 after four months: Revisiting fit, comfort, more

	

For this reason, I recommend trying AirPods Pro 3 before buying them, or buying them from somewhere with an easy return process.

Wrap up

title: Android Auto rolling out fix that stops auto-playing music when you start your car
snippet: Google has confirmed that a fix is rolling out for a bug that leaves Android Auto briefly auto-playing music when your car starts, even if you have autoplay disabled. more…
fullText:
Google has confirmed that a fix is rolling out for a bug that leaves Android Auto briefly auto-playing music when your car starts, even if you have autoplay disabled.

Most of the time you’d want Android Auto to start playing music as soon as it starts up. That’s one of the big benefits of the platform, after all. But if you don’t want music to start playing automatically, there’s a toggle that lets you disable autoplay.

It just hasn’t been working properly for a while.

For some, Android Auto would start playing music briefly when your vehicle starts before ending playback a few seconds later. It’s more than a bit frustrating, but a fix is apparently rolling out.

	

In a post on Reddit, Google confirmed that “unsolicited play commands” will no longer be sent during startup if autoplay is turned off in Android Auto. This is alongside other improvements to autoplay including a prompt to opt out of autoplay if Android Auto notices you frequently pause playback immediately after it starts.

We’ve made a couple of bug fixes so autoplay* works more predictably and accurately based on your listening preferences:

Autoplay app selection: Apps that you haven’t recently or ever used will no longer be selected for autoplay.

One-tap opt-out: If you prefer manual playback and frequently pause autoplay, Android Auto will notice and provide a convenient one-tap notification to quickly disable autoplay.

Infotainment startup handling: We’re rolling out a fix so unsolicited play commands won’t be sent when you have autoplay turned off.

There’s no mention of which Android Auto update fixes autoplay, but it is “rolling out,” Google says.

Over the years, iPhones have evolved into extremely capable cameras, but for both still photos and videos, there has been a significant gap between the quality you can achieve in daylight and that available at night.

Apple has put a lot of work over the years into low-light still photography, and that really shows. Today’s iPhones offer incredibly impressive low-light camera capabilities given the extremely small size of the sensor. That was helped by the inclusion of Night mode portraits back in 2020.

Computational photography in general is the secret to a lot of the iPhone’s night photography abilities. While we think we’re taking a single shot, the phone is in fact taking a whole series of frames and then combining different exposures into a single image.

Video, however, is a far bigger challenge. When we’re shooting at least 24 frames per second, and most typically shooting movement, there’s very limited opportunity for the phone to capture multiple exposures of the same frame in order to combo them. That’s the reason that the quality of night videos inevitably lags significantly behind that of still photos.

Apple does, however, continue to put a lot of work into this, and night video performance does improve with each generation. The iPhone 18 Pro not only benefits from Apple’s annual enhancements to video processing, but also from a wider aperture that lets in more light. It’s less than a stop, but for video work in particular, every extra photon really counts.

The complete clip in normal speed lasted more than nine minutes, and I didn’t want to rely on the impressive video stabilization capabilities of the device for quite that long, so braced a mini tripod on top of a railing. I’ve sped up the video to 10x normal speed to reduce it to 96 seconds, but included a couple of actual-speed sections so you can appreciate the incredibly careful work carried out by the tugboats.

The result? Not perfect, but yes, another step forward in the quality evolution. Sure, people like me can go pixel-peeping and complaining that some of the details are rather muddy when viewed closely, but that’s kind of a “so what?” situation. The average person looks at a video like this and simply enjoys the spectacle, having no complaints about the quality. When I look back at low-light videos from a few generations ago, the difference is … well, night and day.

So yes, night video performance is not yet where I would like it to ideally be, but it continues to improve with each generation, including this one. In truth, we have easily hit the “good enough for most people to enjoy” point even in extremely challenging conditions like this.

title: See for yourself the difference the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes
snippet: Alongside a variable aperture lens, the main camera of the iPhone 18 Pro also opens up to a wider aperture than its predecessors. Apple has been promoting this as enabling a shallower depth of field for portraits and similar shots. The difference, however, is less than a stop, and it’s been unclear how much real life difference this would make on such a small sensor, so I set out to put it to the test … more…
fullText:
Alongside a variable aperture lens, the main camera of the iPhone 18 Pro also opens up to a wider aperture than its predecessors. Apple has been promoting this as enabling a shallower depth of field for portraits and similar shots.

The difference, however, is less than a stop, and it’s been unclear how much real life difference this would make on such a small sensor, so I set out to put it to the test … 

Portraits, not Portrait mode

It’s important to draw a distinction between the optical shallow depth of field enabled by a wide aperture lens and the artificial effect enabled by Portrait mode.

With the latter, Apple uses computational photography and the LiDAR sensor to work out where the subject ends and the background begins in order to apply an artificial blur. The quality of this has improved dramatically over the years, but that’s not what we’re testing here. All of the background blur seen in the sample photos was achieved optically by using the widest possible aperture of f/1.48.

The simple testing method

The iPhone 17 Pro had a widest aperture of f/1.78. This is essentially indistinguishable from f/1.8, which is the second-widest aperture available on the iPhone 18 Pro. What I’ve done here is to use the new manual controls available to take the same photo twice, once at f/1.8 and again at f/1.48, in order to compare the difference. 

There are, however, three other optical factors affecting the amount of background blur of any photo:

The focal length of the lens

The distance between the subject and the background

How close the subject is to the camera

To eliminate these variables, all of the photos are taken at the same focal length (the main camera, which is the only one with a variable aperture), the same framing (ie. same background), and at the same distance. There’s a few seconds gap between the photos as I adjust the aperture, so they are not 100% identical, but both myself and my subject stood still to ensure both were taken at exactly the same distance even if he turned his head between shots.

With these controls in place, any difference in background blur is due entirely to the aperture.

The test shots

All of the test shots are portraits – that is, head-and-shoulder shots – as this is the type of photo for which wide apertures are most commonly used (hence the name Apple applies to the artificial effect available in Portrait mode). 

Additionally, by getting close enough to shoot head and shoulders, we are maximizing the degree of background blur we would expect to see. This makes for the best basis for comparing the shots, versus wider ones where the degree of blur may be harder to assess.

Finally, I’ve included a few shots with graduated backgrounds, so you can see how the focus falls away with distance.

With all of that pre-amble out of the way, let’s take a look at the results. Move the slider all the way to the right to view the f/1.78 version, to the left to view the f/1.48 shot, and anywhere you like to compare different parts of the image.

Conclusions

I think this shot provides the clearest illustration of the impact, as it contains background elements ranging from a few feet to around quarter of a mile:

	

The fountain is the closest element, at around 8-10 feet, and we can see a noticeable difference here. The tree is about 30 feet away, and the difference is smaller but still distinct. The pagoda is maybe 70 feet away, and the difference remains clear but a bit less pronounced. Once we reach the more distant elements – the bridge and buildings on the far side of the river – the difference is more subtle: we can clearly see it when actively looking for it, but I don’t think most people would notice unprompted.

In terms of practical benefit, the shot below is a good illustration. With the f/1.78 aperture, I’d describe the separation of Chris from the background as a little marginal in places, for example, the person eating in the restaurant top right and the section of building top-right of his head. With the wider aperture, the separation is definitely improved.

I’d wondered how much difference we could expect to see from a relatively small change, and now I have my answer. The significance of the difference is something you can judge for yourself from the sample shots; personally, I’d describe it as relatively subtle but in truth bigger than I’d expected – and enough to be useful in some situations. Please share your own thoughts in the comments.

The wider aperture is not the only benefit of the new lens. There are other situations in which it can be useful to take manual control of the variable aperture, and I’ll be looking at these in a follow-up piece.

title: MagSafe Monday: Pelican’s MagSafe Wallet is my go-to wallet for the fall
snippet: As the weather cools off and the fall outdoor season ramps up, I tend to tweak my everyday carry list to match how I ams spending my time. The Pelican MagSafe Wallet & Card Holder is my go-to option when you want something a little more rugged that can handle the outdoors but still works as a great everyday wallet. more…
fullText:
As the weather cools off and the fall outdoor season ramps up, I tend to tweak my everyday carry list to match how I ams spending my time. The Pelican MagSafe Wallet & Card Holder is my go-to option when you want something a little more rugged that can handle the outdoors but still works as a great everyday wallet.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Perfect for outdoor activities

The Pelican wallet is IPX4 water-resistant, which means if you get it wet on a hike or at the lake, it won’t get your credit cards or cash wet. Once it snaps shut, it stays shut. For example, I go to plenty of Falcons games during the fall, and even at football games, I like knowing everything is closed and locked in. That alone makes it a solid pick for fall outdoor activities when the weather can change quickly. It feels more like a tiny hard shell case than a wallet that happens to snap onto your iPhone.

Most MagSafe wallets are designed for a few cards and nothing else. Pelican’s design gives you a little more flexibility. It easily holds an ID and credit cards, and there is also space for some folded cash and a small key. If you want to keep things minimal on a hike, this wallet covers the basics without needing to bring a separate bag.

While the Pelican wallet is great for outdoor use, it is just as useful for everyday carry. Strong magnets attach it securely to the back of your iPhone, and the snap closure means nothing falls out. Compared to less durable MagSafe wallets, this one trades a little bit of slimness for a lot more peace of mind. It’s probably not what I’d reach for in the summer when I want something more minimal, but for hiking, football games, and anything where I am on the go outside and the weather might change, it’s the right call. It’s a great MagSafe wallet for kids with their first iPhone as well. My oldest son has used it for years as well.

Wrap up on Pelican MagSafe Wallet

The Pelican MagSafe Wallet is built for people who prioritize durability. It keeps your essentials safe from the weather and water, carries just enough for a hike or a day trip, and snaps securely in place. If you want a MagSafe wallet that can withstand falls and still work day-to-day, this is it.

You can buy the Pelican MagSafe Wallet from Amazon or directly from Pelican.

title: Google confirms fix for Android Auto’s missing signal icon is rolling out
snippet: After weeks of back and forth, Google has officially confirmed a fix is rolling out for Android Auto’s missing signal icon. more…
fullText:
After weeks of back and forth, Google has officially confirmed a fix is rolling out for Android Auto’s missing signal icon.

The corner of every Android Auto display is meant to show your phone’s battery status, the time, a number of notifications, and your phone’s current cellular connection status.

The last one has been in rough shape.

While it hasn’t been consistent or fully widespread, many have found the cellular signal icon on Android Auto vanishing off and on for several weeks now. Recent updates have seemed to fix the issue for many, but now Google is confirming a fix has been made. In a comment on Reddit, a Google representative explains:

	

We’re aware of reports about the missing cellular signal, and we’re actually currently rolling out a fix that should hopefully address this issue! The fix isn’t widely available yet, though, so it may take some time to reach your device – if you want to receive it sooner, though, you can enroll in the Android Auto beta

The Android Auto beta program, notably, is full at the moment, but you can sideload updates (at your own risk). 

Android Auto 17.8 seems to deliver the fix, at least in part, and is now rolling out via the stable track.

title: Pixel 12 series leak allegedly reveals model numbers, display specs, no wide Fold
snippet: Google’s Pixel 11 series has only been around for a few months now, but Pixel 12 leaks are already surfacing with some key display specs and confirmation of a familiar Fold. more…
fullText:
Google’s Pixel 11 series has only been around for a few months now, but Pixel 12 leaks are already surfacing with some key display specs and confirmation of a familiar Fold.

Citing the GSMA database, OVR+ highlights what appear to be listings for Google’s Pixel 12 lineup. As expected, there are four devices here, presumably to be marketed as Pixel 12, Pixel 12 Pro, Pixel 12 Pro XL, and Pixel 12 Pro Fold. The model numbers listed are:

Pixel 12 – GC0QU

Pixel 12 Pro – GWU59

Pixel 12 Pro XL – G7U1Y

Pixel 12 Pro Fold – G4D5D

Beyond model numbers, the listings point to the screen resolution of each device. The base Pixel 12 is listed at 1080×2400, just shy of the Pixel 11’s 1080×2424. Pixel 12 Pro is listed at 1280×2824 compared to 11 Pro’s 1280×2856. Pixel 12 Pro XL, following the same pattern of very slight differences, is said to be 1344×2952 compared to 11 Pro XL’s 1344×2992. We’d take these with a grain of salt, as the lower pixel counts would suggest a smaller panel, but it could also signal some form of redesign on the main display.

	

Pixel 12 Pro Fold’s inner display is listed at 2296×2404, a considerable bump up from the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s 2076×2152. While that’ll certainly be a welcome upgrade, it’s important to note that this means Google is looking at using the same near-square design for the fourth year rather than switching to a wide format like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or iPhone Duo – the aspect ratio is nearly identical to the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Not really a surprise, but certainly a bit of a shame given Google started this whole foldable journey off with something closer to the new fan favorite. Google is also rumored to be adopting a new display assembly on Pixel 12 Pro Fold.

	

Unsurprisingly, all four devices are listed with Android 18, which will have debuted by the time Google releases its next flagship series.

These early leaks are always subject to change, so take it all with a grain of salt for the time being.

title: Apple TV doc All of Us shows how iPads enable inclusive learning in a unique school
snippet: A new documentary available on Apple TV, All of Us, tells the story of a public elementary school that has taken a unique approach to how education works for students with very different needs. iPads play a key role in enabling what has been described as a powerful example of how inclusive education can work for every child … more…
fullText:
A new documentary available on Apple TV, All of Us, tells the story of a public elementary school that has taken a unique approach to how education works for students with very different needs.

iPads play a key role in enabling what has been described as a powerful example of how inclusive education can work for every child …

Often students who need additional support due to a disability are educated separately from mainstream students. Conventional thinking says that trying to include everyone in the same classroom can be disruptive for the majority.

Ruby Bridges Elementary School took a different view, and the evidence is that, far from being a distraction, inclusive learning benefits all students both academically and socially. Indeed, it worked so well that both the school principal and kindergarten teacher were named Principal and Teacher of the Year in 2025.

A 70-minute documentary available on Apple TV tells the story of “a school that breaks the mold.”

At Ruby Bridges, all students learn in the general classroom. Every child solves math problems, reads books, and sings along in music class. Teachers and specialists work closely together in the classroom, and the results speak for themselves.

So, how do they do it? Ruby Bridges Elementary is a public school. There is no additional funding or staff beyond what the school already has. There is no magic fix. It is simply a group of educators who decided to stop separating children and trust the power of learning together. This is the story of a school that breaks the mold. A school that is unique, but shouldn’t be.

iPads play a key role

Some of the students have severe communication difficulties, and Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) software running on iPads has made a huge difference to their ability to interact with teachers and other students.

A key discovery is that the AAC apps didn’t just prove useful for students with communication challenges – but rather for everyone. Founding Principal Cathi Davis told me:

All learners, including learners with advanced reading and language skills, or our learners at the start of their communication or language journey, show high levels of engagement when they can use the AAC tool to generate, expand or express ideas through AAC. We circumvent challenges in motor skills, writing stamina and even in anxieties about speaking aloud when we have a tool readily supportive of communication while overcoming the barriers that sometimes show up in the classroom or in life […]

It is truly the epitome of what we mean when we say “universal design,” and it is very much a tool for all as compared to almost every other attempt we make at tools for language, communication and vocabulary in the classroom.

As the documentary reveals, the evidence that the approach works for all of the students, not just those with additional needs, is undeniable. A website devoted to the documentary also has a comprehensive set of video resources aimed at other schools who might want to follow the example of Ruby Bridges.

title: John Ternus is taking a more ‘hands-on’ role in Apple’s design teams as CEO: report
snippet: Since Jony Ive’s departure from Apple in 2019, the company hasn’t had much of a true design lead. For a while, former COO Jeff Williams was in charge of design, until his departure last year. Since then, CEO John Ternus has taken a significant interest in both of Apple’s design teams: industrial design and human interface, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. more…
fullText:
Since Jony Ive’s departure from Apple in 2019, the company hasn’t had much of a true design lead. For a while, former COO Jeff Williams was in charge of design, until his departure last year. Since then, CEO John Ternus has taken a significant interest in both of Apple’s design teams: industrial design and human interface, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

This story actually begins prior to John Ternus becoming CEO, which only took place about a month ago. It started with Jeff Williams’ departure as COO. At the time, the company announced that these teams would be reporting to former CEO Tim Cook, but instead, it was reportedly John Ternus. This was one of his key responsibilities while transitioning into CEO.

Of course, it’s no surprise that Ternus is interested in design, seeing as he was formerly in charge of hardware engineering. However, Gurman describes Ternus’ involvement as being “immersed” in the work, and that he often stops by to work with the teams:

Since becoming CEO, however, he has immersed himself in the industrial design and human interface teams. Several people familiar with the department say he works hands-on in the studio several times a week, sometimes visiting multiple times in a single day.

This is in stark contrast to former CEO Tim Cook, who only visited the studio about once a month, per Bloomberg.

Ternus is ‘immersed’ with Apple’s design teams

Ternus as also devoted much attention to refilling the design team’s roles, as the company has lost much talent to outside companies poaching talent. Most notably, Alan Dye left to join Meta, and OpenAI has poached many Apple employees. To rejuvenate the team, Apple has promoted many junior designers and hired new talent from the outside.

Throughout all of this, the company still hasn’t sought out a true Jony Ive replacement to serve as a Chief Design Officer of sorts. According to Bloomberg, no search is underway. Instead, the company has highlighted Molly Anderson and Steve Lemay as respective design leads for industrial design and human interface, with Ternus himself serving as the overarching decision maker for design.

While Ternus lacks a traditional design background, his dedication to it means one thing: design will remain a key cornerstone at the top of Apple.

title: Google Pixel 2 XL set the stage for a decade of ups and downs
snippet: Google Pixel’s 10-year anniversary has me taking a look back at a bunch of the milestones throughout this lineup’s history and, when picking up the Pixel 2 XL, hindsight really kicked in as to how this phone was very much a sign of the tumultuous roller coaster that would become Google Pixel. more…
fullText:
Google Pixel’s 10-year anniversary has me taking a look back at a bunch of the milestones throughout this lineup’s history and, when picking up the Pixel 2 XL, hindsight really kicked in as to how this phone was very much a sign of the tumultuous roller coaster that would become Google Pixel.

The original Google Pixel hit the ground running and really did a great job pitching itself. A stellar camera was the main selling point, but Google’s thoughtful software, well-designed hardware, and ecosystem as a whole filled in the bigger picture to deliver a product that, outside of minor gripes, was about as “perfect” as you could ask for from an initial debut in a product category.

Fast-forward to a year later and, oof.

The Pixel 2 and Pixel 2 XL both arrived with some welcome upgrades across the board, but it was also abundantly clear that Google made some serious missteps. The smaller Pixel 2 was a tame revision in basically every way and, outside of the mega-thick bezels, was still a perfectly fine phone.

	

Pixel 2 XL, though, had some glaring flaws.

While I can look back fondly now on many aspects of the Pixel 2 XL, it’s wild in hindsight that a company at Google’s scale, even nearly a decade ago, made such a massive blunder. The Pixel 2 XL’s overall hardware stuck the landing. The updated dual-tone design still has that iconic “Panda” look and the colorful accent button that lived on through prior generations, but the glaring flaw on this device was the display. 

The LG-made panel was horribly inconsistent. In the best-case scenario, you’d get a panel with not-great viewing angles, slightly off colors, and burn-in issues. Worst case, a panel with a blue tint, black smears, and/or a grainy look. I still remember feeling like it was playing the lottery with buying this device and exchanging it to get a “good” one. Google tweaked this over time with software as well as by upping the warranty coverage, but it was still a huge problem with an otherwise great design.

And, in hindsight, that was kind of a signal of what was to come for Pixel as a whole.

	

The Pixel 2 XL tried something new and ultimately fell short, leading to a big correction the following year. Pixel 3 had a stunning display by comparison, and even to this day, Google has invested heavily in giving its phones some of the best displays you can find. The same pattern has been found throughout the lineup. New swings lead to new problems, with Google ultimately scrambling to make the best of it through software updates and making corrections later on. A similarly big problem came with 2020’s Pixel 6 series, with the modem in the first Tensor chip being truly terrible, but Google working to make the best of it in later software updates, only to iterate on the modem with each new generation to the point where, today, Tensor’s modem is roughly on par with anyone else in the ways that matter most.

Google Pixel remains a series that delivers ups and downs through each new generation, but it’s also clearer that the company has finally settled into something that works in 2026. Where the Pixel 2 XL was still in an era where Google would pivot on a whim, the Pixel 11 series comes from a place of stability, predictability, and at least mild success.

The original Google Pixel hit the ground running and really did a great job pitching itself. A stellar camera was the main selling point, but Google’s thoughtful software, well-designed hardware, and ecosystem as a whole filled in the bigger picture to deliver a product that, outside of minor gripes, was about as “perfect” as you could ask for from an initial debut in a product category.

title: Vivo X Fold 6 skips the wide form factor, but will launch globally with strong cameras
snippet: Vivo’s new X Fold 6 doesn’t join in on the wide foldable trend, but it has some pretty wild camera promises. more…
fullText:
Vivo’s new X Fold 6 doesn’t join in on the wide foldable trend, but it has some pretty wild camera promises.

The Vivo X Fold 6 packs a punch with an 8.02-inch inner display, a 6.51-inch outer display, and is running on a MediaTek Dimensity 9500 Super Edition chip. That’s with 12GB or 16GB of RAM and 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB of storage.

The cameras are perhaps the biggest standout here, though, as foldables usually have to make some serious compromises in that department. 

The main camera is a 200MP Samsung HPB Large Sensor backed up by a 50MP 3x periscope shooter and a 50MP ultrawide. Everything uses ZEISS imaging and Vivo has a teleconverter add-on to extend the range of the camera. Vivo also says to expect a more responsive shutter and improvements to portrait mode and subject tracking.

	

Rounding out the package is a 6,900 mAh battery, IP58/59 dust and water resistance, and Android 17-based OriginOS 7 out of the box. 

Vivo has confirmed the X Fold 6 will see a global debut though, as always, don’t expect a US release.

title: Apple event is reportedly happening next week, per Mark Gurman
snippet: Apple is expected to launch several new products next week on October 13, and per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product unveilings will happen at “an event.” Here’s what he said. more…
fullText:
Apple is expected to launch several new products next week on October 13, and per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product unveilings will happen at “an event.” Here’s what he said.

Apple will unveil three new products at October 13 event, says Gurman

We’re nearly a month out from the last Apple event, which featured the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and more.

But it sounds like an October event could be on the way as early as next Tuesday, October 13.

Per Mark Gurman, writing in his Power On newsletter:

Apple is planning to hold an event on Oct. 13 to unveil its long-awaited smart home hub with a screen, the new HomePod mini and an updated Apple TV. All three devices will have Siri AI at the core.

Gurman previously reported that these three products would be launching October 13, but at the time he made no mention of an event.

There’s been plenty of speculation about whether these new Home products would merit an event or not. John Gruber, for example, said there was “No way” that the rumored HomePad would be released via a press release only. He wrote, “if this is coming, it has to be unveiled with a keynote video and some sort of media event with hands-on demos.”

And based on his latest newsletter, Gurman clearly believes that’s what’s happening. “Apple is planning to hold an event on Oct. 13” sounds pretty straightforward.

If an event does happen, we would expect to see press invites go out in the next day or so. Unless, of course, new CEO John Ternus plans to shake up the way does product introductions and bucks prior patterns.

fullText:
Apple CEO John Ternus, as well as former CEO Tim Cook, have shared posts in remembrance of Steve Jobs today on the 15th anniversary of his passing. Here’s what they said.

Apple’s current and former CEOs reflect on Steve Jobs’ impact

Exactly 15 years ago today, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs passed away after a battle with pancreatic cancer.

To mark the anniversary of his passing, Apple’s current and former CEOs have posted brief reflections commemorating Jobs and his impact on their lives and Apple.

Here’s what Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wrote on X:

The way Steve taught us to care about every detail, every experience, every person, still guides our work today. Forever grateful.

— John Ternus (@johnternus) October 5, 2026

Posted at the same time, Apple’s former CEO and now Executive Chairman Tim Cook published his own thoughts.

Here’s what Cook wrote on X:

There are people who leave a mark on the world, and then there are people who change it entirely. Steve changed the world and so many lives in the process. He certainly changed my life forever. His spirit lives on in everything he created and everyone he inspired. pic.twitter.com/8p08BcSlTS

— Tim Cook (@tim_cook) October 5, 2026

title: 15 years after his passing, nobody is ‘The Next Steve Jobs’
snippet: Today marks 15 years since Steve Jobs passed away after a long battle with pancreatic cancer. Every year, memories come flooding back, and this one is no different. When I was contemplating what I wanted to say about Steve today, it occurred to me that much of what I or anyone has ever wanted to say about him has already been said. more…
fullText:
Today marks 15 years since Steve Jobs passed away after a long battle with pancreatic cancer. Every year, memories come flooding back, and this one is no different. When I was contemplating what I wanted to say about Steve today, it occurred to me that much of what I or anyone has ever wanted to say about him has already been said.

He changed my life, and he rewrote the fabric of society. But there’s one part of his legacy that’s worth reflecting on: he introduced hundreds of millions of people to the simple idea of making something great for others.

Of course, he did it on a much grander scale than many of us ever will. He saw it as ‘expressing appreciation for the species.’ We often talk about his belief that we should strive to put a “dent in the universe,” but we don’t talk enough about how there are many ways to do that, at varying levels, and with different motivations. It can mean so many different things to so many people. 

As I’ve been reading through Ron Johnson’s new book “Shop Different,” I’ve been transported back through some vivid storytelling to when Ron and Steve were gearing up to debut the first Apple Stores. The book paints a detailed, arguably beautiful picture of Steve; complicated as ever, but meticulous and thoughtful. 

He’s often remembered for how hard he pushed people to do their best work, but what’s crystal clear is how much he loved learning from those same people.

Ron Johnson says he proposed the idea of ‘loving your customers’ when they were planning Apple’s retail philosophy. Steve was uncomfortable with the word “love” in that context, but years later, from the Town Hall stage during the iPhone 4 ‘antennagate’ press conference, he laid it out on a simple slide that said, “We love our users.” Looking back, it feels as though the love and care were there all along, even if Steve didn’t realize it. His curiosity and care for the people who would use his products feel increasingly rare today. Apple’s original phrase, ‘enrich lives,’ expressed the same aspiration in more secular terms. Making something easier or simpler isn’t the same as enriching a life.

	

Ever since he passed away, it’s been a common refrain to call someone ‘the next Steve Jobs’. I always look to those who knew him the best. They had the clearest view of his motivations. No one else in the industry comes close to earning the mantle of ‘the next Steve Jobs’ because no one can check every box. I’m not sure today’s tech culture could foster someone with that same extraordinary combination of traits. You can be a visionary, you can make incredible products, you can put a ‘dent in the universe,’ but there was more to Steve than just that. 

Looking for ‘the next Steve Jobs’ misses what made him so special. He cared about every detail more than anybody else, learned humility, took responsibility, and focused on unlocking creativity rather than how many eyeballs he could claim or keystrokes he could collect. Steve simply wanted to make the best products to help people unlock their creativity. His high standards were certainly a part of his success, but so was his heart. The more we learn about Steve, the clearer that becomes.

Maybe the point shouldn’t be to find ‘the next Steve Jobs,’ but to remember what he showed us: that technology can be ambitious and earthshaking while still being deeply human. The best products are driven by love for the people who will use them, as much as by business metrics.

There are many ways to put a ‘dent in the universe,’ but I believe Steve was referring to one: making wonderful tools that could help anyone create something of their own and feel the care that went into making those tools. More of us should strive to model his mission.
